events.inundation_area: About 100,000 km² (67% of the country)
events.name: 1998 Bangladesh flood
events.notes: 1,050 is the Floods-in-Bangladesh table figure. Separate from 1998 China already in the database.
events.what_happened: The 1998 monsoon inundated about 100,000 km² — 67% of Bangladesh, including half of Dhaka — a larger flooded area than 1988. Wikipedia's Floods in Bangladesh table lists 1,050 deaths and notes about 30 million people made homeless. Water contamination produced cholera and typhoid. Distinct from the 1998 China / Yangtze floods already in the database.

events.name: 1998 China floods
events.geo_source: Wuhan, principal city on the flooded middle Yangtze
events.what_happened: Summer 1998 monsoon rains produced severe flooding along the Yangtze and other Chinese rivers. Official Chinese figures recorded 4,150 deaths, 18 million people made homeless, and about 180 million people affected.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 180 million affected; 18 million homeless (official figures cited on Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Prolonged monsoon rainfall over the Yangtze basin.
events.notes: 4,150 is the official nationwide figure commonly cited (not Yangtze-only).

events.affected_or_evacuated: 680,000 houses damaged or destroyed in Poland; 7,000 people lost all possessions (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Stalled Genoa low produced 300–600 mm of rain, a roughly 1-in-1,000-year event on parts of the Oder.
events.economic_damage: About $4.5 billion (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Wrocław, a principal city on the flooded Oder
events.name: 1997 Central European flood (Oder / Millennium Flood)
events.notes: 114 is the Wikipedia total (56 Poland, 50 Czech Republic; remainder Germany/other).
events.rainfall_mm: 300–600 mm over a few days in the core zone
events.return_period: Popularly called a 1,000-year flood in Poland and Germany

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of floods in Europe

events.what_happened: Two pulses of extreme rain (3–10 and 17–22 July 1997) from a stalled Genoa low dropped 300–600 mm in days over the Czech Republic and southwestern Poland. Flash floods then a flood wave down the Oder hit Kłodzko, Opole and Wrocław. Wikipedia records 114 deaths (56 in Poland, 50 in the Czech Republic) and about $4.5 billion damage. In Poland it is the 'Millennium Flood' (powódź tysiąclecia).

events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 50,000 evacuated in Grand Forks; 28,000 in Manitoba
events.cause_summary: Heavy winter snow and a rapid south-to-north melt on the flat, north-flowing Red River.
events.economic_damage: About US$3.5 billion regional; about $500 million CAD in Manitoba (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Grand Forks, the hardest-hit US city
events.inundation_area: About 1,840 km² of river at the Canadian peak; more than 2,560 km² underwater (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1997 Red River flood
events.notes: 0 deaths is sourced (Wikipedia infobox). 0 is not a default for unknown. Damage $3.5 billion.
events.region: Red River of the North / Grand Forks–Winnipeg

sources.label: NWS / NOAA disaster survey: 1997 Red River flood executive summary

events.status: Historical. Greater Grand Forks Greenway and an enlarged Manitoba Floodway followed.
events.what_happened: Abundant snowpack and a rapid melt produced the worst Red River flood since 1826. The river crested at 54.35 feet at Grand Forks on 21 April, overtopping dikes built to a 49-foot NWS forecast. Mayor Pat Owens evacuated more than 50,000 people. A downtown fire burned 11 buildings during the flood. Manitoba's Floodway kept Winnipeg's losses far lower; 28,000 were still evacuated in the province. Total regional damage about US$3.5 billion. No deaths.

events.affected_or_evacuated: 16,000 people evacuated (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Two weeks of saturating rain then a two-day downpour over the Saguenay graben; poorly maintained dikes failed.
events.economic_damage: CA$1.5 billion (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Wikipedia page coordinates for the Saguenay flood (Chicoutimi)
events.name: Saguenay flood (Déluge du Saguenay)
events.notes: 10 deaths is the Wikipedia infobox and CBC 20th-anniversary figure. Wikipedia cites CA$1.5 billion damage; CBC (2016) cites $300 million. The page also mentions 2 additional deaths in mudslides.
events.river_or_facility: Saguenay and Ha! Ha! rivers and municipal dikes

sources.label: CBC: Saguenay flood remembered on 20th anniversary

events.status: Historical. La petite maison blanche is preserved as a museum.
events.what_happened: After two weeks of rain that saturated soils and reservoirs, extreme rainfall on 19–20 July 1996 produced the largest overland flood in 20th-century Canadian history in the Saguenay graben. Wikipedia records 10 deaths, 16,000 people evacuated, 488 homes destroyed and 1,230 damaged, and about CA$1.5 billion in damage. Over 8 feet (2.4 m) of water flooded parts of Chicoutimi and La Baie. Post-flood inquiries found the dike-and-dam network protecting Chicoutimi poorly maintained. The surviving petite maison blanche became the symbol of the flood.

events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 250,000 residents and 1 million animals evacuated (Rijkswaterstaat)
events.cause_summary: Alpine snowmelt plus prolonged rain on the Rhine and Meuse catchments produced record winter discharges.
events.geo_source: Tiel, principal town of the evacuated Betuwe
events.name: 1995 Netherlands river floods (Rivierenland evacuation)
events.notes: Deaths not given a reliable single figure in the official Rijkswaterstaat account; left unknown. Qualifies as a major named official disaster by the 250,000-person evacuation.
events.region: Gelderland / Limburg river district (Betuwe, Bommelerwaard, Land van Maas en Waal)
events.river_or_facility: Rhine, Meuse, Waal and IJssel dikes

sources.label: Rijkswaterstaat: Thirty years later, the 1995 high-water evacuation

events.status: Historical. Room for the River followed this high-water crisis.
events.what_happened: Meltwater from the Alps plus prolonged rain in the Ardennes, northern France and Germany sent the Rhine, Meuse, Waal and IJssel to record winter levels. On 25 January the Meuse peaked at 45.09 m NAP at Itteren and Borgharen and flooded parts of South Limburg. At Lobith the Rhine reached 16.68 m (usual range 7.2–12 m). From 31 January more than 250,000 residents and 1 million animals were evacuated from Gelderland and Limburg — one of the largest peacetime evacuations in Dutch history. The Waal dike at Ochten shifted and was held with sandbags; primary dikes did not breach. The near-disaster launched the Room for the River and Meuse Works programmes.

events.name: Great Flood of 1993
events.geo_source: St. Louis, a principal city on the flooded middle Mississippi
events.what_happened: Persistent heavy rain from spring into summer 1993 produced a months-long flood on the upper Mississippi and Missouri. NOAA and NWS treat it as one of the most damaging river floods in US history. About 50 people died. Some 54,000 people were evacuated. Damage about $15 billion (1993 USD). Hundreds of levees were overtopped or breached as part of the wider river flood.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 54,000 evacuated (NOAA/NWS summaries)
events.cause_summary: Months of above-normal rainfall over the upper Midwest, saturating the Mississippi–Missouri system.

sources.label: NWS Davenport: The Great Flood of 1993

events.notes: 50 deaths and ~$15 billion are the NOAA/NWS figures. Levee breaches were part of a wider river flood.
events.inundation_area: About 30,000 square miles
events.economic_damage: About $15 billion (1993 USD, NOAA)

events.affected_or_evacuated: 45 million affected; 25–28 million homeless (USAID)
events.cause_summary: Synchronised extreme monsoon peaks on the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna.
events.economic_damage: Preliminary recovery costs about $1.14 billion capital stock plus $1 billion housing (USAID)
events.geo_source: Dhaka, capital severely flooded in 1988
events.inundation_area: 77,700 km² (52% of the country)
events.name: 1988 Bangladesh flood
events.notes: 2,379 is the USAID/Wikipedia table figure (flood plus subsequent diarrheal deaths).
events.return_period: Estimated 50–100 years (Floods in Bangladesh)
events.what_happened: August–September 1988 monsoon floods, with the three major rivers peaking together, inundated about 77,700 km² (52% of Bangladesh) including much of Dhaka. USAID recorded at least 2,379 dead (1,644 officially from the floods and more than 735 from later diarrheal disease) and 45 million affected, of whom 25–28 million were homeless. Return period estimated at 50–100 years. Widely described at the time as the worst flood of the century.

events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 800 people evacuated by helicopter on 1 August (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: A stationary thunderstorm complex over the Front Range produced extreme orographic rain in Big Thompson Canyon.
events.economic_damage: More than $40 million (1976 USD); nearly $150 million in 2016 USD (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Drake, a principal canyon community destroyed along US 34
events.name: 1976 Big Thompson River flood
events.notes: 144 is the USGS and Wikipedia figure. Injured recorded as 250; Wikipedia says more than 250.
events.rainfall_mm: 12–14 inches (300–360 mm) near Estes Park; 7.5 inches (190 mm) in one hour (USGS / Wikipedia)
events.status: Historical. Memorial listing the dead stands on US 34 near Drake.
events.what_happened: On the eve of Colorado's centennial, a stalled thunderstorm dumped 12–14 inches (300–360 mm) near Estes Park, including 7.5 inches (190 mm) in one hour. The Big Thompson River rose in a 30-foot (9.1 m) surge through the canyon at about 15 mph. USGS and Wikipedia record 144 deaths, more than 250 injuries and at least 5 missing. 418 homes, more than 400 vehicles and 152 businesses were destroyed. President Ford designated Larimer County a disaster area. A flash-flood warning was issued hours after flooding began.

events.cause_summary: Severe monsoon on the three great rivers of the Bengal delta.
events.geo_source: Dhaka, capital on the flooded delta
events.inundation_area: 52,720 km² (35% of the country)
events.name: 1974 Bangladesh monsoon flood
events.notes: 1,987 is the Floods-in-Bangladesh table figure for flood deaths. Broader famine-inclusive estimates are far higher and are not used on the pin.
events.what_happened: Monsoon flooding in 1974 inundated about 52,720 km² (35% of Bangladesh). The national flood table on Wikipedia's Floods in Bangladesh lists 1,987 flood deaths. Combined with the concurrent famine, some compilations cite much higher totals. About a third of the country was underwater. It is one of the country's named catastrophic monsoon floods of the 20th century.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 13,000 properties affected; about 2,000 evacuated along the Nerang River / Gold Coast canals
events.cause_summary: Cyclone Wanda drew the monsoon trough south over already-full Brisbane, Bremer and Stanley catchments.
events.economic_damage: Over A$980 million (1974 values); $328 million in insurance claims (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Wikipedia page coordinates for the 1974 Brisbane flood (CBD / Port Office gauge)
events.name: 1974 Brisbane flood (Cyclone Wanda)
events.notes: 16 fatalities is the figure on the Cyclone Wanda Wikipedia page and ABC News. Distinct from the 2010–11 Queensland floods already in the database.
events.rainfall_mm: 642 mm in 36 hours in Brisbane; 1,318 mm at Mount Glorious associated with Wanda (BOM / Wikipedia)
events.return_period: Researchers estimated about 100 years for the associated Corinda–Oxley landslide (Wikipedia citing Granger and Hayne)

sources.label: Bureau of Meteorology: Known floods in the Brisbane and Bremer River basin

events.status: Historical. Wivenhoe Dam was built upstream after the flood.
events.what_happened: After three weeks of monsoon rain, weak Tropical Cyclone Wanda crossed the Queensland coast on 24 January 1974 and dumped 642 mm on Brisbane in 36 hours. The Brisbane River peaked at 6.6 m at the Port Office gauge at 02:15 on 29 January. Sixteen people died (twelve drowned in Brisbane and Ipswich), about 300 were injured, at least 6,700 homes were flooded and about 13,000 properties were affected. Final damage exceeded A$980 million (1974 values). The disaster led to flood-mitigation storage at Wivenhoe Dam and was later named a Q150 Icon of Queensland.

events.cause_summary: Stalled remnants of Hurricane Agnes dumped record rain on the Susquehanna basin.
events.geo_source: Wilkes-Barre on the Susquehanna, a principal inundated city
events.name: Hurricane Agnes floods
events.notes: 122 is a commonly cited US death figure for Agnes (flooding was the main killer). Confirm against NWS local summaries.
events.what_happened: After landfall as a weakening hurricane, Agnes stalled over the Mid-Atlantic in June 1972 and produced record rain. The Susquehanna and tributaries flooded Pennsylvania, New York and surrounding states. NOAA and contemporary accounts treat it as one of the costliest US floods of the 20th century. The US Geological Survey and NWS document more than 100 flood deaths; Wilkes-Barre and Corning were among the hardest-hit cities.

events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 3.6 million directly affected (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Category-4-equivalent cyclone made landfall at high tide, flooding the Ganges Delta islands.
events.economic_damage: About $86.4 million (1970 USD; Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Tazumuddin upazila, where over 45% of residents were killed
events.name: 1970 Bhola cyclone storm surge
events.notes: 300,000 is the commonly cited minimum; upper estimates 500,000. Included as a named cyclone-flood (same class as Mitch, Idai, Yagi already in the database).
events.region: Ganges Delta / Bhola and offshore islands
events.river_or_facility: Bay of Bengal coast and delta islands
events.status: Historical. Led to Bangladesh's Cyclone Preparedness Programme.
events.what_happened: The Bhola cyclone made landfall on East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) on 12 November 1970 with a storm surge about 10 m high at the Ganges Delta. At least 300,000 people died, possibly as many as 500,000, mostly by drowning on low islands. Over 3.6 million people were directly affected. It is the deadliest tropical cyclone on record. The failed relief effort helped precipitate the Bangladesh Liberation War.

events.cause_summary: Prolonged autumn rain on semi-arid wadi catchments.
events.geo_source: Kairouan, a principal inland city in the flooded zone
events.name: 1969 Tunisia floods
events.notes: 540 is the commonly cited Wikipedia list figure.
events.what_happened: Exceptional autumn rains in September–October 1969 produced catastrophic wadi floods across Tunisia. Wikipedia's list of deadliest floods cites 540 deaths. Towns and oases in the centre and east were inundated; it remains Tunisia's benchmark flood disaster of the 20th century.

events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 70,000 families left homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Prolonged autumn rain plus reservoir releases sent a flood wave down the Arno into a poorly prepared Florence.
events.geo_source: Santa Croce, where water reached over 6.7 m
events.name: 1966 flood of the Arno
events.notes: 35 is the lead Wikipedia death figure; some accounts give 101. Reservoir discharge was operational, not a structural dam collapse.
events.peak_discharge: More than 2,000 m³/s released from Levane and La Penna toward Florence

sources.label: New York Times: 50 Years After a Devastating Flood

events.status: Historical. Bilancino Dam and other Arno works built later.
events.what_happened: After prolonged rain, the Levane and La Penna dams discharged more than 2,000 m³/s toward Florence. On 4 November 1966 the Arno flooded the city — the worst flood there since 1557. Water exceeded 6.7 m in Santa Croce. The lead Wikipedia figure is 35 deaths; a later passage cites 101. About 70,000 families were left homeless; 6,000 shops were destroyed; millions of books and artworks were damaged. International 'Mud Angels' led the salvage.

events.cause_summary: Adriatic storm surge coincident with sirocco and high tide — the same weather system as the Arno flood.
events.geo_source: Piazza San Marco, Venice
events.name: 1966 Venice flood
events.notes: Deaths not given a reliable single figure in the sources used; left unknown. Named official disaster with city-wide inundation.
events.status: Historical. MOSE barriers later built for extreme acqua alta.
events.what_happened: The same November 1966 storm that flooded Florence produced Venice's worst modern acqua alta. Water reached about 194 cm above the standard tide gauge, inundating nearly the entire historic city and damaging churches, palaces and art. The event is the reference disaster that later drove the MOSE mobile-barrier project.

events.affected_or_evacuated: 22.46 million affected in Hebei (Chinese official figures cited on Floods in China)
events.cause_summary: Week-long extreme rainfall over the Hai basin from southwest monsoon moisture and a typhoon influence.
events.geo_source: Tianjin, principal city of the Hai basin defended in 1963
events.name: 1963 Hai River flood
events.notes: 5,154 is the official figure cited on Floods in China and the deadliest-floods list (5,119 Hebei/Tianjin + 35 Beijing).
events.rainfall_mm: Seven-day centre 2,050 mm; >1,000 mm over 15,300 km² (Chinese accounts cited via Floods in China)

sources.label: Wikipedia: Floods in China (1963 North China flood)

events.status: Historical. A benchmark Hai flood (the later 2023 event was compared to it).
events.what_happened: Historic rain from 1–10 August 1963 (seven-day totals over 1,000 mm across 15,300 km²; a southern Hai centre recorded 2,050 mm) produced the Hai basin's greatest modern flood. Official deaths are 5,154 (5,119 in Hebei including Tianjin; 35 in Beijing). About 22.46 million people were affected in Hebei; 54.38 million mu of farmland flooded. Tianjin was held but rural Hebei suffered for months.

events.affected_or_evacuated: Homes of about 60,000 people destroyed (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: North Sea windstorm surge overtopped and breached Elbe and coastal dikes.
events.economic_damage: About DM 3 billion in Hamburg (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Hamburg-Wilhelmsburg, the hardest-hit residential district
events.inundation_area: 120 km² in Hamburg (one-sixth of the city)
events.name: North Sea flood of 1962
events.notes: 347 is the Wikipedia overall death toll; 315 in Hamburg.
events.status: Historical. Elbe dikes shortened and strengthened afterward.
events.what_happened: The Vincinette / Great Sheffield Gale drove a North Sea surge into the German Bight on 16–17 February 1962. About 50 dike breaches flooded a sixth of Hamburg (120 km²). Wikipedia records 347 deaths overall and 315 in Hamburg; about 60,000 homes were destroyed. Helmut Schmidt coordinated NATO and Bundeswehr rescue. Damage in Hamburg about DM 3 billion.

events.cause_summary: Mediterranean cold-drop storm produced a flash flood on the Turia through Valencia.
events.geo_source: Historic centre of Valencia on the Turia
events.name: 1957 Valencia flood
events.notes: 81+ is the commonly cited Wikipedia list figure.
events.status: Historical. Turia diverted; old bed is now a park.
events.what_happened: A cold-drop (gota fría) storm on 14 October 1957 sent the Turia through the city of Valencia. Wikipedia's deadliest-floods list cites 81 or more deaths. Large parts of the historic centre were inundated. The disaster led to the Turia being diverted south of the city; the old riverbed is now the Turia Garden.

events.cause_summary: Unusually high and prolonged spring–summer rainfall on the middle Yangtze.
events.geo_source: Wuhan, principal city on the flooded middle Yangtze
events.name: 1954 Yangtze floods
events.notes: 33,000 is the commonly cited estimate including post-flood plague.
events.what_happened: An extraordinarily long rainy season from June to September 1954 raised the middle Yangtze to historic highs of 44.67 m at Jingzhou and 29.73 m at Wuhan. Wikipedia estimates about 33,000 dead, including plague deaths after the flood. The disaster added momentum to later construction of Gezhouba and the Three Gorges Dam.

events.name: North Sea flood of 1953
events.geo_source: Oude-Tonge, one of the highest local death tolls (305)
events.what_happened: A severe European windstorm plus a high spring tide drove a North Sea storm surge on the night of 31 January–1 February 1953. Dutch sea defences failed in many places (67 breaches in Zeeland alone). Wikipedia records 2,551 fatalities overall: 1,836 in the Netherlands, 307 on land in England, 19 in eastern Scotland, 28 in Belgium, and more than 230 at sea including the sinking of MV Princess Victoria. Led to the Delta Works and the Thames Barrier.
events.status: Historical. Defences rebuilt (Delta Works, Thames Barrier).
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 70,000 emergency evacuations in the Netherlands; 30,000+ people forced from homes in the UK.
events.cause_summary: North Sea windstorm coincident with a high spring tide; sea defences overtopped and breached.
events.notes: 2,551 is the Wikipedia infobox total (land plus sea). Dutch land deaths 1,836; UK land 307.
events.inundation_area: 1,365 km² of Dutch land flooded (9% of farmland)
events.economic_damage: About 1 billion Dutch guilders; UK about £50 million (1953)

events.affected_or_evacuated: 420 made homeless
events.cause_summary: Orographic thunderstorm rain on saturated Exmoor; debris jam then release on the West Lyn.
events.geo_source: Lynmouth village at the confluence of the East and West Lyn
events.name: Lynmouth Flood
events.notes: 34 deaths is the standard figure. Not a constructed dam failure; a natural debris jam released.
events.rainfall_mm: 229 mm in 24 hours on Exmoor

sources.label: Met Office / Weather journal: The 1952 Lynmouth floods revisited (McGinnigle, 2002)

events.status: Historical. Village rebuilt with the river diverted around the centre.
events.what_happened: A storm of tropical intensity dumped 229 mm of rain in 24 hours on already saturated Exmoor on 15–16 August 1952. Debris-laden floodwaters cascaded down the East and West Lyn. A debris dam in the upper West Lyn failed and sent a wave through Lynmouth. 34 people died; more than 100 buildings were destroyed or seriously damaged; 28 of 31 bridges were lost; 420 people were made homeless.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 70,000–100,000 evacuated; Canadian Disaster Database 107,000
events.cause_summary: Spring melt on the north-flowing Red River over the flat former lake bed of Lake Agassiz.
events.economic_damage: About $600 million to $1 billion (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Winnipeg, the principal city evacuated in 1950
events.inundation_area: More than 1,400 km² of the Red River Valley (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1950 Red River flood
events.notes: 8 is Wikipedia infobox (Canada 3 + United States 5). Canadian Disaster Database records 1 fatality in Winnipeg (a volunteer pump operator) and 107,000 evacuated.
events.region: Red River of the North / Winnipeg
events.status: Historical. Red River Floodway built afterward.
events.what_happened: The 1950 Red River flood ran from 15 April to 12 June along the Red River in the Dakotas and Manitoba. Winnipeg was inundated on 5 May (Black Friday). The river reached its highest level since 1861 and flooded more than 1,400 km² of the Red River Valley. An estimated 70,000–100,000 residents were evacuated and four of eleven Winnipeg bridges were destroyed. Wikipedia records 3 deaths in Canada and 5 in the United States. Property losses were estimated at $600 million to $1 billion. The disaster led to construction of the Red River Floodway (Duff's Ditch), completed in 1968.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 18,500 residents displaced
events.cause_summary: Columbia spring flood; railroad-embankment levee failed as part of the wider river flood.
events.geo_source: Former city of Vanport on the Columbia floodplain north of Portland
events.name: Vanport flood
events.notes: 15 is the official death toll. Levee/embankment failure was part of a wider Columbia flood, in scope like 1993 Mississippi.
events.status: Historical. Site is now West Delta Park / Portland International Raceway.
events.what_happened: Spring snowmelt and rain raised the Columbia to record stages. On 30 May 1948 a railroad embankment that served as Vanport's dike gave way, destroying the wartime city of Vanport — then Oregon's second-largest city — in about an hour. Officially 15 people died; some later estimates are higher. About 18,500 residents were displaced. The city was never rebuilt.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 5 million living on inundated land until 1947 (Bi Chunfu)
events.cause_summary: Intentional military destruction of the Huayuankou levees; flood then persisted as a diverted Yellow River.
events.geo_source: Huayuankou levee breach site
events.name: 1938 Yellow River flood
events.notes: 450,000 is the midpoint of the 400,000–500,000 total commonly cited by Wang Zhibin (1986) and Bi Chunfu (1995). Immediate drownings 30,000–89,000. A wartime levee breach, treated as a named flood (like Katrina's levee failures), not a structural dam collapse.
events.status: Historical. Course restored at Huayuankou in 1947.
events.what_happened: Nationalist forces breached the Yellow River dikes at Huayuankou in June 1938 to slow the Japanese advance. Immediate drowning deaths are estimated at 30,000–89,000. Professional Chinese sources put total deaths from drowning, famine and plague at 400,000–500,000. About five million civilians lived on inundated land until the dikes were repaired in 1947. The river was diverted south into the Huai system for nearly nine years.

events.cause_summary: Sequential Pacific storms on steep, already wet mountain catchments above a rapidly urbanizing basin.
events.geo_source: Los Angeles civic center, in the flooded basin
events.name: Los Angeles flood of 1938
events.notes: 115 is the commonly cited death figure on Wikipedia's deadliest-floods list.
events.region: Los Angeles Basin / Santa Ana and San Gabriel rivers
events.river_or_facility: Los Angeles, San Gabriel and Santa Ana rivers
events.status: Historical. LA River concrete channel built afterward.
events.what_happened: Pacific storms in late February and early March 1938 dumped extreme rain on the San Gabriel Mountains and Los Angeles Basin. Rivers left their channels; bridges and neighborhoods were destroyed. Wikipedia's list of deadliest floods cites 115 deaths. The disaster accelerated the US Army Corps of Engineers' channelization of the Los Angeles River.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 1 million left homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Six to twelve inches of January rain over the Ohio basin; river remained above flood stage for nearly three weeks.
events.economic_damage: About $500 million (1937 USD; Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Louisville, a principal city with ~70% inundated
events.name: Ohio River flood of 1937
events.notes: 385 deaths and ~$500 million are the Wikipedia figures. Levee overtopping was part of the wider river flood.
events.rainfall_mm: About 150–300 mm (6–12 inches) in Ohio, 13–25 January (Wikipedia)
events.region: Ohio River from Pittsburgh to Cairo

sources.label: NWS Louisville: The Great Flood of 1937

events.status: Historical. USACE reservoir system later reduced Ohio flood heights.
events.what_happened: Near-record January rains from 13–24 January 1937 sent the Ohio over its banks from Pittsburgh to Cairo. Wikipedia records 385 deaths, about one million people left homeless, and about $500 million damage (1937 USD). Cincinnati crested at 79.9 feet on 26 January. About 70% of Louisville was underwater and 175,000 people left their homes. The disaster drove a comprehensive reservoir and levee program on the Ohio.

events.affected_or_evacuated: Millions displaced; 1.5 million hectares of farmland flooded (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Monsoon rains on the middle Yangtze and Han/Li tributaries overwhelmed dikes still weakened after 1931.
events.economic_damage: $333 million (period USD; Wikipedia infobox)
events.geo_source: Xiangyang on the Han River, a core inundated city
events.name: 1935 Yangtze flood
events.notes: 145,000 is the Wikipedia infobox figure. Peak Han flow at Danjiangkou about 50,000 m³/s.
events.peak_discharge: About 50,000 m³/s on the Han at Danjiangkou (Wikipedia)
events.region: Middle Yangtze / Han and Li rivers

sources.label: Kte'pi, Encyclopedia of Disaster Relief: Yangtze River Flood (1935)

events.status: Historical. Among the deadliest Yangtze floods.
events.what_happened: On 6 July 1935 the Han, Li and middle Yangtze rose after monsoon rains and dike bursts. Wikipedia records 145,000 deaths and millions displaced. The Han flooded 427,000 hectares and drowned about 80,000; more than 30,000 drowned along the Li; 23,000 died when the Jing River dike burst. Property damage is given as $333 million (period USD). Affected provinces included Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

events.name: 1931 China floods
events.geo_source: Wuhan, core inundated city on the Yangtze
events.what_happened: From June to August 1931 the Yangtze, Huai, Yellow River and Grand Canal flooded after prolonged rains, inundating a core zone across eight central provinces and hitting Wuhan and Nanjing. On 25 August dikes near Gaoyou Lake failed; in Gaoyou County alone 18,000 people drowned. Fatality estimates vary widely, from Li Wenhai’s 422,420 (media-based) to official figures around 2 million including famine and disease, and some Western claims of 3.7–4 million.
events.status: Historical. Among the deadliest floods on record.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Government estimate 25 million affected; later historians up to 53 million. Inundation about 181,500 km².
events.cause_summary: Prolonged summer rains over the Yangtze–Huai basin, culminating in dike failure at Gaoyou Lake.
events.notes: Deaths left unknown on the pin because sourced estimates span 422,420 to about 4 million (drowning vs famine/disease). Do not treat as zero.
events.inundation_area: 181,500 km² (DisasterHistory.org)

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 700,000 displaced (Red Cross / commonly cited figure)
events.inundation_area: About 27,000 square miles
events.notes: 246 is the American Red Cross figure commonly cited by NOAA. Levee breaches were part of a wider river flood, not a single dam failure.
events.name: Great Mississippi Flood of 1927
events.geo_source: Greenville, a principal city on the flooded lower Mississippi
events.what_happened: The most destructive river flood in US history to that date. After months of rain, the Mississippi broke levees from Illinois to Louisiana in 1927, inundating about 27,000 square miles. The American Red Cross recorded 246 deaths; some later estimates are higher. Hundreds of thousands were displaced. The disaster led to the 1928 Flood Control Act.
events.status: Historical. Federal flood-control system rebuilt after 1928.
events.cause_summary: Months of heavy rain over the Mississippi basin; widespread levee breaches on the lower river.

sources.label: NOAA: The Great Mississippi River Flood of 1927

events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 250,000 left homeless
events.cause_summary: A stalled winter storm pattern dumped 3–9 inches of rain across the Ohio basin in four days.
events.economic_damage: More than $333 million (1913 USD) nationwide (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Dayton, hardest-hit major city (Great Miami River)
events.name: Great Flood of 1913
events.notes: 650 is the commonly cited multi-state flood-death estimate. Ohio official range 422–470. Not a dam-failure event; levee breaches were part of the wider river flood.
events.rainfall_mm: 76–230 mm (3–9 inches) over 23–26 March in the core Ohio–Indiana area
events.region: Ohio River valley / Midwest and East
events.river_or_facility: Great Miami, Scioto, Wabash, White and Ohio rivers

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of floods in the United States (1900–2000)

events.status: Historical. Miami Conservancy District floodworks completed 1922.
events.what_happened: Several days of heavy rain from 23–26 March 1913 flooded rivers across Ohio, Indiana and more than a dozen other states. About 650 flood-related deaths are estimated; Ohio's official range is 422–470. More than a quarter million people were left homeless. Dayton's levees failed and about 123 people died there; downtown stood in 10 feet of water. The disaster led to the Ohio Conservancy Act and modern US flood-control districts.

events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands evacuated from homes in Paris and riverside towns
events.cause_summary: Saturated winter catchment; Seine rose through the city's underground network.
events.economic_damage: About 400 million francs (period estimate; ~US$1.5 billion in later conversions cited on Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Seine through central Paris
events.name: 1910 Great Flood of Paris
events.notes: Wikipedia states no deaths were reported. 0 is sourced, not a default for unknown.

sources.label: BBC: Is Paris prepared if Seine floods?

events.status: Historical. A reference 'flood of the century' for Paris flood planning.
events.what_happened: Winter rains over a saturated Seine basin raised the river far above ordinary level. Water entered Paris through sewers, Metro tunnels and saturated soil rather than by overtopping the quays inside the city. The Seine peaked at 8.62 m above normal on 28 January. Thousands were evacuated; residents moved by boat and wooden walkways. No deaths were reported. Damage was estimated at about 400 million francs.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 2 million left homeless (Gunn / Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Days of heavy rain over a silt-raised, diked Yellow River; breach at Huayuankou.
events.geo_source: Huayuankou dike breach site near Zhengzhou
events.inundation_area: About 50,000 square miles (130,000 km²)
events.name: 1887 Yellow River flood
events.notes: 930,000 is Wikipedia's 'at least' figure. Range commonly cited 900,000–2,000,000 including famine and disease.
events.status: Historical. Among the deadliest floods ever recorded.
events.what_happened: After days of heavy rain, the silt-raised Yellow River overcame dikes at Huayuankou near Zhengzhou around 28 September 1887. Water spread across an estimated 50,000 square miles (130,000 km²) of the North China Plain. Wikipedia records at least 930,000 deaths; estimates range from about 900,000 to 2 million including famine and disease. About two million people were left homeless. It is among the deadliest floods on record.

events.cause_summary: A sequence of atmospheric rivers dumped rain on an existing mountain snowpack, then a warm storm melted the snow.
events.economic_damage: About $100 million (1861 USD); roughly $3 billion in 2021 USD (Wikipedia)
events.geo_source: Sacramento, the inundated state capital
events.inundation_area: About 5,000–6,000 square miles in the Central Valley
events.name: Great Flood of 1862
events.notes: 4,000 is Wikipedia's commonly cited California estimate. Inundation 5,000–6,000 square miles.
events.status: Historical. USGS ARkStorm scenario models a repeat in modern California.
events.what_happened: Weeks of rain and mountain snow from November 1861 into January 1862, capped by a warm atmospheric-river storm, produced the largest flood in the recorded history of California, Oregon and Nevada. The Central Valley became an inland sea 250–300 miles long and about 20 miles wide (about 5,000–6,000 square miles). Sacramento was underwater for months; the state government temporarily moved to San Francisco. Wikipedia cites at least 4,000 deaths in California (about 1% of the state population) and about $100 million damage in 1861 USD.

events.cause_summary: Prolonged rain raised the Murrumbidgee over the original Gundagai floodplain township.
events.geo_source: Gundagai town site on the Murrumbidgee floodplain
events.name: 1852 Gundagai flood
events.notes: 89 is a mid-range figure within the commonly cited 80–100 deaths.

sources.label: National Museum of Australia: Australia's deadliest flood

events.status: Historical. Town relocated to higher ground.
events.what_happened: The Murrumbidgee rose after days of rain and swept through the original town of Gundagai, built on the river flats. The National Museum of Australia describes it as Australia's deadliest flood. About 80–100 people died, roughly a third of the town's population. The settlement was later rebuilt on higher ground.

events.cause_summary: Northwesterly North Sea storm on Christmas night overtopped and breached coastal dikes from the Netherlands to Denmark.
events.geo_source: Groningen, a principal flooded city in the Dutch sector
events.name: Christmas flood of 1717
events.notes: 14,000 is the Wikipedia/Delta Works commonly cited total.
events.region: North Sea coast from the Netherlands to Denmark
events.status: Historical. Last large storm flood of this scale in the northern Netherlands.
events.what_happened: A northwesterly storm on Christmas night 1717 drove a storm surge along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Scandinavia. About 14,000 people drowned. Between Tønder and Emden about 9,000 drowned; the Netherlands had about 2,500 victims. Villages behind the sea dikes in Groningen and East Frisia were devastated. A second storm flood followed in late February.

events.cause_summary: North Sea storm tide breached North Frisian dikes and shattered the island of Strand.
events.geo_source: Nordstrand, a principal island shattered by the 1634 storm tide
events.name: Burchardi flood
events.notes: 12,000 is a mid-range figure within the commonly cited 8,000–15,000 range.
events.what_happened: A catastrophic North Sea storm tide on 11–12 October 1634 (the Burchardi flood, or second Grote Mandränke) struck the coasts of North Frisia, Schleswig-Holstein and southern Denmark. Dikes failed across the region. The island of Strand was broken apart; Nordstrand and Pellworm remain. Death estimates commonly range from 8,000 to 15,000.

events.cause_summary: North Sea storm surge more than four metres above mean high water overran neglected dikes.
events.geo_source: Bergen op Zoom, where the Domain Council issued the first documented flood warning
events.location_label: Bergen op Zoom, North Brabant, Netherlands
events.name: All Saints' Flood (1570)
events.notes: 20,000 is the confirmed drowning figure on the Wikipedia page; the same page says up to 25,000 deaths can be assumed.
events.region: Spanish Netherlands / North Sea coast / East Frisia
events.river_or_facility: North Sea dikes from Flanders to East Frisia

sources.label: Die Welt: Als die Allerheiligenflut Holland verschlang

events.status: Historical. High-water mark at Suurhusen church recorded +4.40 m NN.
events.what_happened: The All Saints' Flood of 1–2 November 1570 is considered the worst North Sea flood disaster before the 20th century. A surge more than four metres above mean high water overran neglected dikes from Calais to Jutland and Norway. Chroniclers reported that 80 percent of the country was under water; the island of Wulpen in Zeeland was permanently lost. Wikipedia states it was confirmed that the floods drowned 20,000 people and that up to 25,000 deaths can be assumed. Between the Ems and Weser about 10,000 people died. A warning had been issued the morning before — the first documented North Sea flood warning.

events.cause_summary: North Sea storm surge overtopped and breached medieval sea dikes in Zeeland and Flanders.
events.geo_source: Former town of Reimerswaal, destroyed in the flood
events.name: St. Felix's flood
events.notes: 100,000+ is the commonly cited Wikipedia list figure. Contemporary counts are uncertain.
events.status: Historical. Parts of eastern Zeeland remained drowned.
events.what_happened: A North Sea storm surge on St. Felix's Day (5 November 1530) breached dikes across Zeeland and Flanders. The town of Reimerswaal was destroyed and never rebuilt as a city. The flood is commonly cited with more than 100,000 deaths and is among the deadliest coastal floods on record in the Low Countries.

events.cause_summary: North Sea extratropical cyclone drove a storm surge that overtopped and breached dikes.
events.geo_source: Dordrecht, principal surviving city of the inundated Grote Hollandse Waard
events.name: St. Elizabeth's flood (1421)
events.notes: Deaths left unknown on the pin because sourced estimates span 2,000–10,000. Do not treat as zero.
events.river_or_facility: North Sea dikes and Grote Hollandse Waard polders
events.status: Historical. Biesbosch National Park occupies much of the still-flooded land.
events.what_happened: On the night of 18–19 November 1421 a North Sea storm surge broke dikes in the Grote Hollandse Waard. Villages were swallowed and the flood created the freshwater tidal wetlands now known as the Biesbosch. Wikipedia records 2,000–10,000 deaths. Most of the area remained flooded for decades; reclaimed remnants include the island of Dordrecht and the Hoeksche Waard.

events.cause_summary: Prolonged rain after a dry period, associated with a Genoa low, produced runoff the dry soils could not absorb.
events.geo_source: Frankfurt, a principal city on the flooded Main
events.name: St. Mary Magdalene's flood
events.notes: Total death toll unknown. About 6,000 is the figure commonly cited for the Danube area alone. Do not treat as zero.

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of floods in Europe

events.status: Historical. High-water marks survive at Frankfurt and Hann. Münden.
events.what_happened: The largest recorded river flood in central Europe. After a prolonged dry spell, days of continuous rain following a Genoa low inundated the Rhine, Moselle, Main, Danube, Weser, Elbe, Vltava and tributaries around the feast of St. Mary Magdalene (22 July 1342). Cologne, Mainz, Frankfurt, Würzburg, Regensburg, Passau and Vienna were seriously damaged. Würzburg's Steinerne Brücke was washed away. In the Danube area alone it is believed about 6,000 people perished. Erosion is estimated at more than 13 billion tonnes of soil.

events.name: St. Lucia's flood
events.geo_source: Harlingen, which became a Frisian seaport after the flood destroyed Griend and opened the coast
events.what_happened: A North Sea storm tide on St. Lucia's Day (13–14 December 1287, Old Style) overran seawalls and dikes in the Netherlands and northern Germany. Wikipedia records approximately 50,000 to 80,000 deaths. The island of Griend was nearly destroyed. Formerly landlocked Harlingen became a major Frisian seaport. The same storm killed hundreds in England, including 180 at Hickling, Norfolk, and contributed to the decline of Dunwich.
events.status: Historical. West-Friesland's ringdike largely held; the flood helped end the Friso-Hollandic Wars.
events.cause_summary: North Sea storm tide: a low-pressure system combined with a high tide overran medieval seawalls and dikes.
events.notes: Deaths left unknown on the pin because sourced estimates span 50,000–80,000. Do not treat as zero.

events.name: St. Marcellus's flood (Grote Mandrenke)
events.geo_source: Site of the lost town of Rungholt on the former island of Strand, destroyed in the flood
events.river_or_facility: North Frisian and Low Countries sea dikes
events.what_happened: An intense extratropical cyclone coinciding with a new-moon spring tide swept the British Isles, the Netherlands, northern Germany and Denmark around 16 January 1362 (the feast of St. Marcellus). The storm tide destroyed the town of Rungholt on the island of Strand, damaged Ravenser Odd and Dunwich, and destroyed 44 villages. Wikipedia records at least 25,000 deaths, with estimates as high as 100,000. The event is also called the Grote Mandrenke (Great Drowning of Men).
events.status: Historical. Contributed to the formation of the Zuiderzee and reshaped the North Frisian coast.
events.cause_summary: North Sea extratropical cyclone on a spring tide; dikes were in disrepair after the Black Death.

sources.label: The Guardian: Weatherwatch — The Grote Mandrenke

events.notes: 25,000 is the Wikipedia 'at least' figure. Infobox range is 25,000–100,000.

events.name: February flood of 1825 (Große Halligflut)
events.region: Groningen / Friesland / Overijssel / North Frisia / Jutland
events.geo_source: Emden, a principal East Frisian town hard-hit by the surge
events.river_or_facility: North Sea dikes from the Netherlands to Jutland
events.what_happened: A North Sea storm surge from 3–5 February 1825 drowned about 800 people along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany, Schleswig and Jutland. The sand spit Agger Tange was breached, giving the Limfjord a western opening to the sea and making North Jutland an island. Pellworm was completely flooded. In the Netherlands it was the worst natural disaster of the 19th century, with the heaviest losses in Groningen, Friesland and Overijssel.
events.status: Historical. Unlike 1953, the disaster produced no lasting coastal-engineering programme.
events.cause_summary: North Sea storm surge; many dikes were already damaged by a November 1824 surge.
events.notes: About 800 drowned is the Wikipedia lead figure. About 200 of those deaths were in East Frisia.

events.name: 1900 Galveston hurricane (Galveston Flood)
events.geo_source: Galveston city centre; the island was overwashed by 8–12 ft of storm surge
events.river_or_facility: Galveston Island (no seawall at the time)
events.what_happened: A Category 4 hurricane made landfall south of Houston on the evening of 8 September 1900. Storm surge of 8 to 12 feet (some accounts more than 15 feet) inundated Galveston Island, then only 8.7 feet above sea level. Official reports most often cite about 8,000 deaths (range 6,000–12,000), the deadliest natural disaster in US history. About 7,000 buildings were destroyed, including 3,636 homes; roughly 10,000 of fewer than 38,000 residents were left homeless. The city later built a seawall and raised the grade.
events.status: Historical. Galveston Seawall and island raising followed.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 10,000 homeless in Galveston (of a population under 38,000)
events.cause_summary: Category 4 hurricane storm surge overwashed a low barrier island that had no seawall.
events.notes: 8,000 is the figure most cited in official reports. Sourced range is 6,000–12,000.
events.economic_damage: More than US$34 million (1900); about US$30 million in Galveston County

events.name: 1939 Tianjin flood
events.geo_source: Tianjin urban area; about 80 percent of the city was inundated
events.river_or_basin: Hai River (Yongding, North Canal, Daqing, Ziya, South Canal)
events.river_or_facility: Hai River dikes including Chentangzhuang embankment
events.what_happened: Torrential August 1939 rains across northern China raised the Hai River system. The Chentangzhuang embankment collapsed on 20 August; floodwaters entered Tianjin the next day and inundated about 80 percent of the urban area for up to a month and a half. More than 100,000 houses were destroyed and about 650,000 people in Tianjin and surrounding areas were made homeless. Japanese forces had also breached 182 dikes on the Daqing, Ziya, Hutuo and Fuyang rivers. Epidemics of cholera, typhoid and dysentery followed. Wikipedia does not give a death toll.
events.status: Historical. Waters receded in early October 1939.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 650,000 homeless in Tianjin and surroundings; more than 8 million affected
events.cause_summary: Concentrated rainfall on the Taihang and Yan slopes plus a fan-shaped Hai basin with limited downstream capacity; wartime dike breaches also cited.
events.notes: Deaths left unknown: the Wikipedia article gives no count. A 20,000 figure appears only on list pages, not on the event article. Do not treat as zero. Economic loss cited as 600 million Chinese National Currency.
events.inundation_area: About 80 percent of Tianjin's urban area
events.economic_damage: About 600 million Chinese National Currency (direct losses)

events.name: 1951 Polesine flood
events.geo_source: Rovigo, provincial capital of the inundated Polesine
events.what_happened: After days of rain over northern Italy, the Po and tributaries breached levees from 11 November 1951. The main Polesine inundation began on the evening of 14 November when the primary levee failed at Paviole and later at Bosco-Malcantone. Floodwater covered more than 1,000 km² for days, up to six metres deep near Adria. Italian Civil Protection records more than 100 deaths and 180,000 evacuees; about 80,000 never returned. An Environment & Society Portal essay cites 84 deaths.
events.status: Historical. Land was not fully drained until May 1952.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 180,000 evacuated; about 80,000 never returned (Italian Civil Protection)
events.cause_summary: Prolonged November rain on a Po basin whose levees had been poorly maintained after the war.

sources.label: Italian Civil Protection: The Polesine flood
Environment & Society Portal: The Great Fear — Polesine Flood of 1951

events.notes: Deaths left unknown because sourced figures are 84 (Arcadia) and 'over a hundred' / about 100 (Civil Protection). Do not treat as zero.
events.inundation_area: More than 1,000 km² (Civil Protection); about 1,080 km² in hydrologic reconstructions

events.name: 1962 Vallès floods
events.geo_source: Terrassa, hardest-hit city (372 dead and missing on the Wikipedia page)
events.river_or_basin: Llobregat / Besòs (Riera de les Arenes, Ripoll)
events.river_or_facility: Riera de les Arenes and Ripoll
events.what_happened: A Mediterranean cold drop (gota freda) dumped 212 mm of rain in less than three hours on 25 September 1962 after a long drought. Normally dry torrents and the lower Llobregat and Besòs overflowed through Terrassa, Rubí, Sabadell and neighbouring towns. The official death toll is 617; estimates run to 800–1,000. Wikipedia calls it the largest natural catastrophe in the history of Spain. Informal housing built in dry beds was worst hit.
events.cause_summary: Cold-drop cloudburst over dry clayey torrent beds and unregulated riverside settlement.
events.notes: 617 is the official Wikipedia figure. Estimates 800–1,000 because many victims were unregistered migrants.
events.rainfall_mm: 212 mm in less than three hours
events.economic_damage: 2,650 million pesetas (Wikipedia)

events.name: 1967 Portugal floods
events.geo_source: Odivelas riverside, among the worst-hit places on the Wikipedia page
events.river_or_basin: Tagus tributaries (Trancão, Alenquer, Grande da Pipa, Odivelas)
events.what_happened: A night-time cloudburst on 25–26 November 1967 dropped more than 120 mm, mostly in five hours, along a 60 km line from Estoril to Alenquer, coinciding with high tide. Flash floods on small Tagus tributaries struck informal riverside housing around Lisbon. The official death toll is 495; unofficial estimates are at least 700. Newspaper compilations list 522 dead among 2,045 people registered as directly affected. It is Portugal's deadliest flood on record.
events.status: Historical. Estado Novo censored casualty figures and student relief work.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 885 lost their homes; 307 evacuated (newspaper compilation on Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Five-hour cloudburst on small steep basins, coincident with high tide; informal housing on floodplains.
events.notes: 495 is the official Wikipedia figure. Unofficial estimates ≥700; a newspaper compilation gives 522 dead.
events.rainfall_mm: >120 mm, mostly in five hours (19:00–00:00)

events.name: 1972 Black Hills flood (Rapid City Flood)
events.region: Black Hills / Rapid City, South Dakota
events.geo_source: Wikipedia coordinates for the flood (Rapid City)
events.river_or_basin: Rapid Creek (Battle, Spring, Bear Butte, Boxelder)
events.what_happened: Stationary thunderstorms dropped 4 to 15 inches (100–380 mm) of rain on the Black Hills on 9–10 June 1972. Rapid Creek and neighbouring streams overflowed. Debris clogged Canyon Lake Dam, which then failed, adding to the midnight flash flood through Rapid City. Wikipedia and USGS-linked accounts record 238 deaths (including 5 missing) and 3,057 injuries. 1,335 homes were destroyed. Keystone was also hit (8 deaths).
events.status: Historical. Floodplain housing was removed and parks created; Canyon Lake Dam was redesigned.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1,335 homes destroyed; 2,820 damaged
events.cause_summary: Orographic stalling thunderstorms on saturated soils; debris-clogged Canyon Lake Dam then failed.
events.notes: 238 is the Wikipedia/USGS figure including 5 missing. This is a named flood; Canyon Lake Dam failure was a contributing release, not a standalone dam-incident pin.
events.rainfall_mm: 4–15 inches (100–380 mm); 15 inches in the core
events.economic_damage: Over US$160 million (1972); Rapid City about $66 million

events.name: Eastern China flood of 1991
events.region: Huai / Chu / Yangtze — Anhui, Jiangsu, Henan
events.geo_source: Hefei, capital of Anhui, the province with the highest UNDRO death count (556)
events.what_happened: Continuous heavy rain from 18 May 1991 overflowed the Huai, Chu and Yangtze. Anhui, Jiangsu and Henan took the worst damage; China requested international aid. UNDRO on 3 September 1991 reported 556 deaths in Anhui, 260 in Jiangsu and 94 in Henan. The New York Times on 27 January 1992 reported the death toll as approximately 3,000.
events.cause_summary: Prolonged summer monsoon rainfall over the Huai–Yangtze lowlands.

sources.label: New York Times: China's Floods of July — Misery Lingers (27 Jan 1992)

events.notes: 3,000 is the later New York Times figure (27 Jan 1992). UNDRO's 3 Sep 1991 provincial tally was 910 (556+260+94).

events.name: Tropical Storm Allison flooding
events.geo_source: Downtown Houston / Texas Medical Center, the core of the flood damage
events.river_or_basin: Buffalo Bayou / White Oak Bayou / Harris County bayous
events.what_happened: Tropical Storm Allison made landfall near Freeport on 5 June 2001, stalled over east Texas, looped, and returned. Rainfall peaked at just over 40 inches (1,000 mm) in northwestern Jefferson County; Houston recorded 38.6 inches in six days. Two-thirds of Harris County bayous had 500-year floods. 73,000 houses were flooded, 2,744 destroyed, and 30,000 people left homeless. The Texas Medical Center lost power and research collections. Wikipedia records 50 deaths (23 in Texas) and $8.5 billion damage (2001 USD). The name Allison was retired.
events.status: Historical. First Atlantic tropical storm to have its name retired without reaching hurricane strength.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 30,000 homeless; 73,000 houses flooded in Harris County
events.cause_summary: A June tropical storm stalled and looped over southeast Texas, dumping extreme rain on urban bayous.
events.notes: 50 is the Wikipedia nationwide total (23 in Texas). Peak rain just over 40 inches in NW Jefferson County.
events.rainfall_mm: Just over 40 inches (1,000 mm) peak; 38.6 inches in six days in Houston
events.economic_damage: $8.5 billion (2001 USD)

events.name: 2007 Jakarta flood
events.geo_source: Jakarta city centre; 80 regions in and around the capital were flooded
events.what_happened: Heavy February rain, upland deforestation and debris-clogged waterways produced a flood that began on 2 February 2007 across Jakarta, West Java and Banten. Wikipedia calls it the worst in three centuries and records a final official death toll of 80. Some 70,000 homes were flooded and about 500,000 people displaced. Losses were reported at Rp 8 trillion; insurance claims were seen at about US$400 million.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 500,000 displaced; 70,000 homes flooded
events.cause_summary: Peak rainy-season rainfall plus clogged canals and settlement on floodplains and riverbanks.
events.notes: 80 is the final official Wikipedia figure.
events.economic_damage: About US$400 million insurance claims (Bernama, cited on Wikipedia); Rp 8 trillion losses also cited

events.name: Tropical Storm Ondoy (Ketsana) floods
events.geo_source: Marikina, the most devastated city (78 deaths; river overbank flooding)
events.what_happened: Tropical Storm Ketsana (local name Ondoy) made landfall on Luzon on 26 September 2009 and produced record rainfall over Metro Manila — 454.9 mm at PAGASA Science Garden in 24 hours. Flash floods reached 20 feet in rural areas and isolated Marikina. An NDCC regional table on Wikipedia lists 671 deaths in the Philippines. The storm later killed 179 in Vietnam. Combined fatalities are given as 921. President Arroyo declared a state of calamity on Luzon.
events.affected_or_evacuated: State of calamity over Metro Manila and 25 Luzon provinces
events.cause_summary: Tropical storm enhanced the southwest monsoon and dumped record 24-hour rain on Metro Manila.
events.notes: 671 is the NDCC regional table on Wikipedia (NCR 448, Region IV-A 160, Region III 56). Lead text also cites 464 Philippine deaths and 921 storm-wide. Using the NDCC table.
events.rainfall_mm: 454.9 mm in 24 hours at PAGASA Science Garden, Quezon City
events.economic_damage: ₱11.16 billion / about $237 million in the Philippines (Wikipedia table)

events.name: 2010 Colombia floods
events.region: Caribbean coast / Magdalena / Canal del Dique
events.geo_source: Cartagena, capital of Bolívar, called the department most seriously hit
events.river_or_basin: Magdalena / Canal del Dique / Sinú / Bogotá
events.river_or_facility: Canal del Dique levees and Magdalena tributaries
events.what_happened: An unusually heavy second-semester wet season, intensified by La Niña and remnants of Hurricane Tomas, produced floods and landslides across about 70 percent of Colombia. Wikipedia records 301 deaths. More than 2.2 million people were left homeless. The Canal del Dique levees failed in Atlántico; the Sinú flooded Montería; Gramalote in Norte de Santander was evacuated after a landslide. President Santos declared a national catastrophe.
events.status: Historical. Reconstruction taxes and World Bank credit followed.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 2.2 million homeless (Wikipedia); 1.5 million also cited earlier
events.cause_summary: Prolonged La Niña wet season plus remnants of Hurricane Tomas; levees and hillside settlements failed.
events.notes: 301 is the Wikipedia infobox figure. An earlier CARE/AFP tally of 174 is also cited in the body.
events.economic_damage: More than $6 billion (Wikipedia infobox)

events.name: 2012 Krymsk flood
events.geo_source: Krymsk, where most victims lived; a 7 m flood wave arrived about 02:00 on 7 July
events.river_or_facility: Krymsk and coastal streams (Neberdzhaevskoe reservoir has no controllable sluices)
events.what_happened: An intense Black Sea storm dropped about 275–280 mm of rain in a few hours over Krasnodar Krai on 6–7 July 2012 — months of typical rainfall overnight. A flood wave about 7 metres high hit sleeping Krymsk around 02:00. Wikipedia records 171 deaths. About 30,000 people were affected and 5,200 homes damaged. Local officials were later convicted of failing to warn residents. Claims that a reservoir sluice was opened were denied; the nearby dam has no controllable gates.
events.status: Historical. 9 July 2012 was a national day of mourning.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Close to 30,000 affected; about 5,200 homes damaged
events.cause_summary: Catastrophic orographic rainfall on the Black Sea coastal ranges; overnight flash flood through Krymsk.

sources.label: BBC: Russia flash floods — 144 killed in Krasnodar region

events.notes: 171 is the EMERCOM/Wikipedia figure. Early BBC reports said 144. Warning was too late for a 02:00 flood.
events.rainfall_mm: 275–280 mm in a few hours
events.economic_damage: Almost 9 billion rubles allocated to restore Krymsk (regional statement on Wikipedia)

events.name: 2013 Argentina floods (La Plata)
events.region: Greater La Plata / Greater Buenos Aires
events.location_label: La Plata, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
events.geo_source: La Plata, where 91 of 101 deaths were reported
events.river_or_basin: Río de la Plata coastal plain / Tolosa streams
events.what_happened: A storm on 1–3 April 2013 dropped 160–190 mm on Buenos Aires and about 400 mm in two hours on La Plata, the provincial capital. Flash floods killed 101 people (91 in Greater La Plata, 10 in Greater Buenos Aires). About 3,000 were evacuated in Greater La Plata. Half the city lost power; the oil refinery caught fire and was shut down. Wikipedia calls it the worst flooding in La Plata's history.
events.status: Historical. Three days of national mourning were declared on 3 April.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 3,000 evacuated in Greater La Plata; 1,200 still evacuated on 4 April
events.cause_summary: Record April cloudburst on a poorly drained city; stormwater works were incomplete.

sources.label: BBC: Argentina floods — dozens dead in La Plata and Buenos Aires

events.notes: 101 is the Wikipedia infobox total. A later La Plata-only official count of 78 is also cited.
events.rainfall_mm: About 400 mm in two hours in La Plata; 160–190 mm in Buenos Aires
events.economic_damage: 530.6 million pesos to shops (about US$104 million) cited on Wikipedia

events.name: 2015 South Carolina floods
events.geo_source: Columbia, where Gills Creek set a record crest and multiple dams failed
events.river_or_basin: Gills Creek / Congaree / coastal South Carolina rivers
events.river_or_facility: Gills Creek and statewide dams (18 breached)
events.what_happened: A stalled frontal low drawing moisture from Hurricane Joaquin produced historic rain over South Carolina on 1–4 October 2015. Some areas saw a 1-in-1,000-year rainfall; 26.88 inches fell near Mount Pleasant. Gills Creek in Columbia rose to 17.08 ft before the gauge failed. Eighteen dams were breached. Wikipedia records at least 19 deaths in South Carolina and 25 in the wider storm complex, with about $2 billion damage.
events.status: Historical. Federal disaster declared for many South Carolina counties.
events.cause_summary: Stalled coastal low plus moisture from Hurricane Joaquin produced multi-day extreme rain.

sources.label: Wikipedia: October 2015 North American storm complex

events.notes: 19 is the South Carolina death toll on Wikipedia. Wider storm-complex total is at least 25. Peak rain 26.88 in near Mount Pleasant.
events.return_period: Up to 1-in-1,000-year rainfall in parts of the Columbia area (Wikipedia)
events.rainfall_mm: 26.88 inches (683 mm) near Mount Pleasant; 11.5 inches in 24 hours at Charleston Airport
events.economic_damage: About $2 billion (Wikipedia)

events.name: 2016 China floods
events.geo_source: Wuhan, which recorded 570 mm in the first week of July and a flooded metro
events.what_happened: Meiyu-front and El Niño rains from mid-June 2016 flooded southern and then much of China. About 32 million people in 26 provinces were affected. Wuhan recorded 570 mm in the first week of July. Wikipedia's infobox gives 449+ deaths (350+ from flooding, 99 from a 23 June Jiangsu tornado). By 28 July, 417 flood deaths and 162 missing were recorded. Aon Benfield put damage at about US$22 billion.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 32 million affected across 26 provinces
events.cause_summary: El Niño–enhanced meiyu rains over the Yangtze–Huai; urban paving and reduced lake storage cited as aggravating factors.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: China — Floods and Landslides Jun 2016

events.rainfall_mm: 570 mm in Wuhan in the first week of July
events.economic_damage: About US$22 billion (Aon Benfield, cited on Wikipedia)

events.name: 2016 Sri Lanka floods (Cyclone Roanu)
events.geo_source: Colombo, where the Kelani River flooded and 26,000 were evacuated overnight
events.what_happened: The precursor depression to Cyclone Roanu stalled over Sri Lanka in mid-May 2016, producing flash floods and landslides. Wikipedia records 105 deaths in Sri Lanka and 99 missing, plus 30 deaths later in Bangladesh, for a storm total of 135. More than 134,000 people were displaced. Landslides at Aranayaka and Bulathkohupitiya in Kegalle District buried villages. Damage in Sri Lanka reached about US$2 billion.
events.status: Historical. Recovery; international assistance from India, Japan, the US and others.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 134,000 displaced in Sri Lanka
events.cause_summary: A Bay of Bengal depression (later Cyclone Roanu) stalled over Sri Lanka, flooding rivers and triggering landslides.
events.notes: 105 is the Sri Lanka death toll on Wikipedia (99 missing). Storm-wide total 135 including 30 in Bangladesh.
events.economic_damage: About US$2 billion in Sri Lanka (Wikipedia)

events.name: Hurricane Florence flooding
events.geo_source: Landfall just south of Wrightsville Beach on 14 September 2018
events.river_or_basin: Cape Fear / Neuse / Pee Dee / Waccamaw
events.river_or_facility: Cape Fear and coastal Carolina rivers
events.what_happened: Hurricane Florence made landfall just south of Wrightsville Beach on 14 September 2018 as a Category 1 storm and then stalled, producing catastrophic freshwater flooding. Elizabethtown recorded 35.93 inches, a North Carolina tropical-cyclone rainfall record; Loris, South Carolina, recorded 23.63 inches, a state tropical-cyclone record. Wilmington was cut off. Wikipedia records 54 deaths (24 direct, 30 indirect) and $24.2 billion damage. The name Florence was retired.
events.cause_summary: A large, slow-moving hurricane stalled over the Carolinas, producing record rain and river flooding.
events.notes: 54 is the Wikipedia total (24 direct, 30 indirect). NC 40, SC 9, VA 3, FL 2.
events.rainfall_mm: 35.93 inches (913 mm) near Elizabethtown, North Carolina
events.economic_damage: $24.2 billion (2018 USD)

events.name: 2020 Jakarta floods
events.geo_source: Jakarta; Ciliwung and Cisadane overflowed after nearly 400 mm overnight
events.what_happened: Overnight New Year rain of nearly 400 mm overflowed the Ciliwung and Cisadane on 1 January 2020. Water reached 30–200 cm in much of the city and 4 m in Cipinang Melayu. Wikipedia records 66 deaths as of 6 January (landslides, hypothermia, drowning, electrocution) and 60,000 displaced. It was the worst flooding in the area since 2007. Halim Perdanakusuma Airport closed briefly. Cloud-seeding aircraft were used to try to break up further rain.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 60,000 displaced; more than 397,000 evacuated at peak (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Record overnight monsoon rain on a low-lying capital with clogged waterways.
events.notes: 66 is the 6 January official figure on Wikipedia/CNN.
events.rainfall_mm: Nearly 400 mm overnight (Wikipedia)

events.name: 2020 Central Vietnam floods
events.region: Central Vietnam (Huế, Quảng Trị, Quảng Bình, Hà Tĩnh, Quảng Nam)
events.geo_source: Huế on the Hương River; A Lưới in the same province recorded 2,290 mm from Linfa
events.river_or_facility: Hương River and central Vietnam rivers
events.what_happened: From early October to mid-November 2020 the northeast monsoon plus a train of storms (Linfa, Nangka, Ofel, Saudel, Molave, Goni, Etau, Vamco) flooded central Vietnam. Hướng Linh, Quảng Trị, recorded 3,245 mm around 20 October. Vietnam issued its first Category IV rain alert. Wikipedia cites 189 deaths and 60 missing in Vietnam as of 15 November, 44 deaths in Cambodia, and nearly ₫35.8 trillion (US$1.57 billion) damage. A 1 December figure of more than 243 dead or missing is also given.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hundreds of thousands evacuated ahead of Molave and Vamco
events.cause_summary: Seasonal monsoon reinforced by a succession of tropical cyclones produced extreme multi-week rain.
events.notes: 189 deaths + 60 missing (15 Nov, Vietnam) is the dated sitrep on Wikipedia. A 1 Dec figure of 243+ dead or missing is also cited. Using 189.
events.rainfall_mm: 3,245 mm at Hướng Linh, Quảng Trị, around 20 October
events.economic_damage: Nearly ₫35.8 trillion / about US$1.57 billion

events.name: 2023 North India floods
events.geo_source: Shimla, capital of the worst-hit state (landslides of mid-August killed at least 57 there)
events.river_or_facility: Yamuna at Delhi; Himalayan hill torrents
events.what_happened: A monsoon surge and western disturbance produced extreme rain across northern India from July 2023, with a further deadly spell in August. Delhi recorded 153 mm on 9 July, its wettest July day in more than 40 years; the Yamuna exceeded a 45-year record (208.08 m). Wikipedia records 422 deaths, at least 100 injured and 38 missing. Himachal Pradesh was worst hit (about 330 dead). About 16,000 people were sheltered in Delhi relief tents.
events.status: Historical. Himachal CM cited about ₹10,000 crore in losses.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 16,000 sheltered in Delhi; 70,000 tourists evacuated from Himachal
events.cause_summary: Monsoon surge plus western disturbance; cloudbursts and landslides in the western Himalaya, river flood on the Yamuna.
events.notes: 422 is the Wikipedia infobox fatality figure. Himachal ~330 of those.
events.rainfall_mm: 153 mm in Delhi on 9 July 2023
events.economic_damage: About ₹10,000 crore in Himachal Pradesh (CM Sukhu, cited on Wikipedia)

events.name: 1607 Bristol Channel floods
events.region: Bristol Channel / Severn Estuary (Devon, Somerset, Gloucestershire, South Wales)
events.geo_source: Cardiff city (Wikipedia coordinates); Wikipedia calls Cardiff the most badly affected town
events.what_happened: Around noon on 30 January 1607 (Gregorian; 20 January 1606/07 Julian) a storm surge flooded the Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary. Low-lying land in Devon, Somerset, Gloucestershire and South Wales was inundated from Laugharne to above Chepstow. Cardiff was the worst-hit town; St Mary's Church foundations were destroyed. Contemporary and later estimates put the death toll at 2,000 or more; about 200 square miles of farmland were destroyed. Sea water reached Glastonbury Tor, 14 miles inland. Modern analysis (Horsburgh and Horritt, 2006) attributes the flood to a high spring tide plus a south-westerly gale, not a tsunami.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 200 square miles (51,800 ha) of farmland destroyed (Wikipedia / RMS 2007 retrospective)
events.cause_summary: High astronomical spring tide (7.86 m at Bristol Channel) combined with a severe south-westerly gale.
events.notes: Deaths 2,000+ estimated on the Wikipedia infobox. Using 2000 as the lower sourced estimate, not a precise count. Date given in Gregorian form used by modern sources.
events.inundation_area: About 200 square miles (52,000 ha) estimated
