events.name: 1872 Baltic Sea flood
events.region: Baltic coast from Denmark to Pomerania (Eckernförde / Lolland / Falster)
events.geo_source: Eckernförde (Wikipedia coordinates); Wikipedia says it was the most heavily damaged German coastal town
events.what_happened: On the night of 12–13 November 1872 a storm tide struck the Baltic coast from Denmark to Pomerania. After a south-westerly gale drove water toward Finland, the wind reversed from the northeast and pushed the piled-up water back onto the Danish–German coast. Peak water was about 3.3 m above sea level. Eckernförde was the worst-hit German town (78 houses destroyed, 138 damaged). Wikipedia records at least 271 deaths on the Baltic coast, 2,850 houses destroyed or badly damaged, and 15,160 people left homeless. On Falster 52 died; on Lolland 28; 32 died on land in Mecklenburg and West Pomerania.
events.status: Historical. The Prerower Strom silted up; Zingst became a peninsula after 1874 dyke work.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 15,160 left homeless; 2,850 houses destroyed or badly damaged (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Baltic storm tide after a wind reversal piled North Sea inflow against the Danish–German coast.
events.notes: 271 is Wikipedia's 'at least' coast-wide total. Highest recorded peak about 3.3 m above NN.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1872 Baltic Sea flood.

events.name: 1878 flood in Miskolc
events.geo_source: Miskolc city (Wikipedia coordinates)
events.what_happened: On 30 August 1878 storms from Transdanubia reached northern Hungary and swelled the Szinva and Pece streams through Miskolc. Water rose by about half a metre per minute; in some parts of the city it was 4–5 metres deep. Bridges, mills and houses were swept away. Wikipedia says the flood destroyed 2,000 buildings and killed almost 300 people, or about 400 if neighbouring areas (including Óhuta, where 73 houses were destroyed) are included. It remains remembered locally as the 'Great Flood' and the deadliest 19th-century flood in Hungary.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 2,000 buildings destroyed in Miskolc (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Intense storms swelled the Szinva and Pece through downtown Miskolc.
events.notes: Deaths left null: Wikipedia gives almost 300 in the city, or about 400 including neighbouring areas. Range stays in notes.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1878 flood in Miskolc.

events.name: Great Vermont Flood of 1927
events.geo_source: Montpelier, the state capital on the Winooski (Wikipedia coordinates)
events.what_happened: After a very wet October that saturated soils, record rain fell across Vermont on 2–4 November 1927 as a coastal low drew moisture from a tropical remnant. The U.S. Geological Survey estimated 53 percent of the state received more than six inches; Somerset recorded 9.86 inches. Rivers flooded statewide. Wikipedia records 85 deaths (84 in Vermont) and more than $50 million damage (1927 USD). The flood destroyed 1,285 bridges. Lieutenant Governor Samuel Hollister Jackson died trying to escape a flooded car. It remains Vermont's worst flood, later compared with Irene 2011 and July 2023.
events.status: Historical. State later assumed a larger role in the statewide road system.
events.cause_summary: Saturated October soils plus 3–4 November orographic rain from a coastal low and tropical remnant.
events.notes: 85 is the Wikipedia infobox total (84 in Vermont). Rain peak 9.86 in at Somerset.
events.rainfall_mm: 9.86 inches (250 mm) at Somerset; 8.71 inches at Northfield (Wikipedia / NOAA)
events.economic_damage: More than $50 million (1927 USD) (Wikipedia)

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: Great Vermont Flood of 1927 (NWS/NOAA cited there).

events.name: 1928 Okeechobee hurricane flood
events.region: Lake Okeechobee / Palm Beach County, Florida
events.geo_source: Belle Glade on the southeast shore of Lake Okeechobee (Wikipedia coordinates); Florida Department of Health compiled 611 deaths in Belle Glade alone
events.what_happened: The Okeechobee hurricane (San Felipe Segundo) made landfall near West Palm Beach on 17 September 1928 as a Category 4. Wind-driven water poured over the small dike at the south end of Lake Okeechobee, flooding hundreds of square miles to depths as great as 20 feet. Towns including Belle Glade, Canal Point, Chosen, Pahokee and South Bay were swept. In 2003 the U.S. death count was revised to at least 2,500. About 75 percent of the dead were migrant farm workers. The storm also killed 1,200 in Guadeloupe and 312 in Puerto Rico; those deaths are not in this Florida pin.
events.status: Historical. Led to the Herbert Hoover Dike around Lake Okeechobee.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Governor Martin estimated 15,000 families homeless in Palm Beach County (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Category 4 landfall drove Lake Okeechobee over a low southern dike.
events.notes: 2,500 is the 2003 NWS revision for the United States ('at least'). Earlier Red Cross figure was 1,836. Storm-wide total including the Caribbean is 4,114+. Using the dated US flood figure for this pin.
events.economic_damage: About $25 million in Florida (1928 USD) (Wikipedia)

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1928 Okeechobee hurricane (NWS 2003 death revision cited there).

events.name: 1936 Northeastern United States flood
events.geo_source: Hartford, where the Connecticut River still holds the 37.6 ft March 1936 record (Wikipedia coordinates)
events.what_happened: A snow-heavy winter followed by two March storm systems produced record floods across the Northeastern United States, the Mid-Atlantic and Ohio. The USGS called it one of the greatest rainfall concentrations on record for the area. The Connecticut River peaked at 37.6 feet in Hartford; the Merrimack set a 68.4-foot record in Lowell. By 21 March about 260,000 people were homeless. Wikipedia cites an estimated 150 to 200 deaths and hundreds of millions of dollars of 1936 damage. The Flood Control Act of 1936 followed.
events.status: Historical. Directly prompted the Flood Control Act of 1936.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 260,000 homeless by 21 March (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Heavy winter snow plus two mid-March rainstorms and ice jams on New England rivers.
events.notes: Deaths left null: Wikipedia gives an estimated range of 150–200. Hartford crest 37.6 ft still stood as of 2015.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1936 Northeastern United States flood (USGS 1936 report cited there).

events.name: Hurricane Camille flooding
events.region: Mississippi Gulf Coast / Nelson County, Virginia
events.geo_source: Bay St. Louis / Waveland landfall (Wikipedia coordinates); 24.6 ft storm surge later measured from debris at Pass Christian
events.river_or_facility: Mississippi coast / Tye and Rockfish rivers in Virginia
events.what_happened: Hurricane Camille made landfall near Waveland, Mississippi, on 18 August 1969 as a Category 5 with a then-record 24.6-foot storm surge at Pass Christian. Wikipedia records at least 343 deaths in the United States (172 in Mississippi, 9 in Louisiana, more than 153 in Virginia, 2 in West Virginia), plus 5 in Cuba, for a storm total above 348. After weakening inland, remnants produced a cloudburst over the Virginia Blue Ridge (27 inches near Massies Mill) that USGS called the worst natural disaster to strike Virginia. About 200,000 people were left homeless from Alabama to Louisiana.
events.status: Historical. Name retired. Contributed to Saffir–Simpson scale and later Disaster Relief Acts.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 200,000 homeless from Alabama to Louisiana; more than 9,000 injured (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Category 5 Gulf landfall surge, then remnant cloudburst over the Virginia Blue Ridge.
events.notes: 343 is the US death toll on Wikipedia (288 direct plus 55 indirect identified in a 2016 death-certificate study). Storm-wide total >348 including 5 in Cuba. Virginia flood deaths >153 are included in the 343.
events.rainfall_mm: 27 inches (690 mm) near Massies Mill, Virginia (Wikipedia / USGS)
events.economic_damage: At least $1.42 billion in the United States (1969 USD) (Wikipedia)

events.name: 1999 Vietnamese floods
events.region: Central Vietnam (Thừa Thiên Huế / Quảng Nam / Quảng Trị)
events.geo_source: Huế (Wikipedia coordinates); 324 of 622 fatalities were in Thừa Thiên Huế province
events.what_happened: Tropical Storm Eve (Storm No. 9) and later cold-surge rains produced Vietnam's worst flooding in 40 years from 18 October to 7 November 1999. Streets in Huế were under up to three metres of water; the Perfume and Bồ rivers rose to 8–9 m. As of 14 November the Government of Vietnam reported 622 fatalities, 70 missing, more than 470,000 households affected, 41,846 homes destroyed and over 1 million people needing relief. Damage was 3.3 trillion đồng (US$237 million). A second episode in early December added further deaths (132 as of 8 December) that are not added into the 622 pin.
events.status: Historical. December rains caused a second flood wave while relief was underway.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 1 million needing relief; 15,000 evacuated in Thừa Thiên Huế as of 9 November (Wikipedia / CCFSC)
events.cause_summary: Tropical Storm Eve plus a November cold surge over central Vietnam river basins.
events.notes: 622 fatalities and 70 missing are the Government of Vietnam figures as of 14 November 1999, cited on Wikipedia. December flood deaths (132 as of 8 Dec) are a later episode and not added here.
events.economic_damage: US$237 million / 3.3 trillion đồng (Wikipedia)

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1999 Vietnamese floods (OCHA/CCFSC figures cited there).

events.name: 2003 Santa Fe flood
events.geo_source: Santa Fe city (Wikipedia coordinates)
events.what_happened: After several days of heavy rain the Salado River rose almost two metres in three hours and on 28 April 2003 overflowed into Santa Fe, the provincial capital. Wikipedia records about 100,000 people evacuated, 154 deaths, and 28,000 houses damaged or destroyed. More than 30,000 km² of farmland were lost. A dyke was blown to let water out of the city. A UN assessment requested by the governor put damage at about US$1 billion, about 12 percent of the province's GDP. The provincial government was criticised for ignoring warnings.

events.affected_or_evacuated: About 100,000 evacuated (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Rapid rise of the Salado after multi-day rain; flood defences on that river were incomplete.
events.notes: 154 deaths and 100,000 evacuated are the figures on the Wikipedia article. UN damage about US$1 billion (Newsfront, 23 July 2003, cited there).
events.inundation_area: Over 30,000 km² of farmland destroyed (Wikipedia)

events.name: 2010 Var floods
events.geo_source: Draguignan (Wikipedia coordinates); 12 of 27 deaths were there
events.what_happened: Heavy rain on the evening of 15 June 2010 caused flash and river floods in the Var, the worst in the region since 1827. More than 400 mm fell in less than 24 hours. Wikipedia's infobox gives 27 deaths (12 in Draguignan, 4 in Trans-en-Provence, 3 at La Motte, 2 each in Roquebrune-sur-Argens and Saint-Aygulf, one each in Montauroux and Le Luc). Over 1,000 people were evacuated and 175,000 houses lost electricity. A TGV was stranded near Le Luc. Prime Minister Fillon announced a natural-catastrophe declaration for nine cantons.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 1,000 evacuated from houses; 1,500 rescued in Fréjus (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: More than 400 mm in under 24 hours on the Argens basin.
events.notes: 27 is the Wikipedia infobox total, with a municipal breakdown. Early BBC reports said at least 25.

events.name: 2012 Nigeria floods
events.geo_source: Lokoja at the Niger–Benue confluence (Wikipedia coordinates); Kogi was the worst-affected state
events.what_happened: Seasonal rains from early July 2012, worsened in September by a release from Cameroon's Lagdo Reservoir, produced what NEMA called Nigeria's worst floods in 40 years. Thirty of 36 states were affected. Reuters reported 363 deaths and more than 2.1 million displaced as of 5 November 2012. About seven million people were affected. Kogi State was worst hit (623,900 displaced; 152,575 hectares of farmland destroyed). President Jonathan called it a national disaster. NEMA later put damages and losses at ₦2.6 trillion.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 2.1 million displaced; about 7 million affected (Reuters / NEMA, cited on Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Seasonal rains plus Lagdo Reservoir releases on the Benue; poor drainage in cities.
events.notes: 363 deaths and 2.1 million displaced are the Reuters/NEMA figures as of 5 November 2012. A September Lagdo release killed 30 in Benue; those deaths are inside the 363.

events.name: 2013 Jakarta flood
events.geo_source: Jakarta city centre (same Wikipedia-style pin as flood-jakarta-2007 and flood-jakarta-2020)
events.what_happened: Heavy rain and clogged waterways flooded Jakarta from 15 January 2013. A 30-metre section of the West Flood Canal dike in Menteng collapsed and flooded nearby districts. Wikipedia records 41 deaths. About 20,000 people were evacuated on 17 January. Commuter trains and buses were suspended; flooding reached the presidential palace and postponed a meeting with Argentina's president. Seasonal flooding also hit other islands; those extra deaths are not added here.

ONEMI figures cited on Wikipedia: more than 27,413 people affected, 5,585 in shelters, 26 dead and 101 officially missing (later 125 missing in one ONEMI balance), and more than 28,000 houses damaged. President Bachelet declared a constitutional state of catastrophe for Atacama and later Antofagasta.

events.what_happened: Unusually heavy monsoon rain from 16 July 2015, worsened by Cyclone Komen in late July, flooded 12 of Myanmar's 14 states and regions. The government declared a state of emergency on 30 July in Magway, Sagaing, Chin and Rakhine. Wikipedia records at least 103 deaths and up to 1 million people affected, most casualties from the Irrawaddy Delta. The Ministry of Agriculture reported more than 1.29 million acres inundated. OCHA recorded 15,239 houses destroyed.

More than 14.9 million people in 10-plus provinces were affected; 18,100 houses were destroyed. The Xiangjiang at Changsha stood at 39.21 m on 2 July, 3.21 m above warning level. events.what_happened: Typhoon Hagibis (Reiwa 1 East Japan Typhoon) made landfall on the Izu Peninsula on 12 October 2019 and caused severe flooding across eastern Japan. Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency, cited on Wikipedia, confirmed 139 dead (118 direct, 21 post-disaster) and 3 missing, with 388 injured. More than 270,000 households lost power. Ten Hokuriku Shinkansen trains in Nagano were written off after the yard flooded. National damage was ¥1.88 trillion (US$17.3 billion). It was Japan's deadliest typhoon since Fran in 1976.

events.what_happened: Continuous 2020 rains, much of them over the Ethiopian highlands, drove the Blue Nile in Sudan to more than 17 metres — the highest in nearly a century according to the Ministry of Irrigation. Floods hit 17 of 18 states, destroyed more than 100,000 homes and affected more than 3 million people. The Security and Defense Council declared a three-month state of emergency. FAO said 2.2 million hectares of cropland were flooded. A UNDP Rapid PDNRA put damage at LS 243.4 billion (US$4.43 billion). Wikipedia's infobox gives about 100–500 deaths.
events.status: Historical. Some farmlands were still flooded as of April 2023 per a cited ABC report.

events.what_happened: On 15 February 2022 Petrópolis received 258 mm of rain in three hours — more than the prior 30 days and the city's largest storm since records began in 1932 (Cemaden). Floods and mudslides destroyed hillside neighbourhoods. As of 28 February Wikipedia records 231 dead and 5 missing, exceeding the 1988 event (171 dead). Cemaden had issued a moderate landslide-risk alert two days earlier. Reconstruction costs exceeded R$1 billion.

events.what_happened: Sudan's 2022 rainy season from May flooded 16 of 18 states. The Nile at Khartoum reached 16.42 m on 23 August (critical 16 m; flood 16.5 m), described as a 70-year high. Africanews on 15 September 2022, cited on Wikipedia, reported 134 deaths and 16,900 homes destroyed. OCHA later put people affected above 314,500, exceeding 2021. IOM recorded 97,227 newly displaced by 20 October, many already IDPs. Worst-hit states included South Darfur, Gedaref, Central Darfur, White Nile and Kassala.

events.name: 2023 Slovenia floods
events.geo_source: Ljubljana (Wikipedia coordinates); the Sava flooded in the capital on 4 August
events.river_or_basin: Sava / Savinja / Sora / Gradaščica / Drava / Mur

The Sava, Savinja, Sora and other rivers flooded Upper Carniola, Carinthia and Styria. Wikipedia records at least 7 deaths and at least €7 billion damage. Highways and rail lines closed; about 16,000 lost power. Neighbouring Austrian Carinthia and Croatian Drava/Mura reaches also flooded. ARSO issued a red warning.

events.name: Great Vermont Flood of July 2023
events.region: Vermont / Hudson Valley / Northeastern United States
events.geo_source: Montpelier (Wikipedia coordinates); downtown was flooded and the city issued a travel ban
events.what_happened: Slow-moving thunderstorms on already-saturated ground produced the event the National Weather Service in Burlington named the Great Vermont Flood of 10–11 July 2023. Downtown Montpelier flooded; I-89 closed. Calais recorded 9.20 inches. Wikipedia records 11 fatalities across several states and at least $2.2 billion damage. Two deaths were in Vermont (Barre and the Appalachian Trail near Stockbridge). Officials compared Vermont damage to worse than Irene. Further rounds hit the Northeast through 29 July, including a 15 July flash flood in Upper Makefield, Pennsylvania, that killed 7.

events.what_happened: On 19 November 1824 (7 November Old Style) a Baltic storm surge drove the Neva to 421 cm above datum at 14:00, the highest flood on the city's gauge record. Wikipedia's event stub and the Floods in Saint Petersburg article call it the deadliest flood in the history of Russia and St. Petersburg and the flood that inspired Pushkin's The Bronze Horseman. events.name: 1999 Pentecost flood
events.geo_source: Sonthofen (Wikipedia coordinates); event page says Iller causeways failed and flooded Sonthofen
events.what_happened: The Pfingsthochwasser of late May 1999 was a named 100-year flood on already high Alpine meltwater. Wikipedia says causeways on the Iller failed, flooding Sonthofen, parts of Augsburg and Neustadt; Hindelang-Hinterstein reached a 250-year peak. The Rhine flood hit Lake Constance at Hard and Bregenz; Pflach in the Lechtal was flooded. The Sylvenstein reservoir lowered the Isar through Munich. A BBC report cited on the page recorded two deaths in Bavaria.

Romania's damage was put at more than 5 billion lei (€1.5 billion), with 31 districts and over 500 villages affected.

events.name: 2018 European floods
events.geo_source: Carcassonne (Wikipedia coordinates); event page says all roads were inaccessible there during the 15 October Aude floods
events.what_happened: From 4 October into early November 2018, Mediterranean storms flooded Calabria, Mallorca, southwest France, Sardinia, parts of Portugal and the United Kingdom, then Italy again. Wikipedia records 69 deaths: 36 Italy, 16 France, 13 Spain, 2 United Kingdom, 2 Portugal. On 15 October at least 14 people died in the Aude; a bridge collapsed at Villegailhenc and Carcassonne's roads were cut. Aude damage was about €200 million. Mallorca's 9 October flood killed 13, including six foreign tourists. Late-October Italian storms left Venice under a 156 cm acqua alta.

events.what_happened: Early 2016 seasonal rains produced deadly floods across Ethiopia after the 2015 El Niño drought. events.name: June 2025 South Africa floods
events.geo_source: Mthatha (Wikipedia coordinates); event page centres the 3–4 m floodwaters and the school-bus deaths there
events.what_happened: A cold front from 10 June 2025 brought torrential rain, wind and snow. Rivers around Mthatha burst their banks with floodwaters 3–4 metres deep; homes, vehicles and a high-school bus were swept away. Wikipedia tracks the toll from 57 on 12 June to 103 on 4 July (Eastern Cape Provincial Government: 32 school-going children among 40 children and 63 adults). A national disaster was declared on 18 June. By 4 July, 4,724 people were homeless and 2,145 dwellings partly damaged. Officials dismissed a rumour that Mthatha Dam sluices had been opened; the dam has no sluice gates.

events.name: Great Flood of 1951
events.region: Eastern Kansas / Missouri (Kansas / Neosho / Marais des Cygnes)

events.what_happened: Mid-July 1951 rains raised the Kansas, Neosho, Marais des Cygnes and Verdigris. Wikipedia records 17 deaths, 518,000 people displaced, and more than $935 million damage (about $11.6 billion in 2025 dollars). Eight to 16 inches fell between 9 and 13 July; 13 July was the peak. Manhattan's downtown was under 8 feet; Topeka evacuated about 24,000; Kansas City levees overtopped in Argentine and Armourdale and wrecked the stockyards. On 13 July about 1,074,000 acres in Kansas and 926,000 acres in Missouri were flooded. President Truman called it one of the worst water disasters the country had suffered.

events.economic_damage: More than $935 million then / about $11.6 billion in 2025 dollars (Wikipedia)

events.name: All Saints' Flood (1170)
events.geo_source: Amsterdam city centroid; event page says the flood marked the beginning of Amsterdam and pushed seawater to the walls of Utrecht
events.river_or_facility: North Sea coastal barriers / Creil Woods
events.what_happened: A storm surge on the night of 1–2 November 1170 flooded large parts of the northern Netherlands. The Annales Egmundenses, the only contemporary chronicle of the Kennemerland inundation, say livestock drowned and people climbed onto the beams of their houses; ships from Diemen rescued stranded people, and seawater reached the walls of Utrecht. The flood created the islands of Wieringen and Texel, swept away the Creil Woods peat forest between Stavoren and Enkhuizen, and opened the freshwater Almere to the North Sea — the start of the Zuiderzee. It rendered Rotta (predecessor of Rotterdam) uninhabitable and, by dropping the Almere level, dried the mouth of the Amstel enough for Amsterdam later to emerge.
events.status: Historical. Landscape-forming North Sea surge; no sourced death count on the event page.
events.cause_summary: All Saints' Day North Sea storm surge that breached peat barriers and opened the Almere to the sea.
events.notes: Deaths unknown: the dedicated English Wikipedia event page gives no figure. A Europe flood list cites 'probably many thousands'; that estimate is unsourced on the event page and is left in this note only.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: All Saints' Flood (1170).

events.name: First St. Marcellus's flood (1219)
events.geo_source: Groningen, a principal flooded city in the Dutch sector (same pin as Christmas flood of 1717); Dutch Wikipedia names Noord-Nederland and the Zuiderzee area
events.what_happened: On 16 January 1219, the feast of St. Marcellus, a North Sea storm surge flooded large parts of the northern Netherlands and the Zuiderzee region, as the earlier All Saints (1170), St. Nicholas (1196) and 1214 surges had done. Dutch Wikipedia says the water barely fell with the ebb and the next tide then finished off the remaining dikes. Together with four great storm floods in fifty years this helped open two inland seas, the Zuiderzee and the Wadden Sea. Abbot Emo of Wittewierum left the first surviving eyewitness account of a North Sea storm surge.
events.status: Historical. First St. Marcellus flood; the 1362 Grote Mandrenke is already in the archive.
events.cause_summary: St. Marcellus's Day North Sea storm surge; water stayed high through the ebb so the next tide completed the dike breaches.
events.notes: Dutch Wikipedia infobox lists 36,000 dead. German chronicles cited on secondary pages give ~36,000 (Saxon World Chronicle) or 50,000 (Colmar Annals) and call the figures unreliable. Deaths left null; range 36,000–50,000 stays in this note.

events.name: St. Martin's flood (Sint-Maartensvloed 1686)
events.geo_source: Groningen (Wikipedia coordinates used on Christmas flood of 1717); Dutch Wikipedia says the city lay on the sea after the dikes failed and names Pieterburen and Uithuizen as fully submerged
events.what_happened: On the night of 12–13 November 1686, just after St. Martin's Day, a northwesterly storm surge struck the Dutch province of Groningen and neighbouring East Frisia. Dutch Wikipedia records that every dike along the Ems and the Dollart was swept away; all of North Groningen and the Oldambt flooded; Pieterburen and Uithuizen disappeared under water; and Groningen itself lay on the sea. The same page gives 1,558 people, 1,387 horses and 7,861 cattle drowned, 631 houses washed away and 616 damaged. The Mariakerk in Uithuizermeeden was heavily damaged despite standing on a terp.
events.cause_summary: Northwesterly North Sea storm on the night after St. Martin's Day that destroyed the Ems and Dollart dikes.
events.notes: 1,558 is the Dutch Wikipedia infobox and body figure, matching the contemporary Groningen ministers' damage register tradition.

events.name: 1921 Pueblo flood
events.geo_source: Pueblo, Colorado (Wikipedia coordinates 38.2544°N, 104.6091°W); USGS WSP 487 and Colorado Encyclopedia name Pueblo as the worst-hit city
events.what_happened: Cloudbursts on 3–5 June 1921 sent the Arkansas River and Fountain Creek through Pueblo, Colorado. USGS Water-Supply Paper 487 says the official list of bodies recovered in Pueblo was 78, with more washed downstream and never recovered, and that more than 57,000 acres were inundated below the city. The Colorado Encyclopedia calls it the worst flood in Pueblo's history: 300 square miles inundated, more than 500 houses carried away, and about $25 million damage. Telephone lines failed, so Pueblo was cut off from the rest of the state.
events.cause_summary: Cloudbursts over the Arkansas–Fountain confluence after two days of intense local rain.

events.name: 1935 Republican River flood
events.region: Republican River basin, Colorado / Nebraska / Kansas
events.geo_source: McCook, Nebraska (Wikipedia coordinates); NWS Topeka says the river rose nearly ten feet in twelve minutes at McCook
events.what_happened: On 30–31 May 1935, in the Dust Bowl, 20–24 inches of rain fell at the head of the Arikaree and Republican rivers. NWS Topeka records that at McCook the river rose nearly ten feet in twelve minutes; at Concordia, Kansas, USGS measured 207,000 cubic feet per second against a typical 1,260 cfs, and the channel through town changed. The river ran one to four miles wide. NWS estimates 110–113 dead, more than 20,000 cattle lost and over 270,000 acres of farmland destroyed. Wikipedia's Republican River article calls it Nebraska's deadliest flood and cites 113 killed, 74,500 acres inundated, 341 miles of highway and 307 bridges destroyed.

events.name: 1949 Eastern Guatemalan floods
events.region: Southern and eastern Guatemala / Lakes Atitlán and Amatitlán

events.river_or_facility: Lakes Atitlán and Amatitlán / Coyolate River
events.what_happened: Seventy-two hours of torrential rain on 14–16 October 1949, in a wet spell that ran from 28 September to 18 October, made Lakes Atitlán and Amatitlán spill into surrounding towns and burst rivers and mountain streams. Wikipedia's dedicated event page says estimates of the death toll ranged from 1,000 to 40,000, with reliable estimates suggesting 4,000, and monetary losses of $15–40 million (1949 USD). More than fifty bridges and 1,200 miles of highways were destroyed; San Juan Osculcalco was reported destroyed by landslides; Tzununa on Lake Atitlán had to relocate housing. Escuintla, San Marcos, Quezaltenango, Jalapa, Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Sacatepéquez were among the worst-hit towns.

events.cause_summary: Seventy-two hours of torrential rain overflowing Lakes Atitlán and Amatitlán and bursting rivers and mountain streams.
events.notes: 4,000 is the Wikipedia infobox figure ('reliable estimates'). Contemporary government figure was about 1,000; some modern writing cites up to 40,000. U.S. Ambassador Patterson told Truman the press had exaggerated the loss of life. Range stays in this note.
events.economic_damage: $15–40 million (1949 USD; Wikipedia infobox)

events.name: Hurricane Hazel flooding in Toronto
events.geo_source: Toronto city centroid; event page names the Humber River, Raymore Drive, Woodbridge, Long Branch and Holland Marsh
events.river_or_basin: Humber River / Etobicoke Creek / Holland Marsh
events.what_happened: After weeks of saturating autumn rain, the extratropical remnants of Hurricane Hazel stalled over Toronto on 15–16 October 1954 and dropped up to 214 mm at Snelgrove. Rivers and creeks rose 6–8 m. The Humber River flash flood swept away 366 m of Raymore Drive and 14 homes, killing 35 of the 81 Canadian dead; Woodbridge had nine dead; Etobicoke Creek at Long Branch killed seven when houses were swept into Lake Ontario. Over 50 bridges and many roads and railways were destroyed. Wikipedia and the Canadian Hurricane Centre give 81 Canadian deaths — still Canada's deadliest natural disaster — and more than 4,000 families left homeless.
events.status: Historical. Canadian inland flood from Hazel; U.S. landfall and Haiti deaths are not copied onto this row.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 4,000 families left homeless (Wikipedia / Canadian Hurricane Centre)
events.cause_summary: Extratropical Hazel stalled over already-saturated southern Ontario and produced a Humber River flash flood.

sources.label: Canadian Hurricane Centre: Hurricane Hazel — Impacts

events.name: 1955 Connecticut floods
events.region: Connecticut river valleys (Naugatuck, Farmington, Quinebaug, Mad, Still)
events.geo_source: Waterbury, Connecticut (Wikipedia coordinates); event page names Waterbury among the towns that suffered the most and says water there reached an estimated 35 feet
events.what_happened: Back-to-back rains from Hurricanes Connie (4–6 in on 13 August) and Diane (another 13–20 in over two days) saturated Connecticut and overflowed the Mad and Still Rivers in Winsted, the Naugatuck, Farmington and Quinebaug. Wikipedia's dedicated event page says 87 people died and damage exceeded $200 million (1955 USD). In Waterbury the water reached an estimated 35 feet and up to 500 people were lifted out by helicopter. President Eisenhower declared Connecticut a major disaster area at noon on 20 August. The state recovery report listed 668 dwellings destroyed and more than 200 New England dams damaged or destroyed.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hundreds rescued by helicopter in the Waterbury area alone (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Successive rains from Hurricanes Connie and Diane on already-soaked New England river valleys.
events.notes: 87 is the Wikipedia infobox and body figure from the Connecticut Flood Recovery Committee / Hartford Courant accounting, including heart-attack deaths during rescue.
events.rainfall_mm: Connie 4–6 in on 13 August; Diane 13–20 in over two days (Wikipedia / NOAA)
events.economic_damage: More than $200 million in 1955 USD (Wikipedia infobox / state recovery report)

events.name: 1982–83 Peru El Niño floods
events.region: Northern coastal departments of Piura and Tumbes
events.geo_source: Piura (same Wikipedia coordinates already used for the 2017 Peru coastal El Niño floods); UPI names Piura and Tumbes and files from Chulucanas
events.what_happened: The 1982–83 El Niño reversed the usual cool Humboldt current and dropped unprecedented rain on Peru's northern coastal desert. A 28 June 1983 UPI dispatch from Chulucanas said 13 feet of rain fell in less than six months on Piura and Tumbes after seven years of drought, flooding farmland, dissolving adobe roads and homes, and killing 230 people. Damage already exceeded $700 million and about 300,000 people were homeless; the government said the twin northern floods and southern drought had devastated 30 percent of the nation's settled land. Academic papers describe localized storms above 100 mm/day focused near Chulucanas.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 300,000 homeless (UPI, 28 June 1983)
events.cause_summary: 1982–83 El Niño rains on the northern Peruvian desert after a multi-year drought.

sources.label: UPI: 230 die in six months of rain (28 June 1983)

events.notes: 230 is the UPI 28 June 1983 Peru flood death figure for Piura and Tumbes. Global El Niño death estimates of 1,300–2,000 (WHOI) are worldwide and are not copied onto this row.
events.rainfall_mm: 13 feet (~4 m) in less than six months on Piura and Tumbes (UPI, 28 June 1983)
events.economic_damage: More than $700 million in Peru as of June 1983 (UPI)

changelog.change: Added from UPI 28 June 1983 archive and Wikipedia: 1982–83 El Niño event.

events.name: 1987 Bangladesh flood
events.region: Western Brahmaputra / Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence / north of Khulna
events.geo_source: Dhaka (Wikipedia coordinates already used for the 1974/1988/1998 Bangladesh floods); Floods in Bangladesh names the western Brahmaputra, the Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence and areas north of Khulna
events.what_happened: Catastrophic monsoon floods through July and August 1987 inundated 57,300–57,491 km² (about 39–40 percent of Bangladesh), a 30–70 year event on the Floods in Bangladesh page. The worst-hit ground was west of the Brahmaputra, below the Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence, and north of Khulna. The same page's historic-flood table lists 1,657 deaths and 57,491 km² flooded. A companion damage table puts crop losses at 1.5 million tons and financial loss at 35,000 million taka. The Geographical Journal paper by Brammer (1990) is the cited background source for the 1987 and 1988 events.
events.cause_summary: July–August monsoon over the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna basin; 30–70 year flood.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Floods in Bangladesh (1987 section and historic table)
Brammer 1990, The Geographical Journal (cited on that page)

events.notes: 1,657 is the death figure in the Floods in Bangladesh historic table (Okayama University compilation cited there). No dedicated English Wikipedia event article; the named 1987 section plus the table are the source.
events.return_period: Once in 30–70 years (Floods in Bangladesh / Brammer 1990)
events.inundation_area: 57,300–57,491 km² / about 39–40% of the country (Floods in Bangladesh)
events.economic_damage: 35,000 million taka total financial loss (Floods in Bangladesh damage table)

events.name: 1994 Piedmont / Tanaro flood
events.geo_source: Asti (Wikipedia coordinates 44.90000°N, 8.20694°E); Italian Wikipedia event page photographs and text centre on Asti and names Alessandria (14 dead, ~50% of the city flooded)
events.what_happened: On 4–6 November 1994 torrential rain over southern Piedmont and Liguria sent the Po, Tanaro and tributaries (especially the Belbo) over their banks. Italian Wikipedia's dedicated page records 69 dead, 500 injured and 2,226 displaced in Cuneo, Turin, Asti and Alessandria. Two-day rain peaked at 293.8 mm at Levice (CN); 24-hour totals exceeded 200 mm across the Tanaro, Bormida and Belbo basins. The Tanaro flood wave formed above Ormea on 5 November and reached the Po early on the 7th, with 3,400 m³/s at Farigliano, 4,000–4,200 m³/s at Alba, Asti and Alessandria, and nearly 5,000 m³/s at Montecastello. Ceva, Alba and Asti were about one-third flooded; Alessandria almost half, with 14 dead there.
events.status: Historical. First large emergency for Italy's National Civil Protection Service.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 2,226 displaced (it.wikipedia infobox); Protezione Civile page cites about 5,500 evacuated
events.cause_summary: Three-phase November rainstorm over the Tanaro, Belbo, Bormida and upper Po, with 200–300 mm in 24–48 hours.

sources.label: Dipartimento della Protezione Civile: L'alluvione del Piemonte

events.notes: 69 is the Italian Wikipedia infobox. Protezione Civile's memorial page says 68 victims. Using the dedicated event-page figure; 68 stays in this note.
events.peak_discharge: Nearly 5,000 m³/s on the Tanaro at Montecastello; 3,400 m³/s at Farigliano (it.wikipedia)
events.rainfall_mm: Maximum 264.6 mm in 1 day and 293.8 mm in 2 days at Levice (CN) (it.wikipedia / Luino 1999)

changelog.change: Added from Italian Wikipedia: Alluvione del Tanaro del 1994 and Protezione Civile.

events.name: 2001 Bab El Oued floods
events.geo_source: Bab El Oued (Wikipedia coordinates 36.7907°N, 3.0497°E); OCHA names Bab-El-Oued and Oued Koriche as the worst-hit communes
events.river_or_facility: Oued Koriche / Bab El Oued collectors
events.what_happened: From the evening of 9 November 2001, torrential rain and wind hit northern and western Algeria. In Algiers the Oued Koriche produced a flash flood and mudflow through the hillside communes of Bab El Oued and Oued Koriche. OCHA Situation Report No. 7 (26 November 2001) gave the latest provisional official toll as 751 killed, 700 of them in Algiers, with 170 still missing and 10,000 families (40,000–50,000 people) affected. Seven Algiers communes were seriously hit, four partially. French Wikipedia's Bab El Oued page says torrents of mud engulfed housing and the Place du marché Triolet, killing more than 700 in about three hours. USAID later put damage at more than $300 million.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Up to 10,000 families / 40,000–50,000 people (OCHA sitrep 7, 26 Nov 2001)
events.cause_summary: About 200 mm in 24 hours over the steep, densely built Oued Koriche catchment above Bab El Oued.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Algeria floods OCHA Situation Report No. 7 (26 Nov 2001)

events.notes: 751 is the Algerian authorities' provisional toll in OCHA sitrep 7 (26 November 2001), of which 700 in Algiers. Academic papers later cite 781 dead and 115 missing, or 750 dead and 120 missing. Later unofficial figures stay in this note.
events.return_period: Described as the Oued Koriche hundred-year flood (Persée / PNUD-FEM 2002)
events.rainfall_mm: On the order of 200–214 mm in 24 hours over Algiers (Persée / weather services cited in academic papers)
events.economic_damage: More than $300 million (GOA / USAID OFDA fact sheet FY2002)

events.name: 2006 Dire Dawa flood
events.geo_source: Dire Dawa (Wikipedia coordinates 9.600°N, 41.867°E); OCHA sitreps name the Dechatu River through the city centre
events.what_happened: On the night of 5–6 August 2006 very heavy rain sent the usually dry Dechatu River through the centre of Dire Dawa, spreading up to 200 m from either bank and sweeping homes, trees and concrete fences. A ReliefWeb Horn of Africa overview (citing figures as of 21 August) said the Dire Dawa flood had left at least 254 people dead with 244 still officially missing; OCHA sitrep 1 had first reported about 200 dead and 300 missing. UNICEF/OCHA Focus on Ethiopia (August 2006) gave 256 dead and 244 missing and said the homes of over 9,000 people were destroyed. The same seasonal floods later killed hundreds more on the Omo and elsewhere; those deaths are not copied onto this row.
events.status: Historical. Named Dire Dawa flash flood, distinct from the wider 2006 Ethiopian season (2016 Ethiopian flood is already in the archive).
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 9,000 displaced in Dire Dawa town plus 7,500 around the city (OCHA/UN appeal figures cited on ReliefWeb)
events.cause_summary: Night-time flash flood on the Dechatu after very heavy rain over a deforested catchment with houses built too close to the channel.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Regional overview of flooding in the Horn of Africa (Dire Dawa 254 dead as of 21 Aug 2006)
ReliefWeb: Ethiopia Dire Dawa Floods — OCHA Situation Report No. 2

events.notes: 254 is the confirmed Dire Dawa toll as of 21 August 2006 on the ReliefWeb Horn overview. Focus on Ethiopia (Aug 2006) cites 256 dead. Wider 2006 Ethiopia season deaths (639 nationwide as of 27 August in that overview) are not used here.

changelog.change: Added from ReliefWeb OCHA Dire Dawa sitreps and Horn of Africa flood overview (Aug 2006).

events.name: 2007 South Asian floods
events.geo_source: Patna city centroid; Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were the hardest-hit Indian states on the dedicated event page (same pin style as flood-south-asia-2017)
events.what_happened: From 3 July to 15 August 2007 monsoon floods struck India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan. Wikipedia's dedicated event page, citing Indian and Bangladeshi governments, puts the death toll in excess of 2,000, with about 20 million affected by 3 August and 30 million in India, Bangladesh and Nepal by 10 August. A USAID/OFDA regional fact sheet compiled later official tallies: India 2,253 dead and 43 million affected (Government of India, 28 August); Bangladesh 563 dead and 10.7 million affected (IFRC, 4 September); Nepal 146 dead (OCHA, 21 August); Pakistan 420 dead (OCHA, 27 August). In Bangladesh the Padma and Brahmaputra flooded; the Dhaka highway was cut; by 15 August about five million people were still displaced.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 43 million affected in India (GOI 28 Aug 2007); ~30 million in India, Bangladesh and Nepal by 10 August (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Exceptionally heavy South Asian monsoon from early July 2007 on the Ganges–Brahmaputra system.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: South Asia Regional Floods Fact Sheet #2 FY2007 (USAID/OFDA)

events.notes: 2,253 is the Government of India figure as of 28 August 2007 (USAID/ReliefWeb Fact Sheet #2). Wikipedia infobox says 2,000+ regional. Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan sitrep totals are not added onto this India-pinned row.
events.economic_damage: More than $2 billion in India (GOI / USAID fact sheet); Bangladesh agriculture about $294 million (DAE / IFRC)

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 2007 South Asian floods and USAID/OFDA Fact Sheet #2 FY2007.

events.name: 2009 European floods
events.region: Czech Republic / Austria / Poland / Slovakia / Hungary / Romania
events.geo_source: Nový Jičín city centroid; the event page describes 24 June flash floods on the Jičínka (5.5 m, 2 m above the 1997 flood) with multiple deaths in that district
events.what_happened: June 2009 rain from a slow-moving upper low flooded the Oder, Vistula, Elbe and Danube basins in the Czech Republic, Austria, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Germany, Romania, Serbia and Turkey. Wikipedia's infobox lists 33 fatalities. In the Czech Republic persistent rain from 22 June and a 24 June two-hour flash flood (up to 80 L/m²) on the Jičínka and Zrzávka killed people in Nový Jičín district; the page later says fourteen people died in the Czech Republic. Austria had its wettest June on record in the north (Lunz am See 207 mm/48 h; St. Pölten 311 mm in June). Turkey's 9 September Istanbul flash flood, treated as a further storm on the same page, killed 20.
events.status: Historical. Named Central European June 2009 floods; a Czech complement to 1997/2002/2013 already on file.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands of firefighters deployed in Austria; 50 families evacuated in Kraków (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Quasi-stationary June upper low (Quinton) over the Alps, Balkans and Black Sea, then local thunderstorms on saturated ground.
events.notes: 33 is the English Wikipedia infobox total for the dedicated 2009 European floods page. The lead cites at least 12 dead in the Czech Republic and one in Poland; the Czech section later says 14. The same page's 'Further storms' section includes the 9 September 2009 Istanbul flash flood (20 dead), which is not the June Central Europe wave. Using the page infobox; composition stays in this note.
events.rainfall_mm: Lunz am See 207 mm in 48 h; Nový Jičín area up to 80 L/m² in two hours on 24 June (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: First Czech estimates 5–6 billion Kč (~€230 million); Lower Austria claims about €60 million (Wikipedia)

events.name: 2025 Yemen floods
events.geo_source: Sana'a city centroid; ReliefWeb disaster page covers a nationwide season across 19–20 governorates
events.what_happened: Yemen's second rainy season produced widespread flash floods from 1 August 2025. OCHA's mid-September sitrep recorded about 50,600 households (around 354,400 people) affected in 125 districts in 19 governorates, with 62 deaths and 95 injuries, mainly from drowning, lightning and falling debris. ECHO's 30 September Daily Flash, citing UN OCHA as of 29 September, raised the tally to 82 dead, 100 injured and nearly 455,500 people affected across 156 districts in 20 governorates. IDP sites were among the worst hit. April–July 2025 rains (20 deaths) were a separate earlier spell.
events.status: Season closed; recovery ongoing in a pre-existing humanitarian crisis.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Nearly 455,500 people across 156 districts in 20 governorates as of 29 September 2025 (UN OCHA via ECHO Daily Flash 30 September)
events.cause_summary: Second-season (July–September) rains and flash floods across Yemen, hitting IDP sites especially hard.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Yemen Key Message Update, September 2025 (FEWS NET)
ReliefWeb: ECHO Daily Flash 30 September 2025 (OCHA 82 dead)

events.notes: 82 deaths and 100 injured are the 29 September 2025 UN OCHA figures as cited by ECHO on 30 September. The 17 September OCHA/FEWS NET sitrep had 62 dead and 95 injured; that earlier dated figure stays in this note.

changelog.change: Added from ReliefWeb Yemen Floods Aug 2025 disaster page, FEWS NET September update, and ECHO Daily Flash 30 September 2025.

events.name: 2026 Yemen floods
events.region: Taiz (Al-Mokha) and more than ten governorates
events.geo_source: Taiz city centroid; IFRC/ECHO name Al-Mokha, Mawza and Al-Wazeyah districts of Taiz as the worst-hit coastal ground
events.what_happened: Yemen's 2026 rains began early (from 20 March) and intensified from 27 March, flooding more than ten governorates including Taiz (Al-Mokha), Al Jawf, Ibb, Abyan, Al Bayda, Lahj, Marib, Al Hodeidah, Hadramout, Aden and Al Dhale'e. The IFRC DREF (MDRYE017, 6 April 2026) cited Yemen Red Crescent Society figures of 83,713 people (11,959 households) affected, at least 30 dead and 47 injured, and 254 incidents logged at the YRCS emergency centre. ECHO's 31 March flash said at least 15 dead and 9,820 households affected on the west coast, including 49 IDP sites. A later ECHO note (30 April) gave at least 24 dead and 7,900 households along the west coast.
events.status: Ongoing seasonal flooding as of April 2026 sitreps.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 83,713 people / 11,959 households (YRCS / IFRC DREF 6 April 2026)
events.cause_summary: Early, intense first rainy season from 27 March 2026, worst on the Taiz–Hodeidah west coast and in IDP sites.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Yemen Flood 2026 — DREF Operation MDRYE017

events.name: 2025 Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei floods
events.geo_source: Miyun District (Wikipedia coordinates 40.37444°N, 116.83944°E); Chinese Wikipedia and Reuters name Miyun (Taishitun nursing home) as the deadliest site
events.river_or_facility: Miyun Reservoir / Panjiakou Reservoir / Qingshui River
events.what_happened: From 23–29 July 2025 a stalled trough, with indirect influence from Typhoon Co-May (Zhujiecao), produced extreme rain over Beijing, northern Hebei and northern Tianjin. Chinese Wikipedia records at least 64 dead and 39 missing: 44 dead in Beijing (all at a Taishitun, Miyun, elderly-care centre), 16 dead in Luanping County, Hebei, and 4 dead in Tianjin, mainly in Jizhou mountain floods. Reuters on 31 July reported at least 60 dead, including 31 at the Miyun care home, and 573.5 mm in parts of Miyun — about a year's rain in a few days. Hebei reported 356,000 people affected and 44,000 relocated by 29 July. A June 2026 emergency-management investigation blamed the care-home deaths on a Qingshui River extreme flood inundating a low-lying site.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hebei 356,000 affected and 44,000 relocated as of 29 July; Beijing more than 80,000 evacuated (zh.wikipedia / Xinhua cited there)
events.cause_summary: Week-long July rainstorm over the Yanshan hills, indirectly steered by Typhoon Co-May, with a Qingshui River flash flood through Miyun.

sources.label: Reuters: Care home residents among at least 60 killed in north China flooding (31 July 2025)

events.notes: 64 is the Chinese Wikipedia body total (44 Beijing + 16 Hebei + 4 Tianjin). The infobox says at least 60; Reuters on 31 July also used 60. Using the later summed official local figures on the Chinese event page.
events.peak_discharge: Luan River 2025 No. 1 flood: Panjiakou inflow 2,270 m³/s (zh.wikipedia / ministry briefing)
events.rainfall_mm: Miyun local maxima 573.5 mm in a few days (Reuters); 254–321 mm in 22 hours over Huairou/Miyun on 25–26 July (zh.wikipedia)
events.inundation_area: Hebei crops 72,000 ha affected as of 29 July (zh.wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: Direct losses in the north described as exceeding 100 billion yuan on the Chinese Wikipedia page

events.name: Cyclone Ditwah floods
events.region: Sri Lanka (worst in Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Badulla) / Tamil Nadu
events.geo_source: Kandy (Wikipedia coordinates 7.2931°N, 80.635°E); Cyclone Ditwah page lists 234 of 644 Sri Lankan deaths in Kandy District
events.what_happened: Cyclonic Storm Ditwah crossed Sri Lanka from 26 November 2025 and then paralleled the Tamil Nadu coast. Wikipedia's dedicated storm page records 647 fatalities (644 in Sri Lanka, 3 in India), 21 injured, 183 missing and more than $4.14 billion damage. Sri Lanka had 234 deaths in Kandy District, 90 in Badulla, 89 in Nuwara Eliya and further deaths across 18 districts; 6,200 homes were destroyed and 96,545 damaged; about 1.46 million people (407,594 families) were affected and 59,000 families sheltered in 1,529 centres. The Mavil Aru bund breached in Trincomalee District. It was Sri Lanka's deadliest disaster since the 2004 tsunami. A DMC sitrep of 16 December 2025 is cited for the district table.
events.status: Recovery ongoing into 2026 (bailey bridges still being installed under Operation Sagar Bandhu).
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1.46 million people / 407,594 families affected; 59,000 families in 1,529 centres (Wikipedia / DMC)
events.cause_summary: Slow-moving cyclonic storm that stalled over Sri Lanka and dumped extreme rain on central-highland catchments.
events.notes: 647 is the Wikipedia infobox (644 Sri Lanka + 3 India). A DMC sitrep of 16 December 2025 is the cited source for the Sri Lankan district table. Not a dam failure; the Mavil Aru bund breach is noted as a tank overflow, not copied as a structural dam-collapse toll.
events.economic_damage: World Bank about Rs 1.3 trillion / US$4.1 billion; government Rs 1.03 trillion / US$3.4 billion (Wikipedia)

events.peak_discharge: About 4,500 m³/s on the Vltava at Prague (cs.wikipedia / Prague city history)
events.name: 1845 Czech flood (Velká povodeň 1845)
events.geo_source: Prague (Wikipedia coordinates 50.0875°N, 14.42138889°E); Czech Wikipedia event page and Prague city history name the Vltava through the Old Town and Karlín as the measured crest
events.what_happened: The March 1845 snowmelt-and-rain flood was one of the largest modern floods on the Vltava and Elbe in Bohemia and Moravia, exceeded in Prague only in 2002. Czech Wikipedia estimates the Vltava peak through Prague at about 4,500 m³/s. Prague city history records the crest on 29 March at 5.77 m above the Old Town gauge, with 114 streets and 946 of 3,106 houses flooded and 1,657 families left without shelter; almost all of Karlín was underwater. The dedicated event page does not give a death toll.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1,657 families without shelter in Prague; 946 houses flooded (Prague city history)
events.cause_summary: Late-March thaw and rain on a snow-rich Vltava–Elbe catchment.

sources.label: Praha.eu: Povodně v Praze — ohlédnutí do historie

events.notes: Deaths null: the dedicated Czech Wikipedia event page and the Prague municipal history give houses, families and the 4,500 m³/s estimate, but no sourced fatality count. Do not invent.

changelog.change: Added from Czech Wikipedia: Povodeň v Česku (1845) and Praha.eu flood history.

events.rainfall_mm: San Bernardino 1,118 mm in 8 days; 467 mm in 2 days (Oeschger / Storm Archive)
events.name: 1868 Switzerland floods
events.geo_source: Bodio TI (German Wikipedia coordinates 46.38°N, 8.907°E); Swiss Storm Archive names Bodio in the Leventina as the deadliest site (22 of 51 deaths)
events.what_happened: Two extreme rain spells (27–28 September and 1–5 October 1868) on already wet Alpine catchments flooded Ticino, Graubünden, Valais, Uri and St. Gallen. The University of Bern Oeschger Centre reconstruction records 1,118 mm in eight days on the San Bernardino pass and the highest Lago Maggiore stage ever measured (199.98 m a.s.l. on 4 October). The Swiss Storm Archive and the Oeschger brochure both give 51 deaths nationwide, 41 of them in Ticino, including 22 at Bodio where 30 houses were destroyed. Damage is estimated at about one billion francs in year-2000 prices.
events.cause_summary: Two multi-day autumn rainstorms plus föhn snowmelt on both sides of the Alpine crest.

sources.label: University of Bern / Oeschger Centre: Ein Extremhochwasser, das die Schweiz prägte

events.notes: 51 is the nationwide figure on both the University of Bern Oeschger Centre page and the Swiss Storm Archive. The archive breaks out 41 Ticino / 22 Bodio. No dedicated German Wikipedia event page; this uses the national academic reconstruction plus the storm archive.

events.peak_discharge: 1,890 m³/s at Murcia; more than 2,000 m³/s estimated at Orihuela (Wikipedia)
events.rainfall_mm: About 600 mm in one hour estimated at the Guadalentín headwaters (Wikipedia)
events.name: Santa Teresa flood (Riada de Santa Teresa)
events.region: Murcia / Vega Baja del Segura / Guadalentín
events.geo_source: Murcia (Wikipedia coordinates 37.9833°N, 1.1303°W); English and Spanish event pages name the Segura through the city centre after it overtopped the Malecón
events.what_happened: On 15 October 1879 the Segura and Guadalentín rose after extreme rain at the Guadalentín headwaters (an estimated 600 mm in one hour). Wikipedia records 1,890 m³/s at Murcia and more than 2,000 m³/s at Orihuela. The Segura overtopped the Malecón and flooded the city centre; streets in Orihuela reached 3.80 m. The catastrophe left more than a thousand dead: 761 in Murcia, 300 in Orihuela, 13 in Lorca, two in Librilla and one in Cieza. 5,762 houses were destroyed and 22,469 animals died.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 5,762 houses destroyed in Murcia and Lorca (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Extreme convective rain on the Guadalentín–Segura headwaters, producing a flash flood through Murcia and Orihuela.
events.notes: 1,077 is the sum of the locality table on the English and Spanish event pages (761+300+13+2+1). Infoboxes say more than 1,000. Using the summed named localities.

events.inundation_area: More than 150,000 ha in Bavaria; 2,000 ha in Linz; Eferding basin about three times Lake Traunsee (de.wikipedia)
events.name: 1954 Danube flood (Donauhochwasser 1954)
events.geo_source: Linz (Wikipedia coordinates 48.30583333°N, 14.28638889°E); German Wikipedia event page records the 9.62 m Linz gauge on 11 July, not reached again in 2002
events.what_happened: Rain from 7–11 July 1954 over the Bavarian and Austrian Alpine foreland, after weeks of wet weather, produced an extreme Danube flood from Regensburg downstream. German Wikipedia records more than 400 mm in south-east Bavaria, 9,000 people evacuated and 12 deaths in Bavaria, and more than 150,000 ha inundated. In Upper Austria it was the strongest flood of the 20th century: 2,000 ha of Linz underwater, 5,500 people evacuated, and a 9.62 m gauge on 11 July that the August 2002 flood did not reach (8.20 m). Vienna's Handelskai and Prater were flooded.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 9,000 evacuated in Bavaria; 5,500 in Linz (de.wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Multi-day July rain on the Bavarian–Austrian Alpine foreland, with the Inn almost three times the Danube at Passau.
events.notes: 12 is the Bavarian death toll on the German event page. The page does not give a separate Austrian fatality figure. Using the only sourced count; Austrian deaths if any are unknown here.

events.inundation_area: Willamette 152,789 acres; Central Valley 375,000 acres (Wikipedia)

events.name: Christmas flood of 1964
events.geo_source: Oregon City (Wikipedia coordinates 45.3569°N, 122.6067°W); the event-page lead photograph is Willamette Falls at Oregon City
events.river_or_facility: Willamette Falls / Eel River at Scotia
events.what_happened: A mid-December freeze and snowpack was followed by a warm atmospheric river from 18 December 1964 into early January 1965. Every Oregon river went above flood stage; the Willamette inundated 152,789 acres. In California the Eel at Scotia peaked at 752,000 cfs, towns along the Eel, Klamath and Smith were destroyed, and 34 counties were declared disaster areas. USGS's 50th-anniversary feature gives 47 deaths, thousands homeless and more than $540 million damage ($3.9 billion in later dollars). Wikipedia separately cites 17 or 18 deaths in Oregon and 19 in California.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands homeless (USGS)
events.cause_summary: Rain-on-snow atmospheric river on frozen ground across Oregon, California, Washington, Idaho and Nevada.
events.notes: 47 is the USGS 50th-anniversary nationwide figure. Wikipedia's state splits (17–18 Oregon, 19 California) sum lower and omit other states. Using the later USGS total; the state splits stay in this note. Hell Hole Dam (then unfinished) failed as a secondary effect and is not treated as a structural dam-collapse event here.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: Christmas flood of 1964 and USGS featured story.

events.economic_damage: At least $500 million; perhaps over $1 billion (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1970 floods in Romania
events.geo_source: Alba Iulia (Wikipedia coordinates 46.06694444°N, 23.57°E); the event-page lead photograph is flood victims in Alba Iulia, May 1970
events.river_or_basin: Danube / Someș / Tisza / Olt / Prut / Siret
events.what_happened: From about 12 May into mid-June 1970, torrential rain, wind and a Carpathian snowmelt heatwave produced the deadliest modern Romanian floods. Wikipedia records 209 deaths, 41,000 houses damaged or destroyed, at least 265,000 homeless, more than a million arable acres inundated and at least 240,000 evacuated. Thirty-seven of 39 counties were hit; Sighișoara, Mediaș, Sibiu, Satu Mare, Galați and Brăila were among the threatened cities. Damage was at least $500 million and perhaps over $1 billion.
events.affected_or_evacuated: At least 240,000 evacuated; 265,000 homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: May–June rain plus a heatwave melt of Carpathian snow, swelling the Danube and Transylvanian tributaries.
events.notes: 209 is the Wikipedia infobox and body figure. A 3 June 1970 New York Times piece cited on the page had 161 on the Danube earlier in the event.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: 1970 floods in Romania.

events.name: 1987 Ötztal flood
events.geo_source: Längenfeld (Wikipedia coordinates 47.06666667°N, 10.96666667°E); ORF and Tiroler Tageszeitung name the Ferdinandsbrücke between Umhausen and Längenfeld as the site of the 13 deaths
events.what_happened: After a hot day, prolonged rain on 24–25 August 1987 sent the Ötztaler Ache over its banks. ORF Tirol records that a bridge between Umhausen and Längenfeld was torn away and 13 people died in the night of 24–25 August when warnings reached drivers too late. The rear valley was supplied by army helicopter for days; the Timmelsjoch was used as the road link. Tiroler Tageszeitung later called it a roughly 300-year event. There is no dedicated Wikipedia event page; the river article and national/regional outlets document the named disaster.
events.cause_summary: Prolonged August rain and glacier melt on the Ötztaler Ache, destroying the Längenfeld bridge.

events.what_happened: On 22 September 1992 a stationary storm on the west flank of Mont Ventoux produced a roughly 100-year flash flood of the Ouvèze. About 183 mm fell in the afternoon at Vaison after a quieter morning; Entrechaux recorded 300 mm in six hours. The municipal campsite and the Théos estate on the right bank were swept away; water at the Roman bridge rose about 15 m above normal. French Wikipedia's most commonly cited toll is 46 dead (34 at Vaison) plus four missing; the lede also gives 37 dead and four missing in four communes. Sixty-three Vaucluse communes were hit. Damage was later put at about €460 million.

events.what_happened: Tropical Storm Alberto made landfall near Destin, Florida, on 3 July 1994 and then stalled over Georgia and Alabama. Wikipedia's NHC-based infobox records 33 deaths (31 Georgia, 2 Alabama) and $1.03 billion damage (1994 USD). Up to 27.85 in (707 mm) fell near Americus; the Flint and Ocmulgee exceeded 100-year floods, about 1,000 bridges closed, and Albany and Macon lost water treatment. About 50,000 people fled their homes. Other sources on the page put damage at $1.5–2 billion and deaths closer to 38.

events.cause_summary: Stalling tropical-storm remnants over saturated central Georgia, producing record Flint and Ocmulgee floods.

events.what_happened: Overnight 22–23 July 1998, torrential rain in the Orlické hory raised the Bělá and Dědina by up to three metres and flooded about 100 km² and 30 municipalities in Rychnov nad Kněžnou, Náchod and Hradec Králové districts. Czech Wikipedia records six people drowned (five men and one woman) at Deštné, Skuhrov, Kounov, Dobré, Masty and Pulice, plus a seventh indirect death of a volunteer rescuer in a car accident at Černíkovice. About 800 people were evacuated. Damage was put at 1.927 billion Kč.

French Wikipedia records 35 deaths (26 Aude, 5 Tarn, 3 Pyrénées-Orientales, 2 Hérault), 6,000 evacuated, 14 bridges destroyed in the Aude and 431 communes recognised as natural-disaster zones. About 50 stations exceeded 200 mm in 48 hours; Lézignan-Corbières recorded 624 mm in 36 hours. Damage was about 3.5 billion francs.

events.name: 2000 Alpine flood (Alpenhochwasser 2000)
events.geo_source: Gondo (German Wikipedia coordinates 46.195843°N, 8.139565°E); the German event page names the 14 October Gondo landslide-flood as the single worst site (13 of 16 Valais deaths)
events.what_happened: From 10–16 October 2000 a stalled Mediterranean fetch produced extreme rain on the southern Alps. German Wikipedia records 23 dead, 128 injured and 11 missing in Piedmont, and 16 dead in Valais — the canton's worst 20th-century flood — including 13 at Gondo when a landslide destroyed ten houses on 14 October. Lago Maggiore reached its highest 20th-century stage and flooded Locarno. In the Rhone plain 1,027 ha were underwater after dyke breaches at Chamoson and Sion. Canal 9's anniversary tally for Valais is 16 (13 Gondo, 2 Neubrück, 1 Martigny).
events.cause_summary: Six-day southerly Mediterranean rainstorm on Piedmont, Ticino and Valais, with a landslide-flood through Gondo.
events.notes: 39 is 23 Piedmont + 16 Valais as stated on the German event page. Piedmont also listed 11 missing. Using the summed named-country figures from the same page.

events.what_happened: On 8–9 September 2002 a Cévennes Mediterranean episode produced one of the largest flash floods in modern French records. France 3's 20-year retrospective recorded 687 mm in 24 hours at Anduze, 22 dead, 299 of 353 Gard communes disaster-listed and more than €830 million damage. Encyclopædia Universalis contemporaneously gave 23 dead. The Delrieu et al. OHM-CV monograph used 24 casualties and €1.2 billion. More than 90 percent of Gard communes were affected; Alès's dyke failed on the evening of 9 September.

events.what_happened: At the end of March 2006, rain plus a rapid thaw of a heavy snowpack flooded much of the Czech Republic and neighbouring Central Europe. The dedicated Czech Wikipedia page dates the main wave 25 March–5 April, with Q50–Q100 on some reaches and the worst urban flooding at Veselí nad Lužnicí (up to 400 homes), Planá nad Lužnicí, Znojmo, Ústí nad Labem and Olomouc. Seven regions and several hundred municipalities were hit. Total damage reached about 5 billion Kč. The event page does not itself state deaths; the Czech flood-list article gives 7 victims.

events.geo_source: Cockermouth (Wikipedia coordinates 54.6613°N, 3.362°W); the event page names Cumbria as the worst-hit British county and Cockermouth as the town with more than 200 rescues
events.what_happened: November 2009 was the wettest month in the UK since records began in 1914. On 19–20 November a depression flooded Cumbria: Seathwaite Farm recorded a then-UK record 314.4 mm in 24 hours, Cockermouth saw about 2.5 m of water, and Workington's Northside Bridge collapsed, killing PC Bill Barker. Wikipedia's infobox lists 4 flood deaths (the officer, a Dartmoor canoeist on 21 November, and two in Powys). Cork lost running water for more than ten days after the Lee flooded the treatment plant. ABI damage in Cumbria and Scotland was put above £100 million.

events.cause_summary: Record November rainfall, worst on the Cumbrian Derwent and Cocker and on the Irish Lee and Shannon.

Wikipedia records 37 deaths (Poland 25, Austria 3, Serbia 2, Hungary 2, Slovakia 3, Czech Republic 2) and about 23,000 evacuated. Kraków declared an emergency; the Vistula broke banks at Płock and Sandomierz; Auschwitz-Birkenau closed. Polish damage was estimated at €2.5 billion.

events.name: 2011 Colombia floods
events.geo_source: Manizales (Wikipedia coordinates 5.0675°N, 75.51°W); the event page names the 6 November Manizales landslide (45 dead) as the deadliest single site of the second rainy season
events.what_happened: Colombia's 2011 rainy seasons produced two flood-and-landslide waves. Wikipedia's opening paragraph says the April wave killed at least 187 people, affected 1.2 million, destroyed 1,450 houses and damaged 149,270, and left more than 69,000 homeless, with damage estimated at US$5 billion. A second wave from September killed another 81, wounded 65 and affected about 289,000. The Magdalena reached a then-record level; a 6 November landslide in Manizales killed 45. A nationwide emergency was declared on 23 April.

events.cause_summary: Two 2011 rainy-season waves overflowing the Magdalena and Cauca, with deadly landslides at Manizales.

events.geo_source: Cevio (Wikipedia coordinates 46.31666667°N, 8.65°E); the English event page lead photograph is the destroyed Visletto bridge on the Maggia near Cevio
events.what_happened: June 2024 storms produced a series of Swiss floods, landslides and debris flows. Wikipedia's dedicated page records at least 18 deaths. MeteoSwiss later restated 7 dead and one still missing in the Maggia valley alone. Val Bavona stayed closed to tourism for nine months.
