events.name: 1872 Bohemia flash flood
events.geo_source: Beroun (Wikipedia coordinates 49.96416667°N, 14.07388889°E); Czech Wikipedia event page names the unmatched Berounka crest at Beroun (2,500 m³/s)
events.what_happened: A 25–26 May 1872 convective cloudburst over western and central Bohemia produced a 1,000-year flash flood on the Berounka. Czech Wikipedia records an official count of 337 dead, worst at Holedeč (43) and Nebřeziny (40). The night wave breached five fishpond dikes on the Blšanka and the Mladotice pond, and a landslide dammed Mladotický potok to form Odlezelské Lake. Academic reconstructions put fatalities at 240–300 (NHESS 2026 cites 244).
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands homeless; about 2,900 persons affected in the Natural Hazards floods database
events.cause_summary: Afternoon cloudburst on the Blšanka–Střela front; night flood wave on the Berounka.
events.notes: 337 is the official count on the dedicated Czech Wikipedia event page. Documentary/academic range 240–300 (often 244) stays in notes. Pond-dike failures on the Blšanka and the Mladotice pond were consequences of the rainfall flood, not a standalone dam-collapse row.

changelog.change: Added from Czech Wikipedia Povodeň v Čechách (1872).

events.economic_damage: 150 billion pesetas (Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 1983 Spanish floods (Basque Country)
events.geo_source: Bilbao (Wikipedia coordinates 43.25694444°N, 2.92361111°W); event page names Casco Viejo at the Nervión–Ibaizabal confluence
events.what_happened: Abnormally heavy rain on 25–27 August 1983 burst the Deba, Oria and Urola in Gipuzkoa, then flooded Bilbao at the Nervión–Ibaizabal confluence during Aste Nagusia. Water stood about 3 m deep in Casco Viejo. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 34 deaths and five missing, more than 5,000 evacuated, and 150 billion pesetas in damage — Spain's costliest floods until October 2024.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Over 5,000 evacuated in Bilbao (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Late-August cloudburst on Basque river confluences, worst at Bilbao.
events.notes: 34 deaths plus five unaccounted for on the event page. Distinct from flood-spain-2024 (DANA) and flood-valles-1962 / flood-valencia-1957 / flood-santa-teresa-1879.

events.rainfall_mm: About 160 mm at Biescas; 200–250 mm estimated in the Arás headwaters (es.wikipedia)
events.name: 1996 Biescas campsite flood
events.geo_source: Biescas (Wikipedia coordinates 42.63333333°N, 0.15°W); Spanish Wikipedia event page places Camping Las Nieves on the Arás fan about 1 km downstream of town
events.river_or_facility: Arás torrent at Las Nieves campsite
events.what_happened: On 7 August 1996 a short convective storm sent a debris-laden flash flood down the Arás ravine onto Camping Las Nieves, built on the alluvial fan at the Gállego confluence just below Biescas. Spanish, Catalan and German Wikipedia event pages agree on 87 dead and 187 injured. Sediment-check dams in the torrent were swept out; a 2005 Audiencia Nacional ruling held the state and Aragón liable.
events.cause_summary: Convective cloudburst on the Arás torrent; campsite sited on the fan.

sources.label: Wikipedia (es): Riada del camping de Biescas

events.notes: 87 is the figure on the dedicated Spanish and German Wikipedia pages (English Wikipedia town page says 86). No English event page.

changelog.change: Added from Spanish/German Wikipedia Riada del camping de Biescas.

events.rainfall_mm: 230 mm in three hours (officials, cited on Wikipedia)
events.name: 2009 Messina floods and mudslides
events.geo_source: Giampilieri Superiore (Wikipedia coordinates 38.06666667°N, 15.46666667°E); event page names this frazione as buried in mud
events.what_happened: On the night of 1–2 October 2009 about 230 mm of rain in three hours sent mudslides through Giampilieri Superiore, Scaletta Zanclea, Altolia and Briga Superiore on Sicily's Ionian coast. The dedicated Wikipedia page records at least 31 deaths, six missing and 95 injured; more than 400 people were left homeless. It was Italy's worst landslide disaster since Sarno 1998.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 400 homeless; at least 450 inhabitants of the comuni left homeless (Wikipedia, 8 Oct 2009)
events.cause_summary: Three-hour cloudburst on deforested Ionian-coast slopes; illegal building in torrent beds.
events.notes: Infobox 'at least 31 deaths, 6 missing'. Early press 13–28; Berlusconi briefly said the toll could reach 50. Using the event-page figure 31.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2009 Messina floods and mudslides.

events.name: 1928 Thames flood
events.geo_source: Event-page coordinates 51.484°N, 0.162°W at Chelsea Embankment, where a 75-foot section collapsed opposite the Tate
events.what_happened: A Cotswolds thaw and rain, a high spring tide and a North Sea storm surge combined on 7 January 1928 to produce the highest Thames level then recorded in London (5.55 m). Water overtopped the Embankment from the City to Putney; a 75-foot Chelsea Embankment section collapsed opposite the Tate. Fourteen people died, mostly in Millbank basements, and about 4,000 were made homeless. Last major flood of central London; a driver of the later Thames Barrier.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 4,000 Londoners made homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Snowmelt-and-rain flood wave meeting a North Sea surge and spring tide in dredged tidal Thames.
events.notes: 14 is the Times / Wikipedia death-roll. Distinct from flood-north-sea-1953 and flood-lynmouth-1952.

events.rainfall_mm: 255 mm in one day at Hala Gąsienicowa, a then Polish record (Wikipedia)
events.inundation_area: 1,260 km² (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: About 60 million interwar zlotys / US$12 million (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1934 flood in Poland
events.geo_source: Dobczyce (Wikipedia coordinates 49.88083333°N, 20.09027778°E); event-page image caption is flooded Lesser Poland around Dobczyce on the Raba
events.what_happened: Heavy rain in the Dunajec basin from 13 July 1934, peaking on 16 July (255 mm at Hala Gąsienicowa), spread to the Raba, Wisłoka and Skawa and then the Vistula. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 55 deaths, 1,260 km² flooded, 22,059 buildings damaged or destroyed and about 60 million zlotys of losses. The disaster led to the Porąbka and Rożnów reservoirs.
events.cause_summary: Mid-July cloudburst in the Tatras and Gorce; flood wave on Dunajec tributaries into the Vistula.
events.notes: Biggest flood of the Second Polish Republic on the dedicated event page. Distinct from flood-oder-1997 and flood-central-europe-2010.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 1934 flood in Poland.

events.peak_discharge: Estimated 3,126 or 4,440 m³/s at Zagreb (Wikipedia notes both scholarly figures)
events.inundation_area: About 60 km² of the city (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: 160 billion Yugoslav dinars / more than US$100 million (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1964 Zagreb flood
events.geo_source: Zagreb (Wikipedia coordinates 45.81305556°N, 15.9775°E); event page is the Sava through Trešnjevka and Trnje
events.what_happened: A record Sava wave from rain in Slovenia overtopped Zagreb's embankments on 25–28 October 1964. The gauge at the Sava Bridge crested at 514 cm, 59 cm above 1933. About 60 km² of the city flooded, including working-class Trešnjevka and Trnje. The dedicated page records 17 direct deaths (some sources 14), 183,000 people living in the flooded area and 40,000 homeless. Last devastating river flood in Zagreb; the Sava–Odra canal followed.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 183,000 living in the flooded area; 40,000 lost their homes (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: October rain on a saturated Sava catchment in Slovenia; embankments overtopped at Zagreb.
events.notes: 17 direct deaths on the event-page infobox; some sources say 14. Using 17. Country recorded as Croatia (event was in SR Croatia, SFR Yugoslavia).

events.economic_damage: About 1,520 buildings damaged (Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 2017 West Attica floods
events.geo_source: Mandra (Wikipedia coordinates 38.06666667°N, 23.5°E); event page names 23 of 24 deaths in Mandra
events.what_happened: On the morning of 15 November 2017, Cyclone Numa / low Eurydice dumped extreme rain on West Attica. Flash floods in Mandra, Nea Peramos, Magoula and Elefsina killed 24 people (23 in Mandra, one in Nea Peramos) and damaged about 1,520 buildings. Wikipedia calls it the third-deadliest flood in Attica by fatality count. Three days of national mourning were declared.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 1,520 buildings damaged (1,064 in Mandra; 448 in Megara / Nea Peramos)
events.cause_summary: Cyclone Numa / Eurydice cloudburst over West Attica catchments.
events.notes: 24 is the event-page figure (23 Mandra + 1 Nea Peramos). Distinct from Storm Daniel 2023 Thessaly, which has no dedicated flood page.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2017 West Attica floods.

events.name: 1938 Hanshin flood
events.geo_source: Kobe (Wikipedia coordinates 34.69°N, 135.19555556°E); event page is the Mount Rokkō area including Kobe and Nishinomiya
events.what_happened: Torrential July 1938 rain on Mount Rokkō sent flash floods and debris flows through Kobe and Nishinomiya. The dedicated English Wikipedia page, citing the official government report, says at least 715 people lost their lives. The disaster is remembered as 阪神大水害 and appears in Tanizaki's The Makioka Sisters.
events.cause_summary: Seasonal cloudburst and debris flows off Mount Rokkō into the Hanshin cities.
events.notes: 715 is the official-report figure on the dedicated event page. Older list-of-floods entries citing 925 stay in notes as a higher unofficial tally.

events.rainfall_mm: 1,109 mm in 24 hours (Ministry of Agriculture record cited on Wikipedia)
events.name: 1957 Isahaya flood
events.geo_source: Isahaya, Nagasaki (Wikipedia coordinates 32.84333333°N, 130.05305556°E); event page is the Honmei River through Isahaya
events.what_happened: From 25–28 July 1957 a stalled Baiu front dumped a then-Japanese-record 1,109 mm of rain in 24 hours on the Honmei basin. Debris flows and two flood waves wrecked Isahaya; stone Megane Bridge trapped debris and worsened the second wave. The Fire Services White Paper recorded 586 killed, 136 missing and 3,860 injured. The Isahaya Flood 30th Anniversary book puts dead and missing at 630.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1,564 houses completely destroyed; 24,046 flooded above floor level (White Paper, via Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Stationary Baiu-front cloudburst on the Honmei; debris-choked Megane Bridge.
events.notes: 586 killed is the White Paper figure on the event page. 630 dead-or-missing (anniversary book) and 136 missing stay in notes. Distinct from flood-kyushu-1953 and flood-wakayama-1953.

events.economic_damage: Over $600,000 (1903 USD; Wikipedia)
events.name: Heppner flood of 1903
events.geo_source: Heppner, Oregon (Wikipedia coordinates 45.35472222°N, 119.55583333°W); dedicated event page
events.river_or_basin: Willow Creek / Balm Fork / Hinton Creek
events.what_happened: On 14 June 1903 a thunderstorm on already-wet ground sent a 15-to-50-foot wall of water down Balm Fork and Willow Creek into Heppner, Oregon, after a steam laundry building failed as a debris dam. The dedicated page records 247 deaths — about a quarter of the town, Oregon's deadliest natural disaster, and the second-deadliest US flash flood after Johnstown 1889. Riders warned Lexington and Ione; no one died there, but sewage-contaminated wells later caused at least 18 typhoid deaths.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 140 structures, one-third of Heppner, washed away (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Thunderstorm flash flood on Willow Creek after a laundry building acted as a debris dam.
events.notes: 247 is the event-page death toll. At least 18 later typhoid deaths in Lexington and Ione are not added to the flood figure. Johnstown 1889 stays in incidents.json as a dam failure.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia Heppner flood of 1903.

events.rainfall_mm: Over 20 inches at McEwen, a Tennessee 24-hour record (Wikipedia)
events.name: 2021 Tennessee floods (Waverly)
events.geo_source: Waverly, Tennessee (Wikipedia coordinates 36.08583333°N, 87.78694444°W); event page is Trace Creek through Waverly
events.what_happened: Between midnight and 10:00 CDT on 21 August 2021, 10–20 inches of rain fell across a five-county area of western Middle Tennessee. Runoff down Trace Creek destroyed much of Waverly. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 19 deaths in Waverly and one in nearby Hurricane Mills (20 total). Hundreds of homes and dozens of businesses were swept away. NWS and local officials called it one of Tennessee's worst natural disasters.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hundreds of homes and dozens of businesses destroyed in Waverly (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Record 24-hour cloudburst; Trace Creek flash flood through Waverly.
events.notes: 20 = 19 Waverly + 1 Hurricane Mills on the event page. Waverly town page also says 20 in Humphreys County.

events.rainfall_mm: 363 mm in one day at Sentul; 380 mm reported in Selangor (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: RM5.3–6.5 billion government estimate (Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 2021–2022 Malaysian floods
events.geo_source: Shah Alam (Wikipedia coordinates 3.07222222°N, 101.51666667°E); event page names Taman Sri Muda / Shah Alam as the worst-hit township
events.what_happened: Tropical Depression 29W made landfall near Kuantan on 16 December 2021 and stalled over the peninsula. A 'once in a century' downpour flooded Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Pahang. The dedicated page infobox records 54 dead and two missing (Bernama, 5 January 2022); a state table on the same page sums to 74. More than 71,000 people were displaced at peak. Worst damage at Taman Sri Muda, Shah Alam (14 deaths in that township).
events.affected_or_evacuated: 71,000 displaced at peak; 125,490 cumulative (Wikipedia infobox)
events.cause_summary: Landfall and stalling of Tropical Depression 29W; record Klang Valley rain.
events.notes: 54 is the dated Bernama / infobox figure (5 Jan 2022). A deaths-by-state table on the same page sums to 74 with 17 missing — range stays in notes. Distinct from flood-malaysia-2014.

events.name: 2022–2023 Philippine floods
events.geo_source: Ozamiz (Wikipedia coordinates 8.15°N, 123.85°E); event page names Ozamiz, Oroquieta and Gingoog as the worst-hit cities
events.river_or_basin: Mindanao and Eastern Visayas coastal catchments
events.what_happened: From 18 December 2022 to 5 February 2023 a shear line, northeast monsoon and low-pressure areas flooded Mindanao, the Visayas, Bicol and Mimaropa. Misamis Occidental declared a state of calamity; Ozamiz, Oroquieta and Gingoog were worst hit. Combined NDRRMC sitreps on the dedicated Wikipedia page total 97 dead, 29 injured and 25 missing (52+18+18 in December; 45+7+11 in January–February).
events.cause_summary: Shear line, amihan and LPAs over Visayas and Mindanao.
events.notes: 97 is the combined NDRRMC sitrep total cited on the event page. Distinct from flood-ondoy-2009, flood-washi-2011 and flood-ormoc-1991.

events.rainfall_mm: More than 200 mm in 24 hours in Recife, Olinda, Jaboatão and others (Wikipedia)
events.name: 2022 Northeastern Brazil floods and mudslides
events.geo_source: Recife (Wikipedia coordinates 8.05°S, 34.9°W); event page names Greater Recife / Ibura as 106 of 109 deaths
events.what_happened: From 23 May 2022, rains far above the May average hit Pernambuco, Alagoas, Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte and Sergipe. Greater Recife recorded more than 200 mm in 24 hours; Jardim Monte Verde in Ibura alone had 21 dead. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 109 deaths, with 106 in Greater Recife and at least 10 still missing at the time of writing. About 4,000 people were left homeless in Recife; more than 10,000 were homeless in Alagoas.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 4,000 homeless in Greater Recife; more than 10,000 affected in Alagoas (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Eastern-wave / South Atlantic High rains over Greater Recife and the Zona da Mata.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2022 Northeastern Brazil floods and mudslides

events.notes: 109 is the event-page infobox. Distinct from flood-petropolis-2022, flood-sao-paulo-2023, flood-rs-brazil-2024 and flood-rio-2011.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2022 Northeastern Brazil floods and mudslides.

events.rainfall_mm: 481 mm at Jacobabad in the 5–9 September wet spell, a monthly record (PMD via Wikipedia)
events.name: 2012 Pakistan floods
events.region: Sindh / southern Punjab / Balochistan / Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
events.geo_source: Jacobabad (Wikipedia coordinates 28.27694444°N, 68.45138889°E); event-page rainfall table lists Jacobabad 481 mm, a monthly record
events.river_or_basin: Indus / Kachhi / southern Punjab hill torrents
events.what_happened: A Bay of Bengal monsoon low entered Pakistan on 3 September 2012 and stalled until the 12th, breaking a 24-year rainfall record. Flash floods hit upper Sindh, Dera Ghazi Khan, Rajanpur and five districts of eastern Balochistan. The dedicated Wikipedia page, citing NDMA (17 October 2012), records 455 deaths and about five million people affected.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About five million affected (NDMA via Wikipedia, 17 Oct 2012)
events.cause_summary: Stalling Bay of Bengal monsoon low over Sindh and southern Punjab.
events.notes: 455 is the NDMA 17 October 2012 figure cited on the event page. Distinct from flood-pakistan-2010, flood-pakistan-2022 and flood-pakistan-2025.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2012 Pakistan floods (NDMA 17 Oct 2012).

events.rainfall_mm: Over 400 mm in 48 hours at some stations; models locally to 1,281 mm (Wikipedia)
events.name: 2021 Turkish Black Sea floods
events.geo_source: Bozkurt, Kastamonu (Wikipedia coordinates 41.95888889°N, 34.01305556°E); event section names Bozkurt as the worst-destroyed town
events.what_happened: Thunderstorms from 7–14 August 2021 stalled on Turkey's western Black Sea coast. Water rose about 4 m in Kastamonu, Sinop and Bartın; Bozkurt was largely destroyed by a log-choked torrent. The dedicated section of Floods in Turkey / 2021 coverage records 97 dead, about 228 injured and more than 1,800 evacuated. Interior Minister Soylu called it the worst flood disaster he had seen. The three provinces were declared disaster areas.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 1,800 evacuated; 2,472 in one official tally (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Week-long stalling thunderstorms on the western Black Sea; construction in floodplains.
events.notes: 97 is the lede figure on the 2021 section. Mid-event press 31–81. 2023 Şanlıurfa–Adıyaman floods (21 dead) on the same wrapper page are a different event and are not added here.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2021 Turkish floods (Black Sea).

events.name: 2015 Tbilisi flood
events.geo_source: Tbilisi (Wikipedia coordinates 41.7225°N, 44.7925°E); event page is the Vere through Vake, Saburtalo, Heroes' Square and the zoo
events.river_or_facility: Vere River at Tbilisi Zoo / Heroes' Square
events.what_happened: Hours of rain on 13 June 2015 triggered a landslide above Akhaldaba that twice dammed the Vere in Tbilisi. The resulting flood wrecked the Tbilisi Zoo, Heroes' Square and nearby streets. The dedicated Wikipedia page records at least 20 human deaths, including three zoo workers, and left about half the zoo's animals dead or loose.
events.cause_summary: Rain-triggered landslide temporarily dammed the Vere in central Tbilisi.
events.notes: At least 20 human deaths on the event page. Animal deaths at the zoo are not counted in the human toll.

events.economic_damage: At least US$152 million (Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 2009 West Africa floods
events.geo_source: Ouagadougou (Wikipedia coordinates 12.36861111°N, 1.5275°W); event page names the capital as the worst-hit place (150,000 fled; one-day rain equal to 25% of annual)
events.what_happened: Exceptional West African monsoon rain from June to September 2009 burst the Pendjari, Niger, Volta and Senegal. The dedicated Wikipedia page records at least 193 deaths and 940,000 people affected across 12 countries. Burkina Faso was worst hit: 150,000 people fled their homes, mostly in Ouagadougou, where one day's rain equalled a quarter of the country's normal annual total.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 940,000 people affected across 12 countries; 150,000 fled homes in Burkina Faso (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Above-normal West African monsoon; riverine flooding from the Sahel to the coast.
events.notes: 193 is the event-page 'at least' total. Country pin is Burkina Faso / Ouagadougou as the named worst-hit capital; the event spanned 12 countries.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2009 West Africa floods.

events.rainfall_mm: 372.8 mm at Gunsan on 14 July; monsoon-season average 648.7 mm (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: ₩751.3 billion / US$590 million (Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 2023 South Korea floods
events.location_label: Yecheon County, North Gyeongsang, South Korea
events.geo_source: Yecheon County (Wikipedia coordinates 36.65555557°N, 128.45694445°E); event page names the 15 July Baekseok-ri landslide in Yecheon
events.what_happened: The 2023 East Asian rainy season (25 June–26 July) produced South Korea's heaviest downpour in 115 years. Floods and landslides, mainly in North Chungcheong and North Gyeongsang, killed 47 people with three still missing as of 22 July 2023 on the dedicated Wikipedia page. A 15 July landslide at Baekseok-ri, Yecheon, killed five elderly residents.
events.cause_summary: Record East Asian monsoon rains and landslides in central-eastern South Korea.
events.notes: 47 dead and 3 missing as of 22 July 2023 on the event page. Distinct from 2020/2022/2024 Korea flood seasons, which are not added here.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2023 South Korea floods.

events.name: 2015 Accra floods
events.geo_source: Accra (Wikipedia coordinates 5.55°N, 0.2°W); event page names Kaneshie, Graphic Road and the GOIL station near Kwame Nkrumah Interchange
events.what_happened: Continuous rain from 1 June 2015 flooded Accra — Kaneshie market, Graphic Road and large parts of the city — killing at least 25 people by drowning. On 3 June a GOIL petrol station near Kwame Nkrumah Interchange exploded in the floodwaters and killed about 200 more. President Mahama declared three days of national mourning and released GH₵60 million for victims.
events.cause_summary: Early-June rain on choked Accra drains; GOIL station fire in floodwater treated separately in notes.
events.notes: 25 is the flood-drowning figure on the event page. The GOIL petrol-station explosion the same week killed about 200 more and is not added to the flood death field. Combined contemporary headlines of 150–200+ refer mainly to the fire.

events.rainfall_mm: 580.5 mm near Ormoc, about 500 mm in three hours (PNOC gauge, Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: US$27.7 million (1991 USD; Wikipedia infobox)
events.name: 1991 Ormoc flash flood (Tropical Storm Thelma / Uring)
events.geo_source: Ormoc (Wikipedia coordinates 11.0106°N, 124.6075°E); Tropical Storm Thelma page is the dedicated narrative of the Anilao–Malbasag flash flood through the city
events.what_happened: Weak Tropical Storm Thelma (Uring) stalled over the Visayas on 5 November 1991 and dropped about 500 mm of rain in three hours on the deforested Anilao–Malbasag watershed. A flash flood, worsened by debris dams and the Cogon Bridge constriction, inundated Ormoc in minutes. Wikipedia records 4,922 dead in the city and at least 5,081 confirmed dead nationwide, with another 1,941–3,084 missing and presumed dead. Then the deadliest Philippine tropical cyclone until Haiyan 2013.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 598,454 people affected; about 43,000 homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Orographic cloudburst on a deforested Leyte watershed; flash flood at the Anilao–Malbasag bend.
events.notes: 5,081 confirmed dead on the Thelma page. 4,922 of those in Ormoc. Missing 1,941–3,084 not added. Same sourcing pattern as flood-ondoy-2009 and flood-washi-2011 (storm page that is the flood narrative).

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia Tropical Storm Thelma (Ormoc flash flood).

events.rainfall_mm: About 1,000 mm in Freetown from 1 July to mid-August, nearly triple the seasonal average (NWS CPC via Wikipedia)
events.name: 2017 Sierra Leone mudslides (Freetown)
events.location_label: Regent / Sugar Loaf, Freetown, Sierra Leone
events.geo_source: Event-page coordinates 8.43389°N, 13.22278°W for the Western Area Rural District mudslides (Sugar Loaf / Regent)
events.what_happened: After three days of rain, Sugar Loaf mountain above Freetown collapsed in two stages on the morning of 14 August 2017, sending a debris flood down the Babadorie valley and a second slide through Regent. The dedicated Wikipedia page, citing the World Bank rapid assessment, records a final official toll of 1,141 dead or missing and more than 3,000 homeless. President Koroma declared a state of emergency and seven days of mourning.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 3,000 homeless (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Seasonal cloudburst on deforested Sugar Loaf slopes; debris flood into Freetown suburbs.
events.notes: 1,141 is the final official dead-or-missing figure on the event page (World Bank assessment). Early counts were 205 then ~1,000. Flood-and-mudslide event, same class as Messina 2009 / Petrópolis 2022.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 2017 Sierra Leone mudslides.

events.name: 1955 Hunter Valley floods
events.geo_source: Maitland, New South Wales (Wikipedia coordinates 32.71666667°S, 151.55°E); event page is the Hunter through Maitland
events.what_happened: On 23 February 1955 the Hunter River overwhelmed Maitland, exceeding the August 1952 record by nearly a metre and flooding as many as 5,000 homes with up to five metres of water. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 25 deaths in a week of flooding that also hit Dubbo and Gilgandra on the Macquarie. About 15,000 people were evacuated in Maitland; 58 homes were washed away and 103 damaged beyond repair. Often called one of Australia's most devastating floods.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 15,000 evacuated in Maitland; 2,180 homes invaded by water there (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Late-February rain on the Hunter and Macquarie; record crest at Maitland.
events.notes: 25 deaths on the event page. Distinct from flood-brisbane-1974, flood-gundagai-1852 and flood-australia-east-2022.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia 1955 Hunter Valley floods.

events.rainfall_mm: 907 mm in 24 hours at Crohamhurst, then an Australian record (Wikipedia)
events.name: 1893 Brisbane flood (Black February)
events.geo_source: Brisbane (Wikipedia coordinates 27.46777778°S, 153.02805556°E); dedicated 1893 Brisbane flood page
events.river_or_facility: Brisbane River at the City (Port Office) gauge
events.what_happened: Three major Brisbane River floods in February 1893 — 6, 11 and 19 February, the first and third driven by tropical cyclones — were named Black February. The City gauge reached 8.35 m, second only to 1841 (8.43 m). Crohamhurst recorded 907 mm in 24 hours. The dedicated Wikipedia page records 35 deaths; the third flood left up to one-third of Brisbane's residents homeless.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Up to one-third of Brisbane residents homeless after the 19 February flood (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Three February tropical-cyclone rains on the Brisbane–Stanley catchment.
events.notes: 35 deaths on the dedicated event page. Distinct from flood-brisbane-1974 and flood-australia-east-2022.

events.rainfall_mm: 130 mm in a few hours near Mocoa (Wikipedia)
events.name: 2017 Mocoa landslide and flash flood
events.geo_source: Event-page coordinates 1.15°N, 76.6475°W for the 2017 Mocoa landslide
events.what_happened: Overnight 31 March–1 April 2017 about 130 mm of rain in a few hours burst the Mocoa, Sangoyaco and Mulata rivers and sent mudflows through Mocoa, Putumayo, before dawn. The dedicated Wikipedia page records at least 336 dead (including 92 children), more than 400 injured and 200 missing as of 6 April — Colombia's third-deadliest weather disaster and the worst catastrophe in Mocoa's history.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 200 missing as of 6 April 2017 (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Pre-dawn cloudburst; flash flood and debris flows on three rivers through Mocoa.
events.notes: 336 is the event-page 'at least' figure (301 was an earlier 6 April running tally in some wrap-up articles). Distinct from flood-colombia-2010 and flood-colombia-2011.

events.name: 2014–2015 Malaysian floods
events.geo_source: Kota Bharu (Wikipedia coordinates 6.13333333°N, 102.25°E); event page names Kelantan as the worst-hit state (354,800 affected)
events.what_happened: Northeast-monsoon floods from 15 December 2014 to 3 January 2015 were described as Malaysia's worst in decades. The dedicated Wikipedia page records more than 500,000 people affected — 354,800 of them in Kelantan — and 21 killed. Evacuees nationwide exceeded 200,000 by 28 December. A police helicopter crashed on a Kelantan patrol on 31 December, injuring four crew (not counted in the flood death toll).
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 500,000 affected; 354,800 in Kelantan (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Northeast monsoon over the east-coast peninsula, worst in Kelantan.
events.notes: 21 killed on the event page. Distinct from the larger flood-malaysia-2021. Exact centre figures were acknowledged as uncertain at the time.

events.name: 2025 Philippine monsoon floods
events.region: Luzon / Cagayan Valley / Central Luzon / Calabarzon
events.geo_source: Manila (Wikipedia coordinates 14.5958°N, 120.9772°E); event page names Manila, Malabon, San Miguel and Cavite states of calamity and NLEX flooding
events.what_happened: A July 2025 southwest monsoon, enhanced by Tropical Storms Wipha and Co-may, flooded northern and central Luzon. The dedicated Wikipedia page records a final toll of 30 dead, 10 injured and 7 missing. More than 1.26 million people were affected at one count. States of calamity were declared in San Miguel, Manila, Malabon and Cavite; NLEX was impassable for hours.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1,266,322 individuals affected at the 22 July count (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Southwest monsoon enhanced by Wipha and Co-may over Luzon.
events.notes: 30 is the final reported toll on the dedicated event page. Distinct from flood-philippines-2022 and flood-yagi-2024.

events.name: All Saints' Flood (1304)
events.geo_source: Stralsund (Wikipedia coordinates 54.3092°N, 13.0819°E); event page is the Pomeranian Baltic coast and the Rügen–Ruden land bridge lost in the surge
events.what_happened: A 1 November 1304 Baltic storm surge, named from Johann Berckmann's later Stralsund chronicle, struck Western Pomerania. Water piled in the central Baltic under westerlies then surged onto the Pomeranian coast when the wind shifted northeast. Chronicles say 271 people died. The flood drowned the Rügen–Ruden land bridge, opened a new Baltic channel and flooded villages on Ruden; later writers also link breaches at Usedom and the Swine.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Two villages on Ruden reported drowned; further land-loss along Mönchgut and Ruden
events.cause_summary: Baltic storm surge: westerly setup then a sudden northeasterly shift onto the Pomeranian coast.
events.notes: 271 is the death figure on the dedicated EN event page. The All Saints dating is from Berckmann (d. 1560) and is not independently confirmed, though 1304 is treated as probable. Distinct from flood-all-saints-1170 and flood-all-saints-1570.

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: All Saints' Flood (1304).

events.name: All Saints' Day Flood of 1436
events.geo_source: Tetenbüll (Wikipedia coordinates 54.3539°N, 8.8261°E); the event page says 180 died in this North Frisian village alone
events.what_happened: A 1 November 1436 storm tide hit the entire North Sea coast of the German Bight. In Tetenbüll alone 180 people died. Eidum on Sylt was destroyed and its people later founded Westerland; List on Sylt was abandoned and rebuilt further west. Dykes burst along the Oste and in Kehdingen. Pellworm was separated from Nordstrand and was not re-diked until 1550.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Eidum destroyed; List on Sylt abandoned and rebuilt; Pellworm separated from Nordstrand
events.cause_summary: North Sea storm tide on the German Bight (Allerheiligenflut).

sources.label: Wikipedia: All Saints Day Flood of 1436

events.notes: 180 is the only sourced village count on the dedicated page (Tetenbüll). Europe list says >180; further uncounted deaths likely. Distinct from flood-all-saints-1170, flood-all-saints-1304 and flood-all-saints-1570.

events.name: Storofsen flood
events.geo_source: Lillehammer (Wikipedia coordinates 61.1167°N, 10.4667°E) on Lake Mjøsa, which the event page says rose 10 m above normal
events.what_happened: Storofsen (Ofsen) struck eastern Norway in July 1789. The Glomma and Gudbrandsdalslågen overflowed and Lake Mjøsa rose ten metres above normal. Sixty-three people vanished, thousands of houses were destroyed and thousands of livestock were killed. Kvikne Copper Works were wrecked. Afterwards, fogd Jens Holmboe helped about forty flood-hit families from Gudbrandsdalen and Østerdalen resettle in Målselvdalen between 1791 and 1800.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands of houses destroyed; about 40 families later resettled in Målselv/Bardu
events.cause_summary: Heavy rain and snowmelt on the Glomma and Gudbrandsdalslågen.
events.notes: 63 vanished is the dedicated-page / Store norske leksikon figure. Exact July day not given; using month start. Nordic named historic event with a sourced pin.

events.name: 1910 European floods
events.region: Ahr valley / Kingdom of Hungary / Lake Lucerne
events.geo_source: Schuld (Wikipedia coordinates 50.4458°N, 6.8894°E); event page says the Ahr town lost at least 50 when a bridge gave way, part of ~200 German deaths
events.what_happened: Mid-June 1910 rains flooded Central Europe. The Ahr in Germany killed up to 200, including at least 50 in Schuld after a bridge collapsed; almost every bridge in the valley was destroyed. Switzerland lost at least 26 around Lake Lucerne. Contemporary reports said more than 1,000 died in the Kingdom of Hungary, 'exceeding all records'. Serbia's Great Morava killed 35 around Jagodina. The dedicated page totals 1,200+.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Villages washed away in Germany and Austria-Hungary; Lucerne and Zürich lighting systems failed
events.cause_summary: Several days of heavy rain across Central Europe in mid-June 1910.
events.notes: Infobox 1,200+ (~200 Germany, ~1,000 Hungary, 26 Switzerland, 35 Serbia). Using 1200 as the page total. Distinct from the 1910 Paris flood (0 deaths; not added).

events.name: Autumn 2000 Western Europe floods
events.geo_source: Uckfield (Wikipedia coordinates 50.97°N, 0.10°E); 12 October thunderstorms dropped 150 mm overnight and a lifeboat rescued 20 from a supermarket
events.river_or_basin: Medway / Ouse / Severn / Thames / Trent / Wharfe / Dee
events.what_happened: The wettest UK autumn since records began in 1766, as successive cyclones (including Nicole, Oratia and Rebekka) sat under a southerly jet. Kent and Sussex flooded in October; Shropshire, Worcestershire and Yorkshire followed in November. About 10,000 homes flooded in 700 places. Peak flows on the Thames, Trent, Severn, Wharfe and Dee were the highest in 60 years; York's Ouse was the highest since the 17th century. The dedicated page records 20 deaths and more than $2 billion damage across western Europe.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 10,000 homes flooded in 700 UK locations; 280,000 properties protected by defences
events.cause_summary: Slow-moving Atlantic cyclones and a southerly jet; wettest England-and-Wales autumn on the 1766 series.
events.notes: 20 is the dedicated-page death total. Distinct from flood-uk-2007, flood-uk-2009 and flood-uk-2019.
events.rainfall_mm: 150 mm overnight at Uckfield, 12 October; England and Wales autumn 503 mm
events.economic_damage: Estimated to exceed $2 billion (page infobox); UK flooded-property cost about £1 billion (ICE/Defra review)

changelog.change: Added from Wikipedia: Autumn 2000 Western Europe floods.

events.name: 2011 European floods
events.geo_source: Genoa (Wikipedia coordinates 44.4072°N, 8.9339°E); 356 mm in six hours on 4 November killed about six in the port city
events.what_happened: Autumn 2011 storms including Cyclone Meeno and Tropical Storm Rolf flooded Ireland, Italy, France and Spain. Dublin declared a major emergency after 85 mm in three hours on 24 October; two people died in Ireland. Liguria and Tuscany declared emergencies after floods killed 10 on 27 October. Genoa then took 356 mm in six hours on 4 November. Five died in southern France. The dedicated page totals 17 deaths and more than €926 million damage.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands of homes and businesses flooded in Ireland; ~750 evacuated in Fréjus, Roquebrune and Tourves
events.cause_summary: Autumn Mediterranean and Atlantic storms (Meeno, Rolf) on saturated catchments.
events.notes: 17 is the dedicated-page total (Italy + Ireland + France). Distinct from flood-var-2010 and flood-europe-2013.
events.rainfall_mm: 356 mm in 6 hours in Genoa, 4 November; 85 mm in 3 hours across Dublin, 24 October
events.economic_damage: >€926 million (2011); French preliminary €550–800 million

events.name: 2014 Bulgarian floods
events.geo_source: Asparuhovo, Varna (Wikipedia coordinates 43.179°N, 27.888°E); 13 of 16 deaths were in this district, including four children
events.what_happened: A Mediterranean cyclone dumped 60–155 L/m² — a full June's rain — on northeastern Bulgaria on 19 June 2014. Flash floods killed 16: 13 in Varna's Asparuhovo district (four of them children; the last, a six-year-old, found 26 June), one in Dobrich and two children at Tsani Ganchevo, Shumen. Houses were swept away; Albena hotels were evacuated when the Batova burst. Romania's Constanța coast was also hit. A national day of mourning was held on 23 June.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 1,000 Asparuhovo residents under evacuation orders by 27 June; 860 rescued or evacuated by the army nationwide
events.cause_summary: Mediterranean cyclone; extreme 24-hour and hourly rain on the Black Sea coast.
events.notes: 16 is the final dedicated-page tally after the 26 June recovery in Asparuhovo. Distinct from flood-balkans-2014 (May).
events.rainfall_mm: 90–155 L/m² in 24 h in Dobrich Province; 140–200 mm/h locally in the far northeast
events.warning_issued: NIMH Varna memo to the local administration on 18 June warning of intense rain and hail on the 19th
events.economic_damage: €311 million+ (page infobox); Varna infrastructure at least 30 million leva

events.name: 2016 European floods
events.geo_source: Simbach am Inn (Wikipedia coordinates 48.2667°N, 13.0167°E); the Simbach stream rose from 0.5 m to 5 m in hours; most Bavarian deaths were here
events.what_happened: Late-May and early-June 2016 rains flooded Germany, France, Belgium, Romania and neighbours. Braunsbach was buried under debris on 29 May. At least 11 died in Germany, including seven in Bavaria around Simbach am Inn and Triftern. The Seine closed the Louvre for two days and peaked near 6.3 m in Paris. Belgium lost three, France five and Romania two. The dedicated page totals 21 deaths; Bavarian insured damage alone exceeded €1 billion.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Town evacuated on the Seine; 200 evacuated in eastern Romania
events.cause_summary: Multi-day May–June thunderstorms on the Neckar, Danube, Rhine and Seine.
events.notes: 21 is the page total (table 11 DE + 5 FR + 3 BE + 2 RO). Distinct from flood-europe-2013, flood-europe-2018 and flood-europe-2021.
events.economic_damage: €1 billion+ in Bavaria alone (page infobox)

events.name: 2016 Macedonian floods
events.geo_source: Skopje (Wikipedia coordinates 41.9961°N, 21.4317°E); 93 mm in two hours on the capital, a full August month
events.what_happened: On the afternoon of 6 August 2016 a storm hit Skopje and western Macedonia. About 93 litres per square metre fell in two hours — a typical August month — with more than 800 lightning strikes in the first two hours and water 1.5 m deep. At least 21 people died. Three villages northeast of the city were cut off by landslides. The government declared a state of emergency and 8 August a national day of mourning.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Dozens injured or missing; army deployed; three villages cut off
events.cause_summary: Extreme August thunderstorm over Skopje; a month of rain in two hours.
events.notes: 21+ is the dedicated-page / Reuters / BBC figure. Distinct from flood-europe-2016 (May–June).
events.rainfall_mm: 93 mm in 2 hours in Skopje (Macedonia weather service)

events.name: 2019–20 United Kingdom floods
events.geo_source: Doncaster (Wikipedia coordinates 53.5228°N, 1.1325°W); River Don record levels and Fishlake/Bentley evacuations in November 2019
events.river_or_basin: Don / Derwent / Severn / Taff / Wye / Teme
events.what_happened: Saturated autumn catchments then Storms Ciara and Dennis produced the wettest February in England and Wales since 1766. November flooding killed former Derbyshire High Sheriff Annie Hall in the Derwent at Matlock and swamped Fishlake and Doncaster. Dennis then set record levels on the Wye and Taff; a woman was swept into the Teme near Tenbury and later found dead, and one person died in the Tawe near Swansea. The dedicated page records 11+ deaths and at least £150 million damage.
events.affected_or_evacuated: At least 1,758 properties flooded in November by council counts (Guardian); Fishlake, Pontypridd and Tenbury among the worst-hit
events.cause_summary: Saturated soils plus Storms Ciara and Dennis; wettest February in the England-and-Wales 1766 series.
events.notes: 11+ is the dedicated-page infobox. Distinct from flood-uk-2007, flood-uk-2009, flood-desmond-2015 and flood-autumn-2000.
events.warning_issued: Multiple Environment Agency severe flood warnings; South Wales Police major incident in February
events.economic_damage: At least £150 million (page infobox)

events.name: Storm Gloria floods
events.region: Valencian Community / Catalonia / Ebro delta / Balearics
events.geo_source: Tortosa at the Ebro (approx 40.8125°N, 0.5211°E); the storm surge ran up to 3 km inland through the delta rice paddies
events.what_happened: AEMET named Gloria on 18 January 2020. After landfall near Santander it stalled over the western Mediterranean. Rain, snow and a record surge (8.44 m significant wave height off Valencia) flooded southeastern Spain and the Balearics between 19 and 21 January. The Ebro delta was inundated up to 3 km inland. Across Spain 13–14 people were killed and three or four remained missing. Southern France evacuated about 2,000. Barx recorded 433 mm.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 2,000 homes evacuated in southern France; 130,000 Catalan students missed school; 337,000+ power outages
events.cause_summary: Named Mediterranean storm stalled off eastern Spain; record waves and multi-day rain.

events.economic_damage: At least $200 million (2020)

events.name: 2024 Bosnia and Herzegovina floods
events.geo_source: Jablanica (Wikipedia coordinates 43.6620°N, 17.7618°E); Donja Jablanica landslide and flash flood killed 19 of 27
events.what_happened: On the night of 3–4 October 2024 an Adriatic atmospheric river produced Bosnia's worst floods since 2014. Flash floods and landslides cut Jablanica, Konjic, Fojnica, Kiseljak and Kreševo. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead: 19 in Jablanica (mostly Donja Jablanica, where houses were buried and only a mosque minaret stood above the debris), five in Konjic and three in Fojnica. Entity governments declared 8 October a day of mourning. A quarry above Donja Jablanica was put under investigation.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Towns and villages cut off; Sarajevo–Mostar road closed; EU Civil Protection Mechanism activated
events.cause_summary: Atmospheric river over the Adriatic; flash floods and landslides on the Neretva.
events.notes: 27 is the dedicated-page total (19+5+3). AP 14 Oct still said 26 plus one missing; the page uses the later 27 after the last Konjic recovery. Distinct from flood-balkans-2014 and flood-central-europe-2024.

events.name: 1982 Nagasaki flood
events.geo_source: Nagasaki (Wikipedia coordinates 32.7447°N, 129.8736°E); named 7.23 Nagasaki Flood
events.what_happened: A Meiyu-front cloudburst on 23 July 1982 dumped 100–187 mm an hour on Nagasaki. Rivers overflowed and mudflows ran through the city; water reached 2.05 m above the surface. A Japanese government report recorded 299 dead in Nagasaki Prefecture and 23 in Kumamoto. JMA named the 23–25 July rains the July 1982 heavy rain; the prefecture calls it the 7.23 Nagasaki Flood.
events.cause_summary: Meiyu-front cloudburst; extreme hourly rain and landslides.

events.name: 2017 Northern Kyushu floods
events.geo_source: Asakura, Fukuoka (Wikipedia coordinates 33.4233°N, 130.6656°E); 500 mm in 12 hours on 5 July, a day above the city's July average
events.what_happened: Severe Tropical Storm Nanmadol made landfall near Nagasaki on 4 July 2017 and then stalled as a rainstorm over northern Kyushu. Asakura recorded 500 mm in 12 hours on 5 July and Fukuoka 774 mm in nine hours. Landslides hit 44 places and floods 38; more than 2,600 homes were destroyed. Forty-two people died by drowning or landslide. Damage was about ¥190 billion (US$1.68 billion). Prime Minister Abe cancelled a European trip to visit the area.

events.cause_summary: Nanmadol landfall then extreme orographic rain over Fukuoka and Ōita.

events.name: 2020 Korea floods
events.geo_source: Busan (Wikipedia coordinates 35.18°N, 129.075°E); early-July flooding in the south, where most 2020 fatalities occurred
events.what_happened: The 2020 East Asian rainy season, later extended by Typhoon Hagupit and Tropical Storm Jangmi, flooded southern South Korea from June into mid-August — the second-longest rainy season on record after 2013. Busan flooded in early July. As of 10 August 2020, 32 people had died in South Korea. Damage was put at ₩1.04 trillion (US$875 million). North Korea issued a red rainfall alert; KCNA reported damage but no official fatalities.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hundreds in COVID-constrained shelters; North Korean reconstruction in North Hwanghae later in the year
events.cause_summary: Record-length jangma, then Hagupit and Jangmi rainfall on the southern peninsula.
events.notes: 32 is the 10 August 2020 South Korea figure on the dedicated page. North Korean deaths not given. Distinct from flood-south-korea-2023 and flood-korea-2022.

events.name: 2022 South Korea floods
events.geo_source: Gangnam District (Wikipedia coordinates 37.4967°N, 127.0275°E); capital floods of 8 August, heaviest rain in 80 years
events.what_happened: On 8 August 2022 Seoul's heaviest rain in 80 years flooded Gangnam and neighbouring districts. Dongjak recorded 43 cm (17 in). The Han swelled on 10 August. At least nine people were killed, 2,800 buildings were damaged and 163 people in Seoul were made homeless. Landslide warnings covered 50 cities and towns. President Yoon warned of further rain.

events.cause_summary: Record urban cloudburst on Seoul; Han River overflow.
events.notes: 9 is the dedicated-page death total. Distinct from flood-korea-2020 and flood-south-korea-2023.

events.name: 2016 North Korean floods (Lionrock remnants)
events.geo_source: Hoeryong (Wikipedia coordinates 42.4333°N, 129.75°E); more than 104,000 lost clean water in the city; Tumen basin was the core of the disaster
events.what_happened: Remnants of Typhoon Lionrock combined with a China low to drop what KCNA called the heaviest North Hamgyong rain since 1945 (320 mm in two days at Kyonghung). The Tumen and tributaries flooded about 16,000 ha of farmland. Over 35,500 houses were damaged and about 25,000 destroyed; 107,000 people left their homes. A five-storey collapse in Ryanggang killed 34. Floods related to Lionrock killed at least 525 in North Korea. The government made a rare public appeal for international aid.

events.cause_summary: Lionrock remnants plus a China low; extreme Tumen-basin rain.

events.name: Hurricane Fifi flooding in Honduras
events.geo_source: Choloma (Wikipedia coordinates 15.6333°N, 88.00°W); a blocked Choloma River then a bridge-break flood killed an estimated 2,800–5,000 of the town's 7,000 people overnight
events.what_happened: Category 2 Hurricane Fifi brushed northern Honduras on 18–19 September 1974 and stalled rain on the mountains. About 610 mm fell in three days. A mudslide dammed the Choloma River; when a concrete bridge failed upstream on 20 September the release destroyed Choloma overnight (about 2,800–5,000 of 7,000 residents). Coastal towns including Omoa were wrecked. The banana crop was wiped out. The dedicated page totals 8,210 fatalities (third-deadliest Atlantic hurricane), almost all from freshwater flooding and mudslides, not wind.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 150,000–500,000 homeless (Red Cross vs Honduran government); 350,000 in shelters by 24 September
events.cause_summary: Slow hurricane rainfall and mountain runoff; Choloma landslide dam-break flood.
events.notes: 8,210 is the page's tabulated total (Honduras 8,000–10,000, Guatemala 200, El Salvador 10). Range 8,000–10,000 remains in many summaries. Flood-dominant, same treatment as flood-mitch-1998. Not a dam-structure failure.
events.rainfall_mm: About 610 mm (24 in) in three days over Honduras; 370 mm in four days at Chinandega, Nicaragua
events.economic_damage: $1.8 billion (1974 USD)

events.name: Hurricane Stan floods
events.geo_source: Santiago Atitlán (Wikipedia coordinates 14.6333°N, 91.2333°W); Stan's rainfall triggered the deadly Panabaj mudslide above the town, emblematic of the Guatemala toll
events.river_or_basin: Guatemalan highlands / Sierra Madre de Chiapas
events.what_happened: Hurricane Stan (October 2005) was a modest cyclone inside a much larger Central American rain event. Torrential rain set off mudslides and river floods in Guatemala, southern Mexico, El Salvador and neighbours. Guatemala took most of the 1,673 deaths, many in highland slides that erased villages (including Panabaj above Santiago Atitlán). In Mexico, Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca, Puebla and Quintana Roo flooded; 86 died in Chiapas. Regional damage was about $3.9 billion.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Tens of thousands displaced; 55,038 houses damaged in the five worst-hit Mexican states
events.cause_summary: Stan's broad rain shield; mudslides and river floods, especially in Guatemala.
events.notes: 1,673 is the dedicated-page regional death total, mostly Guatemala mudslides. Flood-dominant, same treatment as flood-mitch-1998 and flood-fifi-1974. Distinct from flood-guatemala-1949.
events.economic_damage: $3.9 billion across the region; Mex$13.7 billion direct damage in five Mexican states

events.name: 2023 Haiti floods
events.geo_source: Port-au-Prince (Wikipedia coordinates 18.5364°N, 72.3464°W); the event page says damage was particularly severe around the capital
events.what_happened: After late-May rains saturated soils, a stationary low flooded Haiti on 2–3 June 2023. Five departments were hit; Port-au-Prince was among the worst. As of 6 June the dedicated page records 51 dead, 140 injured and 18 missing. About 37,375 people were affected and 13,390 displaced; 13,591 homes were flooded and 820 destroyed. Three rivers isolated Jérémie. OCHA and civil protection led relief amid gang violence. Subsequent 4 and 6 June quakes (four more dead) are not in this flood tally.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 37,375 affected; 13,390 displaced; 13,591 homes flooded, 820 destroyed
events.cause_summary: Stationary low on already saturated soils; river overflows and landslides.
events.notes: 51 dead / 140 injured / 18 missing as of 6 June 2023 on the dedicated page (OCHA flash and PAHO sitrep). Distinct from flood-haiti-2004 and flood-matthew-haiti-2016.

events.name: 2022–2023 California floods
events.geo_source: Sacramento (Wikipedia coordinates 38.5817°N, 121.4944°W); Sacramento County had five of the storm deaths, the highest county toll
events.river_or_basin: Sacramento / Cosumnes / Salinas / Pajaro / Tulare Lake
events.what_happened: A train of atmospheric rivers from 31 December 2022 to 25 March 2023 flooded California and neighbouring Nevada. San Francisco had 5.46 in on 31 December, its second-wettest day. Levees failed on the Cosumnes and later the Pajaro; Tulare Lake refilled for the first time since 1997. At least 22 people died. About 200,000 customers lost power in the first storms and 6,000 were ordered to evacuate. Damage was about $4.6 billion. Newsom and Biden issued emergency and major-disaster declarations.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 6,000 ordered to evacuate; 200,000 homes and businesses lost power in December–January
events.cause_summary: Repeated atmospheric rivers after multi-year drought; levee breaks and valley flooding.
events.notes: 22+ is the dedicated-page death total. Distinct from flood-california-1862 and flood-los-angeles-1938.
events.rainfall_mm: 139 mm (5.46 in) in San Francisco on 31 December; 16-day area average 8.61 in to 11 January
events.warning_issued: California state of emergency 4 January 2023; federal emergency 9 January
events.economic_damage: $4.6 billion (2023 USD, NCEI billion-dollar disasters)

events.name: 2020 East Africa floods
events.geo_source: Nairobi (Wikipedia coordinates 1.2864°S, 36.8172°E); Kenya had 237 of the 453 deaths and 29 of 47 counties flooded
events.river_or_basin: Nzoia / East African Great Lakes / Horn catchments
events.what_happened: A positive Indian Ocean Dipole and a wet 2019 short-rains season left East Africa primed. Long rains from March 2020 then flooded Rwanda, Kenya, Somalia, Burundi, Ethiopia, Uganda, DRC, Djibouti and Tanzania. The dedicated page totals 453 deaths: 237 Kenya, 97 Rwanda, 44 DRC, 34 Ethiopia, 21 Somalia, 11 Uganda, 8 Djibouti, 1 Burundi. More than 700,000 people were affected; 100,000-plus were displaced in Kenya alone after the Nzoia overflowed in Busia and Siaya.

events.cause_summary: Positive IOD hangover plus extreme March–May long rains across East Africa.

events.name: Cyclone Freddy floods
events.geo_source: Blantyre (Wikipedia coordinates 15.7861°S, 35.0058°E); 192 of Malawi's 1,216 deaths were in the city, including at least 40 children
events.what_happened: Record-duration Cyclone Freddy made its final landfall near Quelimane, Mozambique, on 11 March 2023 and then dumped a month of rain in a day on southern Malawi. Flash floods and landslides, especially in Blantyre, Phalombe, Mulanje, Chikhwawa and Nsanje, killed 1,216 in Malawi (192 in Blantyre). Mozambique lost 198 and Madagascar 17. The dedicated page totals 1,434 dead, 2,004 injured and about US$1.53 billion damage. Malawi's hydro grid was shut; cholera surged.
events.affected_or_evacuated: ≥1.71 million affected; 508,244 displaced in 534 Malawi camps by 18 March; 180,000 displaced in Malawi at one count
events.cause_summary: Freddy's third landfall and stall; catastrophic Malawi flash floods.
events.notes: 1,434 is the dedicated-page total (Malawi 1,216, Mozambique 198, Madagascar 17, Zimbabwe 2, Mauritius 1). Flood-dominant inland, same treatment as flood-idai-2019. Distinct from flood-malawi-2015, flood-malawi-2026 and flood-mozambique-2026.
events.rainfall_mm: 458 mm in 24 hours in Phalombe District (record); many districts 300 mm/day
events.economic_damage: US$1.53 billion (page infobox); Malawi US$506.7 million

events.name: 2026 Afghanistan spring floods
events.geo_source: Jalalabad (Wikipedia coordinates 34.4342°N, 70.4478°E); OCHA says the east (Nangarhar 22,267 affected) was the worst-hit region
events.what_happened: From 26 March to 6 April 2026, rainfall and flash floods hit 31 of Afghanistan's 34 provinces, 165 districts and 546 villages. OCHA Flash Update #1 (7 April) reported at least 93 killed, 181 injured and four missing, with more than 73,300 people (10,634 families) affected. Some 9,010 homes were hit (1,338 destroyed). The east was worst — Nangarhar, Kunar and Laghman — with landslides on the Kabul–Jalalabad, Jalalabad–Asadabad and Jalalabad–Torkham roads. A 5 April Hindu Kush earthquake (14 dead in Kabul) is listed separately by OCHA and is not in the 93.
events.status: Assessments ongoing as of 7 April 2026; rains easing.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 73,300 people (10,634 families) affected; 1,338 homes destroyed, 7,672 damaged
events.cause_summary: Early-spring heavy rain and flash floods, worst in the east.

events.notes: 93 dead / 181 injured as of 7 April 2026 (OCHA). Distinct from flood-afghanistan-2024 and the 20–23 July 2026 Parun/Nuristan flash floods (23 dead). Earthquake deaths on 5 April are excluded.

events.name: 2023 Rwanda floods
events.geo_source: Gisenyi/Rubavu (Wikipedia coordinates 1.70°S, 29.25°E); most Western Province deaths were near Lake Kivu; the prime minister attended a Rubavu burial on 4 May
events.what_happened: After a wet start to 2023, extreme rain from about 18:00 local time on 2 May flooded north-western Rwanda overnight. The Sebeya burst its banks. Rutsiro, Nyabihu, Rubavu and Ngororero were worst hit; most Western Province deaths were near Lake Kivu. At least 135 people were killed, 110 injured and about 20,000 displaced. Some 5,100–5,963 homes were destroyed. The event sits on the 2023 African Great Lakes floods page, which also records far larger DRC Kalehe losses that overlap flood-drc-2024 and are not double-counted here.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 20,000 displaced; 5,100–5,963 homes destroyed and 2,500 damaged
events.cause_summary: Overnight 2 May cloudburst on saturated north-western hills; Sebeya overflow and landslides.
events.notes: 135 is the Rwanda figure on the dedicated Great Lakes page (Statesman / later tallies). Infobox 130 as of 3 May is stale. DRC Kalehe (~440) is not added — likely overlaps flood-drc-2024.

events.name: 2021 South Kalimantan floods
events.geo_source: Banjarmasin (Wikipedia coordinates 3.32°S, 114.5925°E); among the worst-hit cities on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: From 9 January 2021 South Kalimantan saw its first major flood in fifty years and the worst in ten. Rivers overflowed across Banjarmasin, Central Hulu Sungai and Tanah Laut. Fifteen people died and more than 100,000 were evacuated. WALHI blamed unreclaimed mine pits and oil-palm conversion as well as the rain. President Widodo visited on 18 January after a #KalselJugaIndonesia campaign over thin national coverage.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 100,000 evacuated; CNN Indonesia 18 January: 5 dead and 112,000 displaced at one count, later raised to 15
events.cause_summary: Intense January rain on degraded catchments; mine pits and oil palm cited by WALHI.
events.notes: 15 is the dedicated-page death total. Distinct from flood-jakarta-2007/2013/2020 and flood-sumatra-2025.

events.name: 1997 Badajoz floods
events.geo_source: Badajoz (Wikipedia coordinates 38°52′43″N 6°58′15″W); Cerro de Reyes on the Rivillas–Calamón confluence was the worst-hit barrio
events.what_happened: On the night of 5–6 November 1997 an explosively deepening Atlantic low dumped more than 100 l/m² across Badajoz province, 125 l/m² in the capital and 136 l/m² in Valverde de Leganés, with wind gusts to 130 km/h. The Rivillas and Calamón brooks burst through the southern barrio of Cerro de Reyes; Las Piletas also overflowed in Valverde. Twenty-two people died in Badajoz and three in Valverde de Leganés. Hundreds of families lost homes; later works spent more than €100 million to clear the floodplains and turn the brooks into parks.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hundreds of families; more than 1,000 homes lost in some press tallies
events.cause_summary: Explosive cyclogenesis and torrential rain on already wet soils; overflow of the Rivillas and Calamón.

events.name: 2008 Western Ukraine floods
events.geo_source: Ivano-Frankivsk (Wikidata 48.9228°N, 24.7106°E); worst-hit oblast on the dedicated uk wiki page
events.what_happened: Thunderstorm rains in the Carpathians from 23–27 July 2008 produced the largest flood in western Ukraine in about 60 years. The Verkhovna Rada declared six oblasts (Lviv, Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, Vinnytsia) zones of ecological emergency for 90 days. The Ukrainian Wikipedia page records 30 deaths, including six children. About 40,600 houses and 33,900 ha of farmland were inundated; 360 road bridges and 561 footbridges were damaged. OCHA sitrep 1 put Ukraine deaths at 30 by 31 July (36 across Ukraine/Moldova/Romania).
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 25,000 evacuated in Ukraine (OCHA 31 July); 40,703 houses flooded
events.cause_summary: Intense July thunderstorms on Carpathian catchments; deforestation cited by Ukrainian ecologists as an aggravating factor.

sources.label: Wikipedia (UK): Паводок на заході України 2008 року

events.notes: Dedicated uk wiki: 30 dead (6 children). OCHA IRA 2–4 Aug cited 36 dead (regional). Using the dedicated-page 30. Distinct from flood-europe-2009 and the thinner 2020 Western Ukraine page (4 deaths, not added).
events.economic_damage: UAH 3–4 billion (~US$650–870 million, OCHA)

events.name: July 2026 Nuristan / Parun floods
events.geo_source: Parun (Wikipedia coordinates 35.4167°N, 70.9169°E); provincial capital hit on 20 July
events.what_happened: A sudden flash flood struck Parun, capital of Nuristan, around 15:00 on 20 July 2026 after heavy rain in eastern Afghanistan. OCHA Flash Update 1 (21 July) cited ANDMA: 23 dead, 15 injured, others missing. Pajhwok on 23 July raised the toll to 24, including the provincial mayor and a battalion commander, with 85 injured. AtlasPress on 27 July reported local officials at 25 dead and 125 injured, with about US$40 million in damage and aid reaching 500 families. GloFAS/Floodlist summarised 23 dead and 125 injured, with five still missing on 26 July (WHO). Distinct from the March–April 2026 spring floods already on file.

events.name: 2017 Gujarat floods
events.geo_source: Palanpur (Wikipedia coordinates 24°10′21″N 72°26′05″E); headquarters of Banaskantha, among the worst-hit districts
events.what_happened: Simultaneous Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal lows produced excess monsoon rain across Gujarat from mid-July 2017. IMD: 559.4 mm statewide from 1–28 July against a 339.6 mm normal (+65%); Banaskantha, Patan, Gandhinagar, Morbi, Surendranagar, Mehsana and Sabarkantha saw 267% of normal in the worst belt. The dedicated page records 224 deaths in Gujarat between 1 June and 31 July, plus 16 in neighbouring Rajasthan. Distinct from the regional flood-south-asia-2017 wrapper (1,419).
events.cause_summary: Twin monsoon lows; extreme July rain on North Gujarat catchments.
events.notes: 224 is the dedicated-page Gujarat total (1 Jun–31 Jul). The 2017 South Asian floods page already on file uses 1,419 regional; this is the Gujarat event page.

events.name: 2020 Assam floods
events.geo_source: Guwahati (Wikipedia coordinates 26°10′20″N 91°44′45″E); principal city of the flooded Brahmaputra valley
events.what_happened: The 2020 Brahmaputra monsoon in Assam began in May and ran through the COVID-19 year. By October more than five million people were affected, 5,474 villages inundated and more than 150,000 people were in relief camps. The dedicated page records 123 flood deaths and a further 26 landslide deaths. Assam and Meghalaya had received 1,164 mm by 21 July against an 894 mm normal.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 5 million affected; 150,000+ in camps
events.cause_summary: Above-normal monsoon on the Brahmaputra and hill catchments.
events.notes: 123 flood deaths on the dedicated page; 26 additional landslide deaths left in notes. Distinct from flood-assam-2026 and flood-south-asia-2020 (wrapper, not added).

events.name: 2022 India–Bangladesh floods
events.geo_source: Sylhet (Wikidata 24.9°N, 91.8667°E); core of the 2022 northeastern India–Bangladesh flood
events.what_happened: From May 2022 deadly monsoon floods hit northeastern India and Bangladesh. The dedicated page says more than 9 million people were affected and around 300 were killed. By 22 June millions still needed food and medicine. A La Niña monsoon on the Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna and Barak–Surma–Kushiyara systems drove the inundation. Distinct from flood-pakistan-2022 and flood-assam-2026.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 9 million affected

events.name: 2012 North Korean floods
events.geo_source: Anju (Wikipedia coordinates 39°37′04″N 125°39′45″E); South Pyongan counties took the largest loss of life on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: Tropical Storm Khanun crossed into North Korea in mid-July 2012. The government later raised Khanun flood deaths from 8 to 88, with 134 injured; the worst loss of life was in two South Pyongan counties. About 62,900 people were left homeless. Further torrential rain on 29–30 July and more rain in August killed at least six additional people and prompted an international aid request.

events.name: 2018 North Korean floods
events.geo_source: Haeju (Wikipedia coordinates 38°02′N 125°43′E); capital of South Hwanghae, one of the two worst-hit provinces
events.what_happened: Floods beginning 28 August 2018, driven in part by Tropical Storm Soulik, killed at least 76 people in North Korea, left about 75 missing, destroyed more than 800 buildings and left about 10,700 people homeless. North and South Hwanghae were the worst-hit provinces; Red Cross volunteers ran search and rescue. Landslides followed the rain.

events.name: 2020 Yemen floods
events.region: Marib / Hajjah / Al Hudaydah / Aden / Taizz
events.geo_source: Sanaa (Wikidata 15.35°N, 44.2°E); capital; floods ran April–August across 19 governorates
events.what_happened: Flash floods and torrential rain hit Yemen from April to August 2020. The dedicated page records at least 172 deaths and damage to homes and UNESCO-listed sites. By April about 21,240 families in 13 governorates were affected; by August about 300,000 people had lost homes, crops or livestock. By September nearly 96,000 families were affected in 189 districts of 19 governorates. Marib, Amran, Hajjah, Al Hudaydah, Taizz, Lahj, Aden and Abyan were among the worst-hit, with at least 148 killed in that belt.

events.notes: Lede 172. Sub-tally 148 in the most-affected governorates left in notes. Distinct from flood-yemen-2025 and flood-yemen-2026.

events.name: 2013 Sardinia floods (Cyclone Cleopatra)
events.geo_source: Olbia (Wikipedia coordinates 40°55′N 9°30′E); worst-hit city on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: Cyclone Cleopatra (Ruven) stalled over the western Mediterranean on 17–19 November 2013 and dumped more than 440 mm of rain in 90 minutes on the morning of the 19th. Rivers overflowed around Olbia, Nuoro, Oristano and Gallura; water reached 3 m in Olbia. At least 18 people died and about 3,000 were left homeless. Prime Minister Enrico Letta called it a national tragedy; a national day of mourning was set for 22 November. Damage was put above €1 billion.

events.cause_summary: Slow-moving Mediterranean cyclone (Cleopatra/Ruven) with embedded thunderstorms.
events.notes: 18 deaths on the dedicated page. Distinct from flood-emilia-2023, flood-messina-2009 and flood-europe-2011.

events.name: 2026 Zona da Mata floods
events.region: Zona da Mata / Minas Gerais / Juiz de Fora / Ubá
events.location_label: Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, Brazil
events.geo_source: Juiz de Fora (Wikidata 21.75°S, 43.35°W); principal city on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: Extreme February 2026 rain on already wet ground produced floods and landslides across Minas Gerais' Zona da Mata. Juiz de Fora recorded 752.4 mm in the month against a 170 mm normal, including 227.6 mm in 48 hours around 22–24 February. The Paraibuna overflowed in Juiz de Fora; the Pomba rose in Cataguases. The dedicated page records 73 deaths after the last missing body was found on 17 March. About 5,510 residents were displaced as of 27 February. President Lula visited on 28 February. The deadliest Brazilian rain disaster since the 2024 Rio Grande do Sul floods already on file.

events.name: 2019 South Sulawesi floods
events.geo_source: Makassar (Wikipedia coordinates 5°08′S 119°25′E); provincial capital flooded to roof level; Gowa had 45 of 68 deaths
events.river_or_facility: Bili-Bili Dam (gates opened; not a structural failure)
events.what_happened: Heavy rain from 21 January 2019 overfilled the Jeneberang and forced the opening of Bili-Bili Dam gates in Gowa; other rivers including the Walanae also overflowed. Water reached roof level (over 1.5 m) in parts of Makassar. By 25–26 January 68 people were dead, 47 injured and 6 missing, 45 of the dead in Gowa. BNPB recorded 3,321 evacuees from 78 villages; police counted 7,364 in camps in Makassar, Gowa and Jeneponto. Officials called it the worst flood in a decade. Silting and illegal mining were blamed. Gate opening was an operational release, not a dam collapse.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 3,321 evacuated (BNPB); 7,364 in camps (police); 5,825 'impacted'
events.cause_summary: Extreme January rain; Jeneberang overflow and operational opening of Bili-Bili gates.
events.notes: 68 dead, 6 missing (Channel NewsAsia 26 Jan). Bili-Bili watergates were opened — operational release, not a structure failure, so kept on the flood DB. Distinct from flood-kalimantan-2021 and flood-north-luwu-2020.

events.name: 2020 Kerala floods
events.geo_source: Painavu / Idukki (Wikipedia coordinates 9°50′56″N 76°56′13″E); Idukki was the worst landslide/flood district (Pettimudi)
events.what_happened: The 2020 southwest monsoon was Kerala’s third straight severe flood year. All 14 districts were affected. MHA sitrep 18 August recorded 104 dead, 12 missing and 40 injured, 1,670 villages hit and about ₹19,000 crore damage. The Pettimudi tea-estate debris flow in Idukki on 6 August killed 66. Idukki, Wayanad, Malappuram and Kottayam flooded on 7 August. The dedicated page also mentions the 7 August Calicut runway overrun (21 dead) as a rain-related incident; that crash is not treated here as a flood death.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 6,300 relief camps; 220 houses fully destroyed, 5,190 partly (MHA 18 Aug)
events.cause_summary: August cloudbursts on the Western Ghats; rain-induced debris flows.
events.notes: 104 is the MHA 18 Aug monsoon/flood/landslide total on the dedicated page. Pettimudi landslide 66 is inside that tally. Air India Express 1344 (21 dead) is mentioned on the page but is a crash, not added to deaths. Distinct from flood-kerala-2018.
events.economic_damage: About ₹19,000 crore (page estimate)

events.name: 2021 Niger floods
events.geo_source: Niamey (Wikipedia coordinates 13°30′54″N 2°07′03″E); capital among the worst-hit areas; Maradi had the most affected
events.what_happened: Niger’s 2021 rainy season produced recurring floods from June to September. The Ministry of Humanitarian Action reported 77 dead and more than 238,000 affected by 24 September; UNICEF’s year-end total was 250,331 affected and 77 dead, with Maradi (104,032), Zinder and Tahoua worst hit. About 12,000 houses collapsed and nearly 6,000 ha of cropland flooded. Niamey saw house collapses in Yantala and isolation of some districts. Dam/dike releases are listed as a contributing factor, not a named structure collapse.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 250,331 affected (UNICEF year-end); 12,000 houses collapsed
events.cause_summary: Seasonal rains, blocked channels and river overflow; dam releases cited as a contributing factor, not a collapse.
events.notes: 77 is the dedicated-page / UNICEF year-end figure. Distinct from flood-nigeria-2012/2022. Not the dam-mixed 2025 Nigeria/Mokwa event.

events.name: 2020 Karachi floods
events.geo_source: Karachi (Wikidata 24.86°N, 67.01°E)
events.what_happened: Record monsoon rain on 24–27 August 2020 produced what the dedicated page calls Karachi’s worst flooding in almost a century. At least 41 people were killed. The city drainage system failed under urban rain; streets and neighbourhoods flooded across the port metropolis.
events.cause_summary: Record late-August monsoon on Karachi’s drainage network.
events.notes: 41 on the dedicated page. Distinct from flood-pakistan-2010/2012/2022/2025 and flood-pakistan-afghan-2013.

events.name: Hurricane Jeanne flooding in Haiti
events.geo_source: Gonaïves (Wikipedia coordinates 19°26′44″N 72°41′18″W); 2,826 of 3,006 Haiti deaths
events.what_happened: Hurricane Jeanne passed north of Haiti on 17–19 September 2004 and dropped up to 330 mm of rain in 36 hours. Floods and landslides killed 3,006 people in Haiti, one of the deadliest Atlantic hurricanes on record. In Gonaïves floodwater reached about 5 m and 2,826 people died. Nord-Ouest (mostly Port-de-Paix) recorded 65 deaths and about 300,000 homeless; 47 died elsewhere. About 5,490 houses were damaged or destroyed. Deforestation and the May 2004 Hispaniola floods (already on file) worsened the impact.

events.cause_summary: Jeanne rainfall on deforested Haitian catchments; Gonaïves inundated.

events.name: 1981 Sichuan floods
events.geo_source: Chengdu (Wikidata 30.66°N, 104.0633°E); Anshun Bridge collapse is the city’s emblematic 13 July scene
events.what_happened: A deep southwest vortex and Bengal-Bay moisture produced more than two days of extreme rain over Sichuan in July 1981. Chengdu streets flooded on 13 July and Anshun Bridge was washed away. Chongqing’s Cuntan gauge peaked at 85,700 m³/s and 191.41 m after six days of rain. Jintang county was inundated.

events.name: 2013 Southwest China floods
events.geo_source: Dujiangyan (Wikipedia coordinates 31°00′11″N 103°37′08″E); 94 cm rain 8–9 July and the 10 July landslide

A Tongkou River bridge failed; Qushan (the former Beichuan seat, an earthquake memorial) stood in 7 m of water. A 10 July landslide at Dujiangyan buried homes. The dedicated page records at least 73 dead and 180 missing, about 6 million people disrupted and US$7.52 billion damage. Xinhua on 16 July cited 58 dead and 175 missing in Sichuan alone.

events.name: 2020 Afghanistan floods
events.geo_source: Charikar (Wikipedia coordinates 35°00′47″N 69°10′08″E); site of the 26 August pulse on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: A series of Afghan flash floods began in June 2020; the largest pulse was on 26 August at Charikar, Parwan. That August flood killed at least 179 people and injured 212, destroying hundreds of houses. The Ministry of Disaster Management also reported casualties in Kapisa, Maidan Wardak, Nangarhar, Panjshir and Paktia. events.name: 2013 Pakistan–Afghanistan floods
events.geo_source: Karachi (Wikidata 24.86°N, 67.01°E); hardest-hit Pakistani city on the dedicated page
events.what_happened: Unusually heavy rain from 31 July 2013 brought flash floods to Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan. The dedicated-page infobox records 187 deaths. Pakistan reached 83 dead by 13 August (NDMA), with Karachi the hardest-hit city; more than 66,000 people were affected. In Afghanistan, Surobi District alone lost 61 people and about 500 mud-brick homes; Khost and Nangarhar recorded 24 deaths, and a 10 August flood near Kabul killed 22 more. Afghan deaths were above 90 by 14 August.
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 66,000 affected in Pakistan
events.cause_summary: Early-August monsoon flash floods on both sides of the Durand Line.
events.notes: 187 is the dedicated-page infobox. Distinct from flood-kashmir-2014 (September 2014, 557) and flood-pakistan-2010/2012.

events.name: 2020 Hyderabad floods
events.geo_source: Hyderabad (Wikidata 17.3617°N, 78.4747°E)
events.river_or_facility: Himayat Sagar (floodgates lifted at FRL; not a structural failure)
events.what_happened: Deep Depression BOB 02 made landfall in Andhra Pradesh on 13 October 2020 and stalled over south-central India. Ghatkesar, a Hyderabad suburb, recorded 324 mm in a day. Himayat Sagar gates were lifted at full-reservoir level and the Musi ran over two causeways. The dedicated-page infobox records 104 deaths (72 in Telangana, including 33 in Hyderabad; 28 in Maharashtra; 4 in Vijayawada). Telangana put damage near ₹9,000 crore. A second pulse on 18 October killed two more in Hyderabad.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 40,000 families displaced; 2,100+ evacuated near Gurram Cheruvu
events.cause_summary: BOB 02 remnants; urban flash flood on the Musi. Himayat Sagar gates opened at FRL — operational, not a dam failure.
events.notes: 104 is the dedicated-page infobox total. Telangana-only 72 (ToI 19 Oct) left in notes. Distinct from flood-chennai-2015 and flood-kerala-2020.
events.rainfall_mm: 324 mm in one day at Ghatkesar
events.economic_damage: About ₹9,000 crore in Telangana

events.name: 2012 Luzon southwest monsoon floods (Habagat)
events.region: Metro Manila / Marikina / Calabarzon / Central Luzon
events.geo_source: Marikina (Wikipedia coordinates 14°39′02″N 121°06′09″E); Marikina River peaked at 20.6 m on 7 August
events.what_happened: From 1–8 August 2012 Typhoon Saola (Gener) and later Typhoon Haikui pulled a Habagat (southwest monsoon) over Luzon. Parts of Metro Manila received 1,007 mm in 72 hours. The Marikina River reached 20.6 m on 7 August (banks ~16 m). La Mesa Reservoir overflowed into the Tullahan. NDRRMC sitrep 16 August recorded 89 dead; the lede also cites 95. About 8,428 homes were destroyed and 6,706 damaged. Losses were at least ₱604.63 million. Compared at the time to Ondoy 2009 (already on file).
events.affected_or_evacuated: More than 1 million families affected at the 8 August peak; 250,000 left homes when a third of the city flooded
events.cause_summary: Habagat enhanced by Saola and Haikui; Marikina and Tullahan overflow.
events.notes: 89 is NDRRMC sitrep 16 Aug. Lede 95 left in notes. Distinct from flood-ondoy-2009 and flood-washi-2011.

events.economic_damage: At least ₱604.63 million (US$14.31 million)

events.name: 2020 North Luwu flash flood
events.geo_source: Masamba (Wikipedia coordinates 2°33′11″S 120°19′41″E); North Luwu capital
events.what_happened: On the night of 13 July 2020 more than 300–400 mm of rain produced a flash flood in North Luwu, South Sulawesi. Mud ran up to 5 m thick. Local officials reported 38 dead and 40 still missing. 4,390 houses were damaged and 15,994 people affected; schools, bridges, two dams (damage, not a named collapse) and more than 200 ha of farmland were hit. The regent declared a 30-day emergency.

events.cause_summary: Overnight cloudburst and flash flood at Masamba.
events.notes: 38 dead, 40 missing on the dedicated page (local officials). Distinct from flood-sulawesi-2019 and flood-jakarta-2020.
