events.name: 2025 New South Wales floods
events.geo_source: Taree (Wikipedia coordinates 31°54′S 152°27′E); Manning River ground zero
events.what_happened: A near-stationary Pacific trough sat over the NSW Mid North Coast and Hunter from 20–25 May 2025. Taree had 427 mm in two days and the Manning River passed 6 m, breaking an almost 100-year mark. Five people died (one woman and four men). About 48,000 people were isolated and almost 10,000 homes were at risk. Premier Minns said tributary rises had not been seen since 1920; researchers called it a 1-in-500-year event for the region. SES carried out hundreds of rescues.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 48,000 isolated; almost 10,000 homes at risk
events.cause_summary: Stationary trough and easterly moisture; record May rain at Taree.
events.notes: 5 deaths on the dedicated page. Famous named 2025 event with a pin; kept despite a modest toll. Distinct from flood-australia-east-2022 and flood-hunter-1955.
events.return_period: 1-in-500-year (Natural Hazards Research Australia, via Wikipedia)
events.rainfall_mm: 427 mm in two days at Taree; 533 mm at Careys Peak

events.name: 2006 Mid-Atlantic United States flood
events.geo_source: Binghamton (Wikipedia coordinates 42°05′56″N 75°54′39″W); Southern Tier / Susquehanna was among the worst U.S. belts
events.what_happened: A stalled jet stream and a tropical moisture feed produced prolonged rain from the Carolinas to Upstate New York between 25 June and 5 July 2006. The dedicated page records at least 16 flood-related deaths and about US$1 billion damage — the region’s worst flooding since Hurricane David (1979). The Susquehanna at Bainbridge crested 14 ft above flood stage; more than 5,000 people evacuated in Broome County. Along the Delaware, Trenton and Easton flooded; Wilkes-Barre’s levee saw levels compared with Agnes. Lake Needwood’s leaking earthen dam forced 2,200 evacuations in Maryland; the dam did not fail.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 5,000+ evacuated in Broome County; 1,000+ in Trenton; 200,000 northeastern Pennsylvania residents moved at peak
events.cause_summary: Stalled jet stream and tropical moisture; widespread river flooding. Needwood dam leaked but did not fail.
events.notes: 16 deaths, ~US$1 billion on the dedicated page. Distinct from flood-agnes-1972, flood-irene-2011 and flood-ida-2021. Needwood/Laurel dam scares were evacuations, not failures.
events.economic_damage: About US$1 billion (2006 USD)

events.name: January 2009 Fiji floods
events.geo_source: Nadi (Wikipedia coordinates 17°48′S 177°25′E); western Viti Levu was the worst-hit dry-side belt
events.river_or_basin: Nadi / Ba / western Viti Levu rivers
events.what_happened: Tropical Depression 04F, an active monsoon trough and the South Pacific Convergence Zone produced consecutive January 2009 rain events over Fiji. Floodwaters reached about 3 m on the ordinarily dry west of Viti Levu. Eleven people were killed (six drownings, two in a landslide, three teenagers among the dead). More than 6,000 people went to 114 shelters; a state of emergency and curfews followed. Sugarcane was heavily damaged. The Office of the Prime Minister’s consolidated report put losses at FJD 112.99 million (about US$64.2 million).

events.name: Kopuawhara flash flood of 1938
events.geo_source: Wairoa (Wikipedia 39°02′06″S 177°25′05″E); mass grave of 11 victims is in Wairoa cemetery; camp was on the Waiau / Kopuawhara Stream near Mahia
events.what_happened: A cloudburst sent a 5 m wall of water down the already-high Waiau Stream at 03:00 on 19 February 1938, destroying Public Works railway Camp No. 4 at Kaiangapiri in the Kopuawhara Valley. Twenty men and Martha Quinn were killed; two bodies were never found. About 11 men who took refuge in a works truck were swept away. Downstream Camp No. 2 was warned in time. Rain gauges recorded 8 in the day before and 20 in within 10 hours; peak flow was calculated at 33,900 cusecs against a normal 27. The event exceeded a 150-year rainfall.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Camp No. 4 destroyed; Camp No. 2 (47 men) evacuated
events.cause_summary: Cloudburst flash flood on the Waiau / Kopuawhara Stream through a railway construction camp.
events.notes: 21 (20 men + Martha Quinn) on the dedicated page and NZ History. Distinct from flood-gabrielle-2023 and flood-auckland-2023.
events.return_period: Exceeded 150-year rainfall (event page)
events.rainfall_mm: About 200 mm the day before; 510 mm in 10 hours before the surge (8 in / 20 in)

events.name: April 2014 Solomon Islands floods (Cyclone Ita precursor)
events.geo_source: Honiara (Wikipedia 9°25′55″S 159°57′20″E); Mataniko River burst its banks through the capital on 3 April
events.what_happened: A slow tropical low that later became Cyclone Ita dumped more than 1,000 mm in four days at Gold Ridge (500 mm in 24 hours) and 732 mm at the Honiara gauge. The Mataniko broke its banks on 3 April, washing away houses and the capital’s two main bridges. NEOC sitrep 11 and OCHA recorded 22 confirmed deaths (18 in Honiara, 2 Guadalcanal, 2 Isabel) and about 50,000 affected; peak displacement was around 10,000 in nearly 30 centres. Losses were SI$787.3 million (US$107.8 million), about 9.2% of GDP. The government declared Honiara and Guadalcanal a disaster zone.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 50,000 affected; ~10,000 displaced at peak in nearly 30 centres
events.cause_summary: Precursor tropical low to Cyclone Ita; Mataniko flash flood through Honiara.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Solomon Islands Flash Floods – Apr 2014

events.name: Cyclone Guba floods in Papua New Guinea
events.location_label: Popondetta, Oro Province, Papua New Guinea
events.geo_source: Popondetta (Wikipedia 8°45′56″S 148°14′05″E); provincial capital and worst-hit Oro centre
events.what_happened: Rare Coral Sea Cyclone Guba formed near New Guinea on 13 November 2007 and meandered offshore for a week. Six days of torrential rain — the worst in 30 years, residents said — produced widespread floods and landslides in Oro Province. The dedicated page records 149 confirmed deaths there, about 2,000 evacuated, roads and bridges washed away, and Popondetta’s water, power and air links cut. About 145,000 people were affected in Oro. PNG declared a state of emergency. Infobox damage is US$71.4 million; another passage cites more than 500 million kina.

events.cause_summary: Slow Coral Sea cyclone; six days of rain and landslides in Oro.

events.name: 2023 Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods
events.geo_source: Auckland (Wikipedia 36°50′57″S 174°45′55″E); West Auckland and the North Shore were worst hit
events.what_happened: A stalled atmospheric river dumped a summer’s rain on Auckland in one day on 27 January 2023 — NIWA called it a 1-in-200-year event and the city’s wettest day on record (258 mm at the airport; 265 mm at Māngere). Four people died (two drowned in Wairau Valley, one in a Remuera slip, one drowned at Onewhero). Auckland Airport’s runway and terminals flooded; 6,000–8,000 homes needed assessment. Perils later put insured loss at NZ$2.2 billion. Distinct from Cyclone Gabrielle two weeks later (already flood-gabrielle-2023).
events.affected_or_evacuated: 6,000–8,000 homes assessed; thousands evacuated
events.cause_summary: Stalled atmospheric river; urban flash flooding. Ageing stormwater cited.
events.notes: 4 deaths on the dedicated page. Distinct from flood-gabrielle-2023 (11 deaths, 12–16 Feb). Auckland is thin in Oceania despite being NZ’s costliest non-earthquake weather event at the time.
events.return_period: NIWA: 1-in-200-year daily rainfall
events.rainfall_mm: Auckland Airport 258 mm / 1 day; Māngere 265 mm; Albert Park 299.5 mm / 34 h
events.economic_damage: NZ$2.2 billion insured (Perils); recovery cited around NZ$4 billion

events.name: 2023 Nova Scotia floods
events.geo_source: Halifax (Wikipedia 44°38′51″N 63°35′26″W); deaths recovered in West Hants, Kings and Brooklyn; Halifax–Hants–Lunenburg–Queens were the worst-hit municipalities
events.river_or_basin: Avon / St. Croix / South Shore rivers
events.what_happened: Parts of Nova Scotia received 250–300 mm of rain in 24 hours on 21–22 July 2023. A two-week provincial state of emergency followed. Four people died: a man in West Hants, two children whose remains were found in Brooklyn, and a youth found about 75 km from the disappearance site on 1 August. About 500 road sections and 48 bridges were damaged; the CN line south of Truro washed out. Aon estimated about US$200 million damage. CTV called it beyond a once-in-a-century event.
events.cause_summary: Extreme 24-hour rainfall; flash floods and washed-out roads across central Nova Scotia.
events.notes: 4 deaths on the dedicated page (all four missing recovered). Canada still thin outside Hazel/Saguenay/Red River/Alberta/BC.

events.name: 2022 Chad floods
events.geo_source: N'Djamena (Wikipedia 12°06′19″N 15°02′41″E); Eighth District remained underwater into September
events.what_happened: Chad’s heaviest rains since 1990, from July 2022, flooded large parts of N'Djamena — the Eighth District was reachable only by boat into September. OCHA recorded 22 deaths by mid-August and about 442,000 people affected or displaced by the end of August. About 2,700 ha of cropland was destroyed in August. Officials called the flooding catastrophic. Neighbouring West and Central African countries had the same above-normal rains; this is the Chad-only dedicated page, not the 2022 Africa wrapper.

events.cause_summary: Heaviest rains since 1990; Chari–Logone and urban flooding in N'Djamena.

events.name: 2019 Kerala floods
events.geo_source: Wayanad district (Wikipedia 11°37′35″N 76°05′20″E); Wayanad, Malappuram, Kozhikode and Idukki were among the worst-hit
events.what_happened: A second consecutive August monsoon disaster hit Kerala from 8 August 2019. IMD issued a red alert in nine northern and central districts. As of 19 August, 121 people were dead, about 200,000 were in 1,318 relief camps, 1,789 houses were fully damaged and 14,542 partly damaged, and about 80 landslides occurred in two days. Cochin airport operations were suspended until 15:00 on 11 August. KSDMA damage was put at ₹2,101.9 crore (about US$220 million). Distinct from the larger 2018 Kerala floods already on file.

events.cause_summary: Arabian Sea depression and monsoon convection; floods and landslides across northern/central Kerala.

events.name: 2026 Kerala floods
events.region: Central and southern Kerala / Pamba basin
events.geo_source: Pathanamthitta (Wikipedia 9°15′53″N 76°47′13″E); Vadasserikkara 361 mm and the Pamba basin were the named highland focus

On 1 August several stations exceeded 300 mm (Vadasserikkara 361 mm, Athikkayam 357 mm, Angamoozhy 307 mm). The Pamba, Manimala and Meenachil overflowed. The dedicated page records at least 28 confirmed deaths and 4 missing, plus blocked transport. Distinct from flood-kerala-2018/2019/2020.

events.geo_source: Khartoum (Wikipedia 15°36′N 32°30′E); Kassala, West Kordofan and Khartoum were the worst-hit states
events.what_happened: Extreme rainfall from July to November 2018 flooded Kassala, West Kordofan and Khartoum. By 16 August at least 23 people were dead and over 60 injured (FloodList). Songkhla was declared a disaster zone. Local claims of 550–1,000+ Songkhla deaths are in notes. Distinct from flood-sumatra-2025 (Indonesia 1,201).

events.name: Tropical Storm Talas floods (Kii Peninsula)
events.geo_source: Nachikatsuura (Wikipedia 33°38′N 135°56′E); Wakayama recorded the most deaths
events.what_happened: Slow-moving Severe Tropical Storm Talas made landfall near Aki, Kōchi, on 3 September 2011 and stalled over the Kii Peninsula, dumping record rain (Wakayama/Nara/Mie towns became lakes; one site beat Takachiho’s 1,322 mm September 2005 mark). events.name: Typhoon Kathleen floods (Kantō 1947)
events.geo_source: Kazo (Wikipedia 36°07′53″N 139°36′06″E); Tone River embankment-collapse memorial is in Kazo
events.what_happened: Typhoon Kathleen approached the Bōsō Peninsula on 15 September 1947 and activated a stagnant front, producing record Kantō–Tōhoku rain. The Tone and Arakawa overflowed; Tokyo, Gunma, Saitama, Tochigi, Ibaraki and Chiba flooded, and the Kitakami hit Ichinoseki. The infobox lists 1,077 dead and 853 missing; the lede says the floods killed at least 1,692. A victim memorial stands in Kazo, Saitama, at a Tone breach.
events.cause_summary: Rain-typhoon; Tone and Arakawa riverine flooding across Kantō.
events.notes: Infobox 1,077 dead + 853 missing; lede at least 1,692. Using 1,077. Japan historic gap-fill. Distinct from flood-kanogawa-1958 and flood-hanshin-1938.

events.name: 1958 Kanogawa Typhoon flood (Typhoon Ida)
events.geo_source: Numazu (Wikipedia 35°05′44″N 138°51′48″E); Kanogawa basin on the Izu Peninsula was the namesake worst-hit valley
events.what_happened: Typhoon Ida — the Kanogawa Typhoon — struck the Izu Peninsula and Kantō on 26 September 1958 as a rain-typhoon. It caused more than 1,900 landslides, flooded a record 520,000 homes, destroyed 2,118 houses and killed 1,269 (381 of them missing and presumed dead). JMA gave it a special local name after the Kano River disaster. Damage was about US$50 million (1958) / ¥20.6 billion. Worst Japanese typhoon since the 1934 Muroto storm.

events.name: 2014 Hiroshima landslides and flash floods
events.geo_source: Hiroshima city (Wikipedia 34°23′29″N 132°27′07″E); Asakita and Asaminami wards were hardest hit; page also gives 34°29′13″N 132°29′38″E
events.what_happened: More than 200 mm of rain in a few hours on 20 August 2014 triggered 166 slope failures (107 debris flows, 59 shallow slides) into northern Hiroshima neighbourhoods, especially Yagi and Asaminami/Asakita. Asakita-ku recorded 217.5 mm from 01:30–04:30. The dedicated page records 74 deaths and 69 injuries (infobox; 44 injuries also cited). An evacuation advisory came only at 04:15. The event is also catalogued as the Heisei 26 19 August heavy-rain disaster.

events.name: 2000 Tōkai heavy rain (東海豪雨)
events.geo_source: Nagoya (Wikipedia 35°11′N 136°54′E); Shinkawa breach and Nonami inundation were inside the city

The Shinkawa levee breached for about 100 m; at least 10 other Aichi breaches and Shōnai overflow at Shimonoisshiki followed. Nonami (Tenpaku) saw house-high inundation and a flooded sakura-dōri subway. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen recorded its worst delay (Nozomi 20, 22 h 21 min). ja Wikipedia infobox: 10 dead, 115 injured, 22,894 houses above-floor flooded, about ¥850 billion damage. Gifu’s Ena district (Keinan heavy rain) was also hard hit.

events.name: 1994 West and North River floods
events.geo_source: Wuzhou (Wikipedia 23°28′36″N 111°16′44″E); streets flooded for 45 days, depths over 8 m, peak 25.91 m on 19 June
events.what_happened: The largest West and North River flood since the founding of the PRC, and the second-largest of the 20th century on those rivers, hit Guangdong and Guangxi in June–July 1994. Official figures: 17.765 million people and 18.75 million mu of farmland affected in 109 counties; Wuzhou’s 19 June crest 25.91 m left streets under more than 8 m for 45 days. Sourced split: June flood 371 dead (145 in Guangdong); July flood 109 dead in Guangdong. Combined 480. Direct losses cited from 28.2 to 63.2 billion yuan depending on the table.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 17.765 million affected (official two-province figure)
events.cause_summary: June and July 1994 Xijiang/Beijiang basin floods, largest PRC-era event on those rivers.
events.notes: 480 = 371 (June, two-province) + 109 (July, Guangdong) on the zh page. EN title missing; zh wiki is enough. Distinct from flood-china-1931 and flood-yangtze-1998.
events.return_period: Largest PRC-era Xijiang/Beijiang flood; 20th-century no. 2 on those rivers (zh page)
events.inundation_area: 18.75 million mu farmland (official)
events.economic_damage: About 28.2–63.2 billion yuan depending on the sourced table

events.name: 2011 China floods
events.region: Yangtze basin / central and southern China
events.geo_source: Wuhan (Wikipedia 30°35′42″N 114°17′51″E); Hubei capital flooded and lost power; 12–13 provinces hit
events.what_happened: June–September 2011 rains flooded central and southern China after a spring drought. The National Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters total on 30 June was at least 239 dead, 86 missing, 36.7 million affected, about 106,500 houses and 1.16 million ha of crops destroyed, and 43.2 billion yuan (US$6.65 billion) losses. A Yangtze level-4 alert evacuated 555,000. Wuhan flooded; Guizhou’s Wangmo saw 200-year hourly rain. Same year-event pattern as flood-china-2010/2016/2017/2020.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 36.7 million affected; 555,000 evacuated on the Yangtze level-4 alert
events.cause_summary: Prolonged June rains across 12–13 provinces after drought; Yangtze and southern floods.
events.notes: 239 dead, 86 missing (NFCDRH 30 Jun). Using 239. Distinct from flood-china-2010 and flood-beijing-2012.
events.inundation_area: About 1.16 million ha of crops destroyed
events.economic_damage: 43.2 billion yuan / US$6.65 billion (NFCDRH 30 Jun)

events.name: 2015 Kantō–Tōhoku heavy rain (Kinugawa / Jōsō)
events.geo_source: Jōsō city centre (approx. 36°01′25″N 139°59′38″E); Kinugawa left-bank breach flooded the Mitsukaido downtown
events.what_happened: A linear rainband between an extratropical ex-Typhoon 18 and Typhoon 17 produced the JMA-named Heisei 27 September Kantō–Tōhoku heavy rain (9–11 September 2015). Nikkō-Imaichi recorded 639 mm in 72 hours; Ikarie 551 mm in 24 hours. The Kinugawa left bank breached at Jōsō, flooding the Mitsukaido centre. Fire and Disaster Management Agency final (18 Oct 2017): 20 dead (Ibaraki 15, Tochigi 3, Miyagi 2), 82 injured, 81 houses destroyed, 7,090 half-destroyed. Special warnings covered Tochigi, Ibaraki and Miyagi. About 240,000 evacuation orders and 3.15 million advisories.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 240,000 under evacuation orders; ~3.15 million under advisories (13 Sep tally)
events.cause_summary: Linear rainband; Kinugawa breach at Jōsō and Tōhoku river floods.
